1037-the-life-of-john-bunyan:
Edmund Venables tells the life of John Bunyan, the Bedford tinker who became England's most-read religious writer. Bunyan fought in the civil war, preached in barns and fields when the law barred him, spent twelve years in Bedford jail, and wrote The Pilgrim's Progress there. Venables follows him from youth to fame.

The biography draws on Bunyan's own Grace Abounding and on parish records, and it sets his dreams, fears, and plain speech in their Puritan age. Readers meet a man of low birth and high fire. The book suits those who want the life behind the allegory, told with care and warmth.
106-jungle-tales-of-tarzan:
Between the great adventures, Tarzan's youth holds smaller jungle stories. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Jungle Tales of Tarzan gathers twelve episodes from his early years among the apes. First love, capture, and fights over the young ape Teeka fill the chapters.

Tarzan meets a black boy, a witch-doctor seeking vengeance, and the lion who haunts his dreams. He rescues the moon in one comic tale and battles for Teeka in another. The stories show how the ape-man learned courage, pity, and law. They enrich the main Tarzan novels with quieter days.
1079-the-life-and-opinions-of-tristram-s:
Laurence Sterne tells the life of Tristram Shandy, but Tristram cannot get born until hundreds of pages in. He is too busy with his father's theories, his uncle Toby's sieges, and endless digressions. The novel breaks every rule, with blank pages, black pages, chapters out of order, and jokes aimed straight at the reader.

Beneath the pranks lies a warm portrait of odd, kind men and their hobby-horses. Sterne mocks systems, doctors, and scholars while praising human folly. The book shocked and delighted its age, and it still reads as the first truly modern novel, playful and wise at once.
1099-the-riverman:
Stewart Edward White sends his hero up a Michigan river with a crew of lumberjacks driving logs to the mill. The riverman must fight jams, rapids, and rival crews, and his skill with a peavey and his nerve in white water decide whether the drive pays or breaks. The novel draws on White's own time in the lumber camps.

Love, rivalry, and a feud with a crooked boss give the drive its plot, while the river itself steals the show. White writes the work, the food, and the talk of the camps with firsthand zest. The book stands as the classic novel of the old lumber days.
134-maria-or-the-wrongs-of-woman:
Mary Wollstonecraft died before finishing her novel of a woman locked away by her husband. Maria, or the Wrongs of Woman, published in 1798, follows Maria Venables from a madhouse to a friendship with her guard's wife. Her story exposes marriage law as a trap.

Maria tells her life in chapters written from prison, recalling seduction, betrayal, and a stolen child. An appendix and conclusion complete the fragment as far as it goes. Wollstonecraft's preface defends printing unfinished genius. The novel stands as an early feminist classic. Feminist scholars revived the novel in the twentieth century as a founding text.
1344-the-secrets-of-the-princesse-de-cad:
After the July Revolution of 1830 wrecks many court fortunes, the Princesse de Cadignan keeps her place in Paris by wit and nerve. Balzac's short novel studies this famed beauty, whose past lovers and past scandals are the talk of every salon, and whose present life depends on managing what others believe about her.

Into her circle comes a serious writer, and the princess sets out to win his trust with a frank-seeming confession of her life. Readers must judge how much is truth and how much is art. The tale is a cool study of reputation, charm, and survival in high society.
1373-study-of-a-woman:
Honoré de Balzac tells a short, sharp tale of Mme de Listomère, a virtuous provincial lady. She receives a love letter meant for another woman and, flattered and curious, answers it, only to find herself caught in a game of manners. The story turns on a single letter and its consequences.

Balzac writes the comedy of reputation with wit and precision, and the tale's irony is complete. The study is brief and brilliant. It suits readers who like Balzac in miniature, with society's rules as the plot. Balzac's brief study shows society's rules doing the work of plot.
1377-the-talisman:
Walter Scott sets this Crusader tale in the Holy Land, where Richard the Lionheart lies ill and the Scots knight Kenneth, in disguise, serves as his guard. The tale follows Kenneth's love for the Lady Edith, Saladin's chivalry, and the plots of the Crusader princes.

Scott writes the Crusades as romance, with tournaments, disguises, and a famous meeting between king and sultan. The novel, part of his Tales of the Crusaders, shows his gift for historical color. It suits readers who like Scott's chivalry at its most stirring. Scott's Crusader romance still stirs with tournaments and chivalry.
1385-lin-mclean:
Owen Wister gathers stories of Lin McLean, a Wyoming cowboy of good heart and poor luck, who drifts through roundups, love affairs, and scrapes with the law. The tales follow Lin from a young rider to a man worn by the range, with humor and pathos.

Wister writes the cowboy West with affection and a novelist's eye, and Lin stands beside the Virginian as a classic figure. The stories are episodic and warm. The book suits readers who like Wister's West in short, vivid pieces. Wister's Lin stands beside the Virginian as a classic cowboy figure.
1470-the-fall-of-the-moghul-empire-of-hi:
H. G. Keene writes a short history of the fall of the Moghul Empire in Hindustan, from its height under the great emperors to its collapse before British power. Keene, a colonial historian, keeps the narrative compact. Keene, a British civil servant in India, wrote short histories for English readers.

The book follows weak successors, Maratha and Sikh rivals, and the East India Company's rise, ending with Delhi under British rule. It serves as a clear introduction, though modern readers will weigh its imperial viewpoint. The Moghul fall, from Aurangzeb to Bahadur Shah, took a century of slow decline.
16-peter-pan:
All children grow up, except one boy who refuses to. J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan, the 1911 novel form of Peter and Wendy, follows Wendy Darling to Neverland. Peter breaks through her nursery window in search of his shadow.

Wendy, John, and Michael fly to an island of Lost Boys, mermaids, and pirates. Captain Hook hunts Peter while Tinker Bell guards him with fierce loyalty. The book ends with Wendy grown and Peter returning for her daughter. Its mix of play and loss made Neverland endure. Stage plays, films, and sequels have kept Peter's refusal to grow up in popular culture ever since.
1714-another-study-of-woman:
At any Paris ball, Balzac observes, two parties are always going on at once: the official dance, and the private talk in corners where reputations are made and unmade. The frame lets Balzac's narrator listen to de Marsay act out a woman's airs and graces, to the offense of the women watching. Then turn to other sketches of Parisian wives, widows, and girls.

The studies are less a single plot than a set of portraits, each asking how women live inside marriages, reputations, and money. Balzac's eye for dress, speech, and social rank is sharp throughout. The volume reads as a companion to La Grande Bretèche, which follows it in the same translation.
1729-the-deserted-woman:
In the spring of 1822, doctors sent a young man to Lower Normandy to recover his health. There he met a woman living apart from the world in a quiet house. She is the Vicomtesse de Beauséant, once a leader of Paris society, now in retreat after a love affair that ended her standing.

The story follows their growing closeness and the question of whether she can return to life or must stay in exile. Balzac writes the provincial setting with care — candlelight, country doctors, and long evenings. And the tale's sadness comes from a woman who knows exactly what society took from her and refuses to beg for it back.
1738-statesman:
What does a ruler actually know that a general, a judge, or a merchant does not. That question drives this dialogue, in which the Eleatic Stranger takes up the inquiry with Socrates' friends. Socrates' friends take up the question with the Eleatic Stranger. He compares the king to a weaver, separating the threads of a city as a weaver separates wool and keeping the useful arts apart from rule itself.

The dialogue is a companion to the Sophist, and it is more a study of method than a manual for kings. Readers will find Plato sorting kinds of knowledge with care. The famous image of the statesman as weaver gives the book its lasting picture: ruling as a craft of binding a community together, not of forcing it.
177-the-american:
Christopher Newman, a rich American businessman, lounges in the Louvre in May 1868 and decides to conquer Paris. Henry James's American follows Newman through salons, business deals, and a courtship with Claire de Cintré. Her aristocratic family weighs his money against their pride.

Newman learns French manners, buys art, and befriends the painter Noémie. The Bellegardes accept him, then break the engagement for rank and revenge. James pits American energy against European tradition in a full-length novel. The American announced his international theme. Newman's blunt energy makes him James's most likable American hero abroad.
1823-the-make-believe-man:
Richard Harding Davis tells of a young man of twenty-five who has always wished for adventures and always gone halfway to meet them. He spends his vacation hunting for one in earnest. He finds it in the form of a young woman whose eyes measure him and his shoulders, as if wondering to what weight he could strip.

The story is a light romance of pretending: a holiday hero tries on courage, and the people he meets try it on him. Davis writes it with the ease of a man who knew both society and the field. The tale's charm lies in watching a make-believe man discover that real feeling was waiting behind the game.
1838-a-new-voyage-to-carolina-containing:
John Lawson, Surveyor-General of North Carolina, wrote this account of his travels in 1700, and it remains the classic early description of the Carolina country. Lawson gives the exact description and natural history of the land: its rivers, timber, grapevines, and the great tracts of good ground on the northwest side of the rivers.

A journal of a thousand miles' travel through Indian towns runs alongside the natural history. Lawson records the peoples he met, their customs, and their languages with unusual care for his time. The book is both a settler's guide and an early ethnography, and it is still read as a first-hand record of the Southeast before it changed.
1877-a-mountain-woman:
Elia Wilkinson Peattie's Mountain Woman gathers tales of the West, dedicated to her best friend and kindest critic, her husband. The foreword notes that most of the tales have been printed before, and the stories that follow move through mining camps, ranches, and lonely houses.

One tale turns on a letter from a woman who will never come back. Writing to Jim, she says it is hopeless and that she would not mind standing still to be shot if there were any good in it. Peattie writes the mountain West from a woman's angle, with attention to the lives that hardship left behind. The collection is a strong sample of regional writing of its day.
1897-the-seventh-man:
Max Brand's Seventh Man opens with a reflection on young men and silence: a man under thirty needs neighbors. To stop up the current of his life with a long silence is like damming a river, until the water sweeps the dam away or rises over it. The hero, a gunman turned outlaw, tests that truth when a sheriff's posse calls 'Halt, there. Up with your hands, or I'll drill you. '.

Brand writes the western as a story of character under pressure, with chases, posses, and a man learning what his solitude costs. The novel is fast, lean, and romantic, and it shows Brand, the most prolific of western writers, at the height of his early powers.
1935-the-tremendous-adventures-of-major-:
William Makepeace Thackeray's Tremendous Adventures of Major Gahagan presents a soldier of the Indian wars whose tales grow taller with every telling. Chapters on Allyghur and Laswaree, a peep into Spain, and the Ahmednuggar Irregulars carry Gahagan through battles he may or may not have fought.

Thackeray frames the book as a joke on military memoirs. Gahagan insists his facts are true and leaves his proofs at his publisher's office, beside an extract from the Bengal Hurkaru, for anyone to examine. The comedy lies in the major's perfect confidence, and the novel reads as a warm-up for the satire of Vanity Fair.
1970-a-poor-wise-man:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's Poor Wise Man opens on a city turning its dreariest aspect toward the railway. Blackened walls, irregular and ill-paved streets, gloomy warehouses, and a gray, smoke-laden atmosphere give it mystery. Into that city comes Willy Cameron, a young man whose coming upsets the habits of an entire family.

Lily's father, sitting upright, demands to know who is coming to-night and why he should upset the household. The novel follows Willy's efforts to do good in a world of strikes, politics, and suspicion. Rinehart writes the postwar years with sympathy for both workers and owners, and the book's title names its hero: poor, wise, and out of step with his age.
19750-the-waif-woman:
Robert Louis Stevenson set The Waif Woman in old Norse Iceland. Finnward is a prosperous man who keeps open house. His wife Aud cares more for fine clothes and admiration. She is thought careless in her conduct for a married woman. Their children are Eyolf, a likely boy, and Asdis, a young daughter. Trouble is plainly gathering around the household.

Stevenson loved saga style: flat telling, heavy fate. A waif woman, a castaway stranger, brings the outside world into Finnward's hall. Stevenson's Norse tales show his range beyond Treasure Island. He retells northern material in spare, hard prose. The story stays little known, which makes it a find. It shows a master storyteller testing an ancient form.
19833-the-heroic-enthusiasts-gli-eroici-:
Part the second of Giordano Bruno's Heroic Enthusiasts continues his dialogues on heroic love. Its pages play with the number nine, ninth letter and ninth door. Fifty portals, it says, lead to the concealed mysteries of being. Od is named the pure life-giving light, or magnetic fluid. Bruno's text, in this edition, wears layers of mystical commentary. The result is heady and strange.

Victorian occult interest revived Bruno as a martyr of free thought. Editions like this one fed that revival. The commentary's talk of Od comes from Baron von Reichenbach's magnetism theories. Bruno's own sonnets and arguments sit beneath the gloss. Readers must dig for the philosopher under the mystic. Part two rewards that digging.
1986-life-and-death-of-mr-badman:
John Bunyan published this allegory in 1680, two years after the first part of The Pilgrim's Progress, as its dark mirror image. Where Christian walks toward heaven, Mr. Badman walks the other road, from a bad youth to a bad death. Bunyan wrote from prison experience and Puritan preaching, in language meant for plain readers of his day.

Told as a talk between two friends, the book follows Badman through lying, theft, loose living, and hard dealing, showing each step as a moral choice. Bunyan writes plainly and directly, aiming to warn readers rather than to entertain them with plot. The dialogue form lets a godly friend answer doubts, so the warning lands as talk, not as a sermon alone.
19863-the-old-masters-and-their-pictures:
Sarah Tytler wrote The Old Masters and Their Pictures for the use of schools. Her survey gives many records of Dutch painters in particular. Dutch art, she notes, proved specially popular in England. Some Dutch masters are better represented in England than at home. Flemish art also gets full treatment here. J. A. Crowe revised the art history for this edition.

School art history began with books like this one. Pupils learned painters' lives beside their famous pictures. The canon here is the Victorian canon: Raphael to Rembrandt. Tytler writes clearly for young students without flattening the art. Her selections shaped what schoolchildren thought great painting was. The book documents that teaching tradition well.
19988-little-maid-marian:
Amy E. Blanchard wrote Little Maid Marian in 1908, a story for girls. Marian talks often with her grandmother in its pages. Faith, both feel, is difficult to exercise completely. Marian has made numberless mighty efforts to believe as she should. Yet things did not come out as her efforts promised. The gap between effort and outcome troubles her young conscience. Blanchard writes that trouble gently.

Blanchard's girls' books often carry quiet religious feeling. Marian's doubts are treated as growth, not failure. Grandmother and granddaughter anchor the story's warmth. The setting is a modest, churchgoing American household. Young readers got companionship for their own questions. The book is a soft-spoken period piece for girls.
20132-the-wizard-of-the-sea-or-a-trip-un:
Roy Rockwood wrote The Wizard of the Sea, a trip under the ocean for boys. Young Mont hears he may join a nautical school with a sly grin. A town man calls him the worst boy in town for mischief. Mont takes the charge with more pride than shame, it seems.

Rockwood wrote many sea and adventure tales under that shared name. A school at sea leads, here, to a craft that dives below waves. Undersea travel was still a marvel when the book came out. Readers get boyish fun mixed with wonder at a new kind of ship.
20205-the-maya-chronicles-brinton-s-libr:
The Maya Chronicles gathers native Maya texts in Daniel Brinton's library series. Brinton sought true specimens of native literature for American scholars. Such works are rare and hard to reach, he warns readers. They sit in manuscript with a few collectors, or in costly society volumes.

This volume brings Maya chronicles from Yucatan into print for study. They record kings, wars, famines, and the coming of the Spanish. Brinton's series aimed to save aboriginal American literature from loss. Readers get primary Maya history in translation, with a scholar's care around it.
20279-the-veterinarian:
The Veterinarian is a reference book for those who treat sick and hurt animals. One entry defines creosote, a colorless to yellowish oily liquid. It holds phenols and comes from the destructive distillation of wood tar. Beech wood tar, in particular, yields much of the supply described.

Creosote once served as a medicine for chronic bronchitis in practice. Entries like this one give drugs, doses, and uses in plain order. Farmers and vets kept such books close in stable and surgery. Readers get a practical window on animal medicine of an earlier age.
20439-susan-b-anthony-rebel-crusader-hum:
Alma Lutz wrote this life of Susan B. Anthony, published by Beacon Press in 1959. Its subtitle calls Anthony a rebel, a crusader, and a humanitarian. Lutz had spent years gathering letters and records of the women's rights movement.

Anthony spent her long life fighting for women's right to vote. She spoke, organized, and faced arrest for casting a ballot in 1872. The biography follows her from her Quaker childhood to national fame. It remains a standard life of the leader who did more than any other to win American women the vote.
20555-what-is-and-what-might-be-a-study-:
What Is and What Might Be studies education in general and elementary education in particular. Its author was a school inspector who came to doubt the cramming system of his day. The book argues that schools crush the very powers they claim to train.

Our faculties grow by use, the book holds. Once they reach their fullest growth, we keep them at that level by exercising them. Mental and spiritual powers have no fixed limit, so the need for exercise is more urgent still. To neglect them is to stunt them. The study became a noted plea for freer, fuller schooling.
2070-to-the-last-man:
Zane Grey turns at last to the feud story he had long avoided, setting a tale of pioneer families whose old quarrel shapes a whole corner of the West. Love and loyalty pull against blood and revenge across the range. Grey had long avoided feud stories, fearing they would repeat the same bloodshed without purpose.

Grey argues in his foreword that the violence of the frontier cannot be left out of its history, and the novel follows that belief. The result is a full-blooded western, with gunfights, chases, and a stubborn fight for home. His foreword argues that pioneer history must face violence honestly, or it will tell a false tale.
20754-the-blunders-of-a-bashful-man:
Shyness is the curse of the man who tells The Blunders of a Bashful Man. He hopes no other soul must bear the mishaps his complaint has cost him. Smallpox and scarlet fever, he notes, strike once, but bashfulness strikes for life.

Comic scenes pile up as the poor man trips through calls, meals, and courtship. Each fresh crowd brings a fresh blunder to dread. The humor is gentle, built on pain most readers know at least a little. This slight, funny book shows how Victorian humor could turn a common flaw into a whole tale of woe.
21063-the-missing-merchantman:
Harry Collingwood worked as a ship designer and shipwright, and that trade knowledge runs through this sea novel. The crew of a merchant vessel decide that captains and officers are paid far too much. Convinced they have been robbed of fair wages for years, the deckhands seize the ship.

In taking the vessel the crew make themselves little better than pirates. The officers and passengers, though, are resourceful people who work their way out of the trap. At last they bring their ship home, where she has long been posted as missing. The tale mixes mutiny, seamanship, and a sharp argument about pay and skill.
21065-the-log-of-a-privateersman:
Early in the nineteenth century, with Britain at war against France, privateers worked as licensed sea raiders against enemy shipping. Harry Collingwood's novel opens with a bold French stroke in October 1804. French sailors slip into Weymouth harbour at night and carry off the trader Weymouth, loaded with rum, sugar, and tobacco.

From that capture the hero's career as a privateersman grows. He proves very good at preying on enemy ships and taking prizes. His success at last brings him an offer of a permanent commission in the Royal Navy. The log form keeps the action close to decks, watches, and pay-offs.
21331-the-adventures-of-hajji-baba-of-is:
James Morier's comic novel follows Hajji Baba, a Persian barber's son, through every trade and scrape his country offers. Chapter headings tell the pattern. He is captured by Turcomans, rescues his master's money and keeps it, and becomes a robber in self-defence. Later he works as a water carrier and an itinerant seller of smoke.

Morier had lived in Persia as a British diplomat, and the tale pokes fun at Persian manners and English ones alike. The poet Asker's history and the dervish Sefer's story fill side chapters. George Curzon introduced this 1895 edition. Hajji Baba remains the classic English comic novel of Persia, sharp, episodic, and often unfair in the way of good satire.
21415-the-young-visiters-or-mr-salteena-:
Daisy Ashford wrote The Young Visiters as a child, and it reached print in 1919 with a preface by J. M. Barrie. Mr Salteena, a man of forty-two, loves having guests to stay. His young guest Ethel Monticue, aged seventeen, joins him at the start.

Ashford keeps her child spelling and her grave, funny view of grown-up life. Visits, a trip to the Crystal Palace, grand calls, and a proposal fill the short tale. A wedding brings the plot to its close. The book became a famed curio, loved for the clear young voice that never slips.
21532-the-university-of-michigan:
Wilfred Shaw, the university's alumni chief, wrote The University of Michigan in 1920. Shaw edited the Michigan Alumnus and etched four of the book's pictures himself. Photographs crowd the rest of the volume, from University Hall onward.

Chapters run from the founding and early days to Presidents Angell and Hutchins. Schools of law, medicine, and letters get their own accounts. Student life, fraternities, athletics, and town and campus fill later pages. A chapter on the university in war, and one on its alumni, close the tale. The odd first name of the school, the Catholepistemiad, gets its due at the start.
21576-the-privateersman:
A cruise off Hispaniola in the privateer Revenge opens Captain Marryat's The Privateersman, published in 1846. The narrator hopes his tale, if ever made public, may bring profit to its readers. Privateering, as Marryat notes, is piracy made lawful by a government's licence.

The Revenge takes a French ship early, then holds her course for more prizes. Marryat's twenty-third book draws on the last great age of the privateer. Captures, fights, and the division of prize money fill the log-like tale. No writer knew this world better from the inside than a post-captain turned novelist.
21582-the-mightiest-man:
Patrick Fahy's tale The Mightiest Man, from Worlds of If in November 1961, opens after aliens have left Earth. A few shining metal huts in the Siberian tundra alone prove they came. Earth stood helpless while vast minds slithered over her fields and cities.

They caught up with the mightiest man in Belgrade, the blurb declares, and he feared nothing. A neural plague has spread to Zagreb, Albania, and Italy in the tale's grim reach. Twenty million lunatics fill the Balkans, and the Danube stands dammed into a lake. Fahy asks who betrayed mankind, and at what price, in a stark cold-war nightmare.
21700-don-juan:
Lord Byron turns the Don Juan legend inside out in Don Juan, his great comic epic in verse. The poem runs to seventeen cantos in the copy given here, with a sharp dedication. Juan is no bold seducer here, but a young man whom women pursue.

Byron opens fire on Southey, the poet laureate, and the Lake poets at Keswick. Their narrow circle, he charges, thinks poetry's wreaths belong to them alone. Shipwreck, a slave market, a sultan's court, and the siege of Ismail fill the cantos. Love affairs, war, and English society all take Byron's wit in ottava rima, the poem's dancing, rhyming measure.
21719-blue-lights-hot-work-in-the-soudan:
Miles Milton stands at a turning point in his life as this Ballantyne novel opens. Ballantyne compares him to water at a ridge, where one drop flows to the Atlantic and the next to Hudson's Bay. Miles leans the wrong way, and the book follows where that false step leads. His strong will and hot temper keep causing trouble at home.

The trail leads at last to the Soudan, where British troops fought in desert heat. Ballantyne mixes a young man's moral fall and recovery with scenes of real campaigning. The title's blue lights point to the Christian soldiers whose faith lights the darker parts of the tale.
21743-jeff-benson-or-the-young-coastguar:
Jeff Benson loses his father, a poor schoolmaster in the coastal town of Cranby, as this Ballantyne tale opens. Jeff is fifteen, tall, hearty, and sure he can do anything he sets his mind to. Fun has ruled his life so far, in school and on the playground. His uncle Jacob, a hard and grasping lawyer, cares little for the boy.

Work by the sea gives Jeff his chance, and the coastguard gives him his calling. Ballantyne follows the lad from schoolboy pranks to rescues on a dangerous coast. Smugglers, storms, and duty test the young coastguardsman in turn. It is a steady tale of a boy growing straight under hard knocks and salt air.
2184-unbeaten-tracks-in-japan:
Isabella L. Bird traveled where few Western visitors had gone, into the interior of Japan and among the Ainu people of Yezo. Unbeaten Tracks in Japan records that journey in letters full of hard roads, remote villages, shrines at Nikko, and the daily life of people far from the treaty ports. Bird writes as a keen, practical observer with little patience for easy praise.

Her account covers food, housing, customs, and the strain of travel itself, often on foot or horseback through rough country. The book still reads as a vivid firsthand record of a Japan that was changing fast. Anyone curious about travel before tourism will find it frank, detailed, and full of surprises.
2196-an-iceland-fisherman:
Pierre Loti's Iceland Fisherman follows Breton sailors who leave home each year to fish the cold waters off Iceland. At the center stands Yann, a strong, silent fisherman, and Gaud, the woman who waits and loves him through long absences. The sea gives and takes with indifference, and the village measures life by returns and losses.

Loti writes the Breton coast and the northern ocean with a painter's eye for light, weather, and ritual. The novel is quiet and sad, more elegy than adventure, and its power grows from small scenes of work, prayer, and parting. It remains a beloved portrait of a fishing world now gone.
21962-harvard-classics-volume-28-essays-:
Great essays in English fill this twenty-eighth volume of the Harvard Classics, Dr. Charles W. Eliot's famous five-foot shelf of books, issued in 1910. The frontispiece shows Thomas Huxley, whose Science and Culture stands inside. Swift and Thackeray open the prose line. Newman's lectures on the idea of a university follow, with his account of university life at Athens.

Matthew Arnold's Study of Poetry and Ruskin's Sesame and Lilies carry the Victorian center. Milton, Bagehot, Freeman on race and language, Pepys on truth of intercourse, and Stevenson close the range. Introductions and notes frame each author. The volume is a portable university of English prose, chosen to prove that a busy reader could self-educate from a single shelf.
21997-christie-s-old-organ:
An old barrel-organ man and a lost boy meet in O. F. Walton's Christie's Old Organ, also called Home, Sweet Home. Old Treffy sits alone in his attic in a dreary lodging house, turning his organ with a trembling hand. The tune it plays, Home Sweet Home, mocks every bare bench below. Yet the flowers of love still live in his withered heart, and he gives them all to his antiquated organ.

Walton wrote tales for Sunday school readers, and this is among her best known. Christie, the boy of the story, learns what home means from the old man who has none. The clergyman pictured with Christie carries the tale's gentle preaching. Sentimental in the Victorian way, the little book moved generations of young readers.
22072-folk-lore-and-legends-north-americ:
Folk-Lore and Legends: North American Indian gathers tales told by Native peoples across the continent. The volume belongs to a popular series that sorted old stories by the peoples who told them. One tale concerns a village belle admired by every hunter and warrior. Her suitor, the Beau-Man, trusts his secrets to a friend, and trouble follows.

Other stories tell of spirits, animals, courtship, and revenge in the woods and villages. The tellers' names and tribes stand behind many of the pieces. Such collections preserved tales that might otherwise have stayed only in oral tradition. They also show how nineteenth-century readers liked their folklore: romantic, brief, and framed as a window on a vanishing world.
22073-the-repairman:
Harry Harrison wrote The Repairman, a short science fiction tale from the early days of his career. Harrison later became famous for the Stainless Steel Rat books and Make Room! Make Room! His repairman narrator has fixed hyperspace beacons across the whole Galaxy. He boasts that he has worked on every type or model ever made.

Then a call names a kind of beacon he has never heard of. The job takes him somewhere stranger than his long experience prepared him for. Harrison builds the joke and the puzzle out of one man's professional pride. The story is quick, dry, and typical of the clever short fiction that filled the science fiction magazines of the 1950s.
22140-the-wrong-woman:
Charles D. Stewart published The Wrong Woman in 1912, a novel of the American West. The frontispiece shows a woman who must continue her journey afoot. Stewart opens on ranch matters: a horse that swells itself out when saddled, then lets the girths hang loose. Such stable talk sets the scene among people who live by horses.

A case of mistaken identity drives the plot, as the title promises. The wrong woman arrives where another was expected, and ranch life must sort out the error. Stewart writes comedy and courtship in a Western setting. His books were known for shrewd humour about human nature, and this one keeps that reputation.
22182-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-v:
Volume V of The Best of the World's Classics turns to Great Britain and presents its prose masters. The set was a standard home library of its day, ten volumes strong. Each author arrives with a short life. Boswell's sketch, for example, runs from his birth in 1740 to his Life of Johnson in 1791 in a few brisk lines.

Essays, speeches, and passages from the great prose writers fill the volume. The editors chose what a general reader was expected to know. Such collections built the canon for homes without a scholar's library. This volume shows Edwardian taste in British prose: Johnson's circle, the essayists, and the historians, all in one thick book.
22331-the-chocolate-soldier-or-heroism-t:
C. T. Studd wrote The Chocolate Soldier, a sharp call for braver Christians. Its full title calls heroism the lost chord of Christianity. Studd mocks soft believers with his chocolate soldier figure.

The Chocolate Christian, he writes, shakes at the very thought of war. The call to battle always finds him with the palsy. Such a man says he cannot move, only sing. Studd quotes the man's favorite lines without mercy. The pamphlet argues that faith should produce courage and sacrifice. It still reads as a brisk, stinging challenge. Studd wanted soldiers for Christ, not sweets that melt when heat comes.
22371-the-chief-end-of-man:
The Chief End of Man, dated 1897, takes up life's largest question directly. Its title echoes the old catechism answer about man's purpose. The passage preserved shows a man in deep perplexity, near dismay.

At such a time, the writer counsels looking backward attentively. A guided life can review the steps by which it advanced. Past crises, once recalled, show how they were met. Light may then break on the path ahead. Or the reader may simply take fresh heart and hope. The book offers that counsel at length. It treats purpose as something proved by a whole life's road.
22532-mary-louise-and-josie-o-gorman:
Edith Van Dyne wrote Mary Louise and Josie O'Gorman, published in 1922. Van Dyne was a pen name used for popular girls' series books. Hard news opens this volume for Mary Louise and her friends.

Hope of Danny Dexter's survival was finally abandoned by everyone. His sorrowing little wife and many friends gave up that hope. Colonel Hathaway's comfortable fortune had also mysteriously disappeared by then. Mary Louise thus faced a future of poverty without warning. With native pluck, she rose to the sad occasion bravely. In spite of her sad heart, she showed cheerful spirit. Josie O'Gorman, girl detective, helps drive the mystery plot. Readers get series fiction with courage under loss.
22664-the-severed-hand-from-german-tales:
Wilhelm Hauff wrote The Severed Hand, a dark tale from his fairy-tale almanacs, here taken from German Tales as published for American readers. The catalog record gives no year. Hauff, who died young, filled his brief career with stories of the East, of students, and of quiet horror.

The sample opens in farewell: a father embraces his son and gives him clothes for the journey, plus the weapons his grandfather hung on the father when he went abroad. Use them only when attacked, the father counsels, but then defend yourself bravely. Such blessings arm the hero for a tale of murder, disguise, and a hand that will not rest. Hauff mixes the storyteller's ease with real dread, and this is among his most gripping tales.
22840-honor-o-callaghan:
Schoolgirl rank is serious business in Honor O'Callaghan, a story by Mary Russell Mitford. The excerpt looks inside a fashionable house of education, where a newcomer's place turns on odd details. One mother calls on her daughter attended by only one footman, and the slight is noted. A father's town address and a mother's milliner also weigh in the scale.

Mitford watches this small world with amused precision. Honor, the Irish girl of the title, must make her way among classmates quick to judge surfaces. The story turns school etiquette into a study of class itself. Beneath the manners sits a real question about worth. The tale answers it the Mitford way, through character shown in daily behavior.
22844-miss-philly-firkin-the-china-woman:
A crowded London street opens Miss Philly Firkin, the China Woman, by Mary Russell Mitford. Houses in the best streets let for double their value, goods sell at nearly the same rate, and horse traffic and foot traffic jostle on the pavement. Coaches and phaetons run against each other in the road.

Philly Firkin keeps her china shop inside that crush of commerce. Mitford follows the small tradeswoman through the risks and pleasures of city shopkeeping, where a fragile stock meets a rough crowd. The portrait mixes sympathy with sharp observation of London manners. Village readers of Mitford's sketches got a capital-city counterpart here. Philly's counter becomes a fine post from which to watch the whole town go by.
23152-the-mcbrides-a-romance-of-arran:
John Sillars lays out his chapters in The McBrides, a romance of Arran. Chapter titles promise the Urie's foot as a resting place, a halflin's message, and another ride to McAllan's locker. A doorstep wedding, a kiss from Margaret McBride, Betty's growing pains, and a raking black schooner fill out the list.

Arran, the Firth of Clyde island called Scotland in miniature, frames the McBrides' fortunes. Smuggling schooners, weddings, and messages cross the island's hills in Sillars's Highland manner. The chapter heads alone tell a family saga's rhythm, rest, errands, weddings, and sails on the horizon. Readers who enjoy Scottish regional romance, dialect and all, will find a whole island community between these covers, arranged around one family's name.
23191-count-ulrich-of-lindburg-a-tale-of:
Count Ulrich of Lindburg is a tale of the Reformation in Germany. Its scene is the Castle of Lindburg, on the banks of the river Saal at Merseburg in Saxony. The land then answered to the aged Elector Frederick, praised in the tale as an excellent ruler.

The castle is drawn as a feudal pile from the Middle Ages, proof against the siege tools of older war. Yet such strongholds were bound to crumble before cannon fire. The tale links that fall to a wider change: the old order giving way before the light of Gospel truth.
23194-the-common-man: Guy McCord's The Common Man opens on a small, telling gesture. A man named Braun lets a sentence trail off, then stuffs a paper into a coat pocket that has clearly served as a waste bin for years. He leads the way up a cement walk, with his younger companions close behind him.
23245-ancient-ballads-and-legends-of-hin:
Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan gathers poems retelling old Indian stories. Its introduction tells a sad, striking story about the poet herself. Within four years of her death, it says, her genius had been revealed to the world in many forms and recognised across France and England.

At her death she had published only one book. That book had found only two reviewers in Europe. The gap between those two facts gives the volume its charge. Readers get ballads and legends from a young Indian poet whose name, the editor insists, no well-read person should fail to know.
23269-the-heir-of-kilfinnan-a-tale-of-th:
The Heir of Kilfinnan is a tale of the shore and ocean, told here through a later summary of its plot. After several exciting events, an earl dies. To everyone's surprise, the young hero Denham is revealed as Dermot, a young man met much earlier in the tale.

A lawyer then states that Dermot's father stood in line to the earldom. That makes Dermot the new earl, and the room erupts in cheers. One catch remains: who wants a ruined castle and a bankrupt estate? Readers get inheritance, hidden identity, and sea adventure in a cheerfully spoiled package.
23270-on-the-indian-trail-stories-of-mis:
On the Indian Trail gathers stories of missionary work among Cree and other Indigenous peoples. Its author explains the book's shape at the start. Unlike some of his other books, it is not one continuous narrative of missionary life, but a set of distinct chapters.

Some chapters were written just for this volume. Others had already seen print, in whole or in part, and are gathered here at the request of friends, with the publishers' courtesy. Readers get first-hand period accounts of travel, teaching, and mission stations, told as separate episodes rather than one long story.
2351-john-halifax-gentleman:
Dinah Maria Mulock Craik's John Halifax, Gentleman follows a penniless orphan who rises by honesty and hard work to become a respected manufacturer and family man. The novel's narrator, a disabled friend, watches Halifax's long life unfold: his labors, his marriage, his children, and his quiet heroism in business and in private sorrow. Craik makes goodness itself the plot.

Victorian readers loved the book for its moral earnestness, and it stayed popular for generations. Its view of industry is humane and hopeful. Readers of classic domestic fiction will find a long, satisfying chronicle.
2354-note-on-the-resemblances-and-differ:
Thomas Henry Huxley, Darwin's great defender, compares the brains of humans and apes in this famous scientific note. The essay, printed with Darwin's Descent of Man, argues from anatomy that the differences between human and ape brains are smaller than those between ape species themselves. Huxley writes with clarity and combativeness.

The note became a landmark in the evolution debate, giving Darwin's case its anatomical backbone. Its Victorian science has since been refined, but its logic still impresses. Readers of science history will find a concise classic. Huxley earned the nickname of Darwin's bulldog for defenses like this one.
2520-the-man:
Bram Stoker, best known for Dracula, published this novel in 1897, and it opens in a quiet English churchyard where two children argue about angels and God. From that small scene grows the life story of Stephen Norman, a headstrong young woman raised with unusual freedom by her guardian.

Stephen loves, chooses, and suffers through the rules her world sets for women, while Leonard Everard and her circle test her resolve. Stoker writes with warmth about loyalty, pride, and forgiveness, and the book ends as a plea for judging people by their hearts rather than by custom. It is a gentler, more domestic Stoker than horror readers may expect.
2605-noto-an-unexplored-corner-of-japan:
Percival Lowell wrote this travel book about Noto, a remote corner of Japan he calls unexplored. He addressed it to his friend Basil Hall Chamberlain, the confidant of his hopes for the trip. Lowell's chapters run from first arrivals through the Usui Pass and the temple town of Zenkoji.

He notes new cornice roads, local shrines, and villages few foreign travelers had reached, with the curiosity of a man who loved Japan deeply. The book mixes road narrative with notes on custom and landscape. It reads as a gentle expedition into a Japan already changing, written before the age of mass travel.
2733-romano-lavo-lil-word-book-of-the-ro:
This word book of the Romany, or English Gypsy, language opens with a challenge. It asks the reader, in Romany and in English, whether he can speak the tongue, play the fiddle, eat prison loaf, and cut and whittle. The 1905 John Murray edition pairs vocabulary with specimens of Gypsy poetry.

An account of Gypsy life and speech accompanies the lists, giving the words a human setting. The book serves students of language, folklore, and the traveling people of Britain. It remains a pioneering record of a language once passed only by mouth, now fixed in print.
2774-the-patrician:
John Galsworthy wrote this novel in two parts, following an English patrician through love, politics, and family duty. The hero, born to rank and wealth, must choose between a brilliant match and a woman the world calls unsuitable.

Galsworthy writes with restraint about the codes that bind the upper class, and the costs of breaking them. The novel moves from country houses to London drawing rooms, with his usual moral clarity. It stands as a study of privilege, and of a man learning its price. Galsworthy's patrician learns that rank cannot buy love.
2924-the-perpetuation-of-living-beings-h:
Thomas Henry Huxley gave this lecture on the perpetuation of living beings, hereditary transmission, and variation as part of his working-men series on Darwin. He frames two questions, whether we know anything of the origin of living beings, and whether, granting an origin, we know anything about how forms persist and change. His answer to the first is altogether negative, and the lecture builds from there.

Huxley illustrates spontaneous variation with a man born with an unusual number of fingers and toes on each hand and foot, a case carefully observed at the time. Nobody knows why the variation appeared, he notes, which is why it earns the name spontaneous. The lecture shows Darwin's chief defender explaining heredity to a popular audience with examples rather than jargon.
2933-on-some-fossil-remains-of-man:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote On Some Fossil Remains of Man to ask whether ancient human bones close the gap between humans and apes. He argues that the Anthropini, or man family, form a well-defined group of primates, with no transitional form linking them to the Catarhini in the existing world. Fossil evidence, he suggests, might diminish or even erase those intervals.

Huxley tests that hope against bones found in a thin mud deposit without stalagmite cover, which still kept much of their organic substance. Such preservation argues against great geological age, he warns, and warns against calling a skull the most savage primitive type when living peoples show similar forms. The essay remains a model of cautious reasoning about human origins.
2992-the-middle-class-gentleman:
Moliere wrote Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme, here as The Middle Class Gentleman, translated by Philip Dwight Jones. The comedy-ballet was presented at Chambord for the king in October 1670 and in Paris at the Palais-Royal Theatre on November 23, 1670. Monsieur Jourdain, a bourgeois, hires masters of music, dancing, fencing, and philosophy to remake himself as a gentleman.

Madame Jourdain, their daughter Lucile, her suitor Cleonte, and the scheming Dorante and Dorimene fill the cast. The famous lesson has Jourdain discover, to his delight, what prose is, as his wife calls his conduct scarcely sensible. The play remains the classic comedy of social climbing, with music, dance, and philosophy all pressed into one man's vanity.
315-rhymes-of-a-red-cross-man:
Robert W. Service, poet of the Yukon, turned to the trenches of France in this wartime book. Rhymes of a Red Cross Man, from a New York edition of 1916, is dedicated to his brother Albert, killed in action that August. The foreword and contents promise soldiers' verse.

Poems like The Call, The Volunteer, and The Man from Athabaska mix humor with mud and grief. The Haggis of Private McPhee, Fleurette, and Bill's Grave follow. Service wrote as a stretcher bearer, close to the wounded. The book brought the war home in plain rhyme.
3271-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Charles Farrar Browne, writing as Artemus Ward, opens his complete works with essays, sketches, and letters. Preliminary notes by John Camden Hotten, a biographical sketch by Melville D Landon, and an introduction by T W Robertson frame the set. A prefatory note by Edward P Hingston joins them. Then Ward himself takes over.

Business letters, a piece on forts, and the Shakers lead the contents, with a high-handed outrage at Utica and a celebration at Baldinsville. Among the spirits, on the wing, and the octoroon follow, with experience as an editor and a visit to Brigham Young. Wax figures versus Shakespeare shows Ward's comic method: misspelled wisdom aimed straight at American humbug.
3276-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Part six of Artemus Ward's complete works preserves his Panorama, the lecture that crowned his fame. A prefatory note by Melville D Landon introduces the Egyptian Hall lecture, with a Times notice and the programme of that lecture. An announcement and programme for the Dodworth Hall lecture join them. The panorama itself was illustrated as delivered at Egyptian Hall in London.

Landon notes that Ward's fame peaked in those last lectures at Egyptian Hall, Piccadilly. The final one broke off abruptly on the evening of 23 January 1867, and that night the humorist bade farewell to the public and retired to die. This part is thus both a comic text and a farewell: Ward's last stage, kept in print.
3293-chronicle-of-the-conquest-of-granad:
Washington Irving tells the fall of Granada from the supposed papers of Fray Antonio Agapida, in this author's revised edition. The kingdom of Granada and its tribute to the Castilian crown open the chronicle. An embassy of Don Juan de Vera demands arrears of tribute from the Moorish monarch, and the tale of war begins.

Domestic feuds in the Alhambra follow, with rival sultanas and predictions about Boabdil, heir to the throne. Ferdinand's campaigns close the Moorish kingdom in the end. Irving writes history as romance, with Agapida as his grave, credulous guide. Readers get the last crusade of Spain as a story: sieges, chivalry, and a kingdom falling in slow, splendid ruin.
3301-the-naturewoman:
Upton Sinclair pits a nature cult against Boston society in this play. Oceana, the naturewoman, leads the cast, against Mrs Sophronia Masterson of Beacon Street and her husband Quincy, a doctor. Freddy, their son, and Ethel, their younger daughter, join Letitia, the elder daughter, and her husband Henry Selden. Remson, a butler, keeps order.

Act one sits in the Masterson drawing room on a winter afternoon, and act two returns the next afternoon to the same room. Nature worship meets drawing-room manners there, and neither side yields gracefully. Sinclair uses the clash to mock both camps: the cult's earnestness and society's polish. The play is short, witty, and very much of its reforming age.
3302-the-second-story-man:
Upton Sinclair builds this one-act play around a midnight burglary. Jim Faraday, the second-story man, meets Harvey Austin, a lawyer, and Helen Austin, his wife, in the library of the Austin home at two in the morning. A lamp burns on a center table, the front door shows through the hall entrance, and a cabinet of curios stands in the corner.

Faraday came through a window, but the play turns on talk rather than theft. Lawyer, wife, and burglar argue morals, law, and need across the lamplit room. Sinclair, best known for The Jungle, uses the stage to put class face to face. The piece is short, tense, and pointed: a crime play that asks who the real criminal is.
3351-letters-to-his-son-1746-47-on-the-f:
The Earl of Chesterfield begins his famous correspondence in this volume covering 1746 and 1747. An editor's note opens the book, explaining old style and new style dates. On consultation with specialists, the editor learned that the abbreviations mark the Julian calendar used in England against the Gregorian calendar standard in Europe. In the mid eighteenth century the gap amounted to eleven days.

That note matters, because Chesterfield dated letters across the two systems as his son traveled. The letters themselves open the education: study, manners, and the world, taught by a father who writes as a statesman and a wit. Readers starting the correspondence here get its foundation, with the calendar key supplied before the first lesson.
3357-letters-to-his-son-1753-54-on-the-f:
New Year's Day 1753 finds Chesterfield waiting for a letter, and content to wait, while his son works in Paris. Letter one hundred and eighty-five, dated New Year's Day 1753, opens on a fortnight's silence. It is above a fortnight since the earl received a letter, he writes, but he hopes the boy is well. The boy is likely engrossed by Lord Albemarle's bureau in the mornings, and by business of a genteeler nature in the evenings.

Chesterfield willingly gives up his own claim on the boy's time to that double business: diplomacy by day and society by night. The volume follows a young diplomat finding his footing in Paris. Readers get the earl as a patient correspondent, content to wait for letters and to teach through the waiting itself.
3358-letters-to-his-son-1756-58-on-the-f:
The Seven Years' War reaches the Chesterfield letters in 1756, and the old statesman reads its dispatches like lessons for his son. Letter two hundred and three, dated 15 November 1756, answers a packet received the day before. With it came the Prussian papers, read with great attention. If courts could blush, Chesterfield writes, those of Vienna and Dresden ought to, for their falsehoods stand publicly and undeniably exposed.

The Seven Years' War frames the letters that follow, as father and son track alliances, battles, and diplomacy. Chesterfield, an old statesman, teaches statecraft from the news itself. Readers get the war as a family correspondence saw it: dispatches judged, courts mocked, and a young diplomat learning to read Europe's moves as they happened.
3359-letters-to-his-son-1759-65-on-the-f:
Italian greetings for the New Year open the 1759 letters, and behind the joke stands a father's worry about his son's health. Letter two hundred and thirty-seven, dated New Year's Day 1759, opens with the season's greeting in Italian: many and happy returns. The earl has done with that subject, he jokes, one truth being fair on the most lying day of the year. Before him lies the boy's last letter, of 21 December.

That letter proves a bill of health, which pleases the father, though he warns against presuming on it. Obey and honor your physician, he advises, that your days may be long in the land. The volume follows the correspondence through war, travel, and middle age, with a father's care turning increasingly to health and to time itself.
3360-letters-to-his-son-1766-71-on-the-f:
The Earl of Chesterfield writes to his son from London in this final span of letters, 1766 to 1771. Letter two hundred and eighty-four, dated 11 February 1766, apologizes for delay with weather. The earl received one letter two days earlier and another only ten days earlier, though both were older. Bad weather and bad roads explain the gap, he writes, and he hardly remembers so severe a winter.

The volume's letters grow shorter and more personal as the earl ages. Advice gives way to news, health, and affection, with the tutor's voice softening into a father's. Readers closing the long correspondence here will find its end fitting: a great letter writer, still writing, against winter, distance, and failing strength.
3394-the-white-mr-longfellow-from-litera:
William Dean Howells remembers the white Mr Longfellow in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. The Howellses planned only a short Boston stay until a house in Old Cambridge turned up. That proved less straightforward than it sounds, since the old town had not yet sped its academic tempo up to modern speed.

Howells writes that in spring 1866 no stir of expansion showed itself anywhere yet, and the huge material growth of later years lay still ahead. Into that quiet Cambridge steps Longfellow, white-haired and kind, the poet as neighbor. A famous man at home, before fame hardened into monument: Longfellow white-haired, kind, and neighborly.
3466-the-foreigner-a-tale-of-saskatchewa:
Ralph Connor sets this novel on the Saskatchewan prairie, where a new nation is being made from many peoples. Saxon and Slav, Teuton, Celt, and Gaul meet on snow swept winter plains and flower decked summer fields, drawn by railways to Winnipeg, Empress of the Prairies. The book's foreigner is an immigrant who must find a place among neighbors of other tongues and faiths.

Connor, a Canadian minister and novelist, argues that justice and charity must bind these peoples together, or old lines of race will break the new country. The story mixes frontier hardship, romance, and moral appeal. It gives a vivid view of western Canada at settlement time, when farms, schools, and churches rose beside the railway lines.
3477-the-verse-book-of-a-homely-woman:
Fay Inchfawn, the pen name of Elizabeth Rebecca Ward, writes poems about the daily life of a housewife in this verse book. Contents move from The Housewife and The Little House to A Woman in Hospital, Homesick on Washing Day, When Baby Strayed, and To an Old Teapot. A second part steps outdoors for Early Spring and other country pieces.

The poems find feeling in small things: a carpet that rucks, a tap across the yard, a musty smell in rainy weather, and work made hard by a cramped house. Inchfawn writes in plain, rhymed verse that speaks for women whose labor rarely reached print. The book suits readers who like domestic poetry with humor, tenderness, and a clear eye.
3529-letters-written-during-a-short-resi:
Mary Wollstonecraft writes letters from a trip across Sweden, Norway, and Denmark in the 1790s, after the fame of her Vindication of the Rights of Woman. The letters mix travel notes with reflections on trade, law, manners, and the lives of women. An introduction sketches her early life, including her father, a quick tempered man, and her mother, a rigorous Irishwoman.

Wollstonecraft observes harbors, farms, and towns with a reformer's eye, asking how laws and customs shape ordinary people. She also writes about friendship, including Frances Blood, a gifted young artist who supported her family by drawing. The book suits readers who want early feminist travel writing and a vivid view of Scandinavia before modern industry.
3548-the-pharisee-and-the-publican:
John Bunyan expounds the parable of the Pharisee and the Publican in this Puritan sermon treatise. The text opens with two men who went up to the temple to pray. A Pharisee thanks God he is not like other men, extortioners, unjust persons, or adulterers. Beside him stands a publican who will not lift his eyes to heaven.

Bunyan contrasts proud, self satisfied religion with humble repentance. He warns readers against trusting in fasting, tithing, and outward duties while despising others. The treatise also comforts those who feel their sins deeply, since the publican went home justified. It suits readers interested in Bunyan beyond Pilgrim's Progress, in his plain, searching preaching voice.
3618-arms-and-the-man:
George Bernard Shaw writes a comedy about war and romance set during the Serbo-Bulgarian War. Raina Petkoff, a young Bulgarian woman, shelters a fleeing Swiss mercenary, Captain Bluntschli, who carries chocolate rather than cartridges in his bag. Bluntschli, a professional soldier, mocks the romantic view of battle that Raina learned from operas and novels.

The play follows Raina's engagement to the dashing Sergius, her growing regard for Bluntschli, and the clash between heroic talk and real soldiering. Shaw turns a war comedy into an argument about courage, love, and common sense. The play suits readers who enjoy Shaw at his lightest, with wit that still cuts through fine phrases.
3627-life-of-bunyan:
James Hamilton writes a life of John Bunyan for the 1845 edition of the Works of the Puritan Divines. Hamilton notes the graceful sketches by Southey and Montgomery and the elaborate biography by Philip, whose researches left few gaps, as well as Bunyan's own graphic narrative of his life. His task, he says, is to tell the story once more for readers of Bunyan's collected works.

The life follows Bunyan from a wild youth, when his energy ran to idle play and mischief, through conversion, preaching, prison, and the writing of Pilgrim's Progress. Hamilton writes as a minister admiring a fellow preacher. The book suits readers who want a short, sympathetic life of Bunyan beside his own writings.
3629-the-titan:
Theodore Dreiser continues the story of Frank Cowperwood in this second novel of his trilogy, following The Financier. Cowperwood, now in Chicago, builds a new city life, a new home, and a new empire in gas and street railways. Chapters trace a Chicago evening, a new queen of the home, the fight for franchises, and a declaration of love, ending with the quest for fifty year franchises.

Dreiser follows Cowperwood's ambition, his wife, and his mistresses through boardrooms and bedrooms, showing how money and desire drive the same man. The novel's scale matches its hero's hunger for power. Readers who enjoy large American novels of business and appetite will find Dreiser at his most detailed and relentless.
3741-the-writings-of-thomas-paine-volume:
Moncure Daniel Conway collected this first volume of Thomas Paine's writings from the opening years of the American Revolution. Its heart is the American Crisis papers, a run of pamphlets that urged the colonies to hold firm through defeat and doubt. Crisis papers addressed to Lord Howe, to General Howe, to the people of England, and to the people of America follow one another in order. Notes on taxation, the king's speech, and the coming peace fill the gaps between them.

Paine's prose hits hard and plain, with short sentences and direct appeals that still stir a reader. The volume shows a working pamphleteer at full stretch, answering each new British move as it came. Readers who know Common Sense will find here the longer argument behind it, written week by week while the war hung in the balance.
3804-pierre-and-jean:
Guy de Maupassant sets this short novel among a fishing family at Le Havre, where old Roland, his wife, and their two sons pass idle days on the water. Pierre, dark and restless, and Jean, fair and easy, seem a matched pair until a family friend dies and leaves his whole fortune to Jean alone. The will cracks the household open, since no honest reason explains such a preference.

Pierre turns the facts over in torment, recalling how the dead man first grew close to his parents through his own scarlet fever. Logic points one way, and affection points another, as he weighs whether Jean is truly his brother. Maupassant writes with cold precision, and the novel's power lies in what Pierre cannot bring himself to say aloud.
4008-count-julian:
A verse drama in the old manner tells of Count Julian, the lord whose wrongs and vengeance open Spain to invasion. In the sampled scenes, lovers speak of suspicion planted like a demon whisper, of hope argued back into the heart, and of parting made final by death.

Mountains and seas, the speakers say, are not true separation, since only death divides. The play moves in high, formal speech, with honor, betrayal, and fate as its ruling themes. Readers who enjoy early nineteenth-century verse tragedy will find a stern, grave work, closer to a stage poem than to a modern novel of action.
4011-epicoene-or-the-silent-woman:
Ben Jonson's comedy centers on Morose, a man who hates noise and seeks a silent wife, and on the young wife who turns out to be anything but silent. In the sampled scenes, a household of mutes makes legs and waits in silence, while talk praises the Turk's mute court as a model of order.

Jonson builds the joke through talk, disguise, and a wedding that upends every plan. The play moves at a brisk, farcical pace, with London wits and gallants crowding the stage. Readers who like sharp city comedy will enjoy a work that turns the dream of a quiet wife into a loud, funny defeat.
4026-the-first-man:
A play in four acts centers on a household in Bridgetown, where Martha, Jayson, and Sheffield argue over a woman's place and work. Talk of law as a career, of small-town air, and of catty remarks shows a family testing new ideas against old habits.

Martha presses for a life beyond the home, while the men around her answer with teasing, concern, and pride. The play moves through drawing-room debate toward a hard choice about marriage and freedom. Readers who like serious domestic drama will find a thoughtful, plain-spoken work about a woman asking for more room in her own life.
4036-essays-from-the-guardian:
Walter Horatio Pater's Guardian essays gather literary criticism first written for a newspaper readership. A sampled essay praises a study of Browning that points readers to the best, most solid parts of the poet's work, treating each book or group of poems as a distinct study.

Pater's own essays move with the same care, weighing writers and works in fine, balanced prose. The volume suits readers who like criticism as an art, where judgment grows from close reading rather than from praise or blame. It offers a window on Victorian taste and on Pater's quiet, exact mind.
4285-the-master-christian:
Marie Corelli set this novel in Rouen, where bells of old grey towers ring the Angelus at dusk. Market women, bargemen, and schoolchildren hear the chime over the city. News comes of a cardinal-archbishop from a small French cathedral town. The story grows into a romance about faith and the churches.

Corelli dedicated the book to all those churches who quarrel in the name of Christ. That purpose shapes the plot: a search for a truer Christianity amid ritual, ambition, and division. Readers of Corelli's popular romances will recognize her blend of sentiment, pageantry, and moral argument, set against a richly described French city.
4304-our-friend-the-charlatan:
George Gissing wrote this novel around Mr. Lashmar, a clergyman waiting for a late breakfast at Alverholme Vicarage. He drums on the window and watches a blackbird on the lawn, while his mind runs on human follies. Gissing calls him a man in mild, ceaseless indignation at the tenor of the age.

The charlatan of the title is a figure who trades in fine talk and borrowed ideas, and the novel tests him against honest folk. Gissing uses the vicarage, its parish, and London talk to ask how people judge sincerity. It is a satire with a serious edge, about belief, ambition, and the art of seeming.
4318-reproduction-of-copyrighted-works-b:
The United States Copyright Office issued this circular, number 21, for educators and librarians who ask about fair use and photocopying. It states plainly that the office cannot give legal advice or opinions on what is permitted. Instead it sets out the basic legislative provisions on reproduction by libraries and schools.

The circular covers fair use under section 107 and library copying under section 108, with related documents and the 1983 report of the Register of Copyrights. Teachers and librarians use it as a starting guide to classroom and reserve copying. For a specific case, readers must still seek counsel, but the rules themselves are laid out here.
4585-god-s-country-and-the-woman:
James Oliver Curwood opens God's Country and the Woman with Philip Weyman in the far north, where water flows north and a man can feel like several people at once. Philip laughs and sings, talks to himself, and tries to sing Radisson's La Belle Marie in a heavy bass, even though he has lately looked on Radisson's unpleasant death. Two years along the rim of the Arctic have taught him how a man becomes acquainted with himself.

From that lonely, buoyant start grows a northern romance in which a woman enters Philip's wilderness world and changes its terms. Curwood writes the cold, the rivers, and the long light with his usual vigour, while loyalty, love, and survival are tested. Readers get a popular Canadian adventure with a strong romantic thread, in which the north itself acts as both danger and judge.
4748-baree-son-of-kazan:
James Oliver Curwood wrote Baree, Son of Kazan, as his third animal book, after Kazan, the Wolf Dog, and The Grizzly King. His preface says hundreds of letters from friends of wild animal life asked questions about his earlier books. Those letters encouraged him to say more about his hope in writing of wild life, and about the foundation of fact beneath this book and its companions.

Curwood says he has always disliked preaching sermons in romance, comparing it to placing a halter about a reader's neck and dragging him down paths he may not like. If fact and truth produce a message in the reader's mind, then a work has been done, and that is what he hopes for in his nature books. He adds bluntly that Americans have gone after Nature with a gun. Readers get an animal story grounded in observed wild life, not a sermon.
4786-zone-policeman-88-a-close-range-stu:
Harry A. Franck, author of A Vagabond Journey Around the World, wrote Zone Policeman 88 as a close-range study of the Panama Canal and its workers. He dedicates it to a host of good fellows, the Zone Police, opening from Quito, December 31, 1912. His first chapter follows the Thousand Stairs up to the red-roofed Administration Building, where Panama and its bay lie below.

Underneath, tight-packed roofs and plazas with three tops nestle in a bright curve of Pacific water, with tree-covered peaks reaching toward distant Taboga. Behind, low, uneven, jungle-clad hills fade hazily toward South America. At the third-floor landing he stops to mop perspiration from his brow and hatband, then enters through the screen door into police headquarters. Inside, the Captain glances up from a letter and asks what military service he has seen. Readers get Franck's firsthand account of joining the Zone Police.
4943-the-river-war-an-account-of-the-rec:
Winston S. Churchill's River War recounts the reconquest of the Sudan, beginning with the Mahdi's rebellion and the Nile country that made it possible. The Egyptian Sudan lies five hundred miles from the sea on every side, divided by mountain, swamp, and desert, and the great river alone carries its commerce and lets European civilization penetrate.

Churchill, who rode in the campaign, describes the provinces along the Nile's headstreams and the forces that clashed over them. The narrative combines geography, history, and battle with a young officer's eye. Readers get a classic of imperial war writing, vivid on the ground and frank about the costs of reconquest.
4961-our-mr-wrenn-the-romantic-adventure:
Sinclair Lewis's Our Mr. Wrenn follows a gentle, lonely clerk who walks with Miss Theresa, starts for the land of elsewhere, and becomes the great little Bill Wrenn. Chapters trace his quaint English flavor, his orphanhood, his meetings with temperaments and intellectuals, and his gipsying, orange tie, and discovery of America.

Wrenn enters society, studies five hundred and savoir faire, grows mildly religious, and finally becomes our Mr. Wrenn, a man transformed by travel and company. Lewis writes with affectionate irony about a nobody finding a self. Readers get an early Lewis novel, comic and tender, about ordinariness turning romantic.
5068-on-being-human:
Woodrow Wilson's On Being Human argues that reading should open up a narrow, shut-in inner life rather than simply increase the knowledge a person holds. Books may instruct, inform, startle, arouse, reform, provoke, or amuse, Wilson concedes, but true readers take pleasure rather than laboriously seeking instruction.

What readers seek is companionship, a renewed spirit, richer thought, and complete mental adventure, enjoyed in congenial company and in a broader world where all of these can be found. Lovers of the masters, Wilson insists, understand this at once. Readers get a short meditation on reading itself, by a scholar-president who believed books enlarge the self.
5336-stories-by-foreign-authors-scandina:
Stories by Foreign Authors: Scandinavian gathers short stories from the North, translated for American readers. Its contents include The Father and The Railroad and the Churchyard by Bjornstjerne Bjornson, When Father Brought Home the Lamp by Juhani Aho, The Flying Mail by M. Goldschmidt, Two Friends by Alexander Kielland, and Hopes by Frederika Bremer.

The Father, from Bjornson's Bridal March and translated by R. B. Anderson, opens the book with the story of the wealthiest and most influential person in his district. Readers get a compact anthology of Scandinavian realism, in which fathers, friends, railroads, and churchyards carry the weight of ordinary lives.
5397-dr-jonathan:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, wrote Dr. Jonathan as a play in three acts during the First World War. Managers declined to stage it at the time, so Churchill published it instead, believing its theme would grow more timely once the fighting ended. That theme is self-determination, the right of peoples to choose their own government, which he saw as the true issue of the war.

The preface argues the point directly, drawing on American ideals and on Churchill's own return from abroad late in 1917. Readers get a wartime drama of ideas rather than battles: a playwright using the stage to argue what the war was really about, and what peace should honor.
5637-literary-and-philosophical-essays-f:
Literary and Philosophical Essays, volume thirty-two of the Harvard Classics, gathers French, German, and Italian essays in translation. Montaigne leads with pieces on judging happiness only after death, philosophizing as learning how to die, the education of children, friendship, and books. Sainte-Beuve asks what a classic is, and Renan writes on the poetry of the Celtic races.

Lessing contributes The Education of the Human Race, Schiller his Letters upon the Aesthetic Education of Man, and Kant his Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals. Readers get a compact library of European thought, from Renaissance essay to German philosophy.
5659-stories-by-foreign-authors-polish-g:
Stories by Foreign Authors gathers Polish, Greek, Belgian, and Hungarian tales in translation. It opens with Henryk Sienkiewicz's The Light-House Keeper of Aspinwall, from Yanko the Musician and Other Stories, translated by Jeremiah Curtin and published by Little, Brown in 1893. It begins when a lighthouse keeper in Aspinwall, near Panama, vanishes without trace during a storm, his boat missing from its rocky niche.

Demetrios Bikelas's The Plain Sister, Maurice Maeterlinck's The Massacre of the Innocents, Camille Lemonnier's Saint Nicholas Eve, and Maurice Jokai's In Love with the Czarina complete the set. Readers get five short masterpieces from four literatures, in one slim volume.
5728-stories-by-foreign-authors-italian:
Stories by Foreign Authors: Italian gathers short fiction in English translation by leading Italian writers. Its contents include A Great Day by Edmondo de Amicis, Pereat Rochus by Antonio Fogazzaro, San Pantaleone by Gabriele D'Annunzio, It Snows by Enrico Castelnuovo, and College Friends again by de Amicis. Each story offers a distinct Italian scene, from school and church to village life.

Readers meet Italian realism, irony, and lyric feeling in compact form, without needing to commit to a full novel. The collection suits readers sampling European short fiction, and students of translation who want to compare national styles. Together the stories show a literature of strong feeling and sharp observation, rooted in towns, families, and faith.
5741-stories-by-foreign-authors-russian:
Stories by Foreign Authors: Russian gathers short fiction in English translation, opening with an officer's garrison life in a small town. Mornings bring drill and the riding school. Dinners come with the colonel or at a Jewish restaurant. Evenings bring punch and cards, in a town with no open house and no marriageable girl. The catalog title points to Turgenev's Mumu among the tales collected here.

Readers get Russian short fiction in compact, accessible form, with army routine, village life, and strong feeling rendered plainly. The collection suits readers sampling Russian literature beyond the great novels, and students who want to compare translators' English. Together the stories show a tradition of close observation, moral pressure, and sudden reversals of fortune.
5745-she-and-allan:
Rider Haggard reunites Allan Quatermain with the mysterious She in She and Allan, a romance of Africa and ancient power. Chapters open with a talisman and messengers, then bring Umslopogaas of the axe, a lion and an axe, Inez, a sea-cow hunt, an oath, pursuit, a swamp, and an attack. Through a mountain wall waits the White Witch, and Allan hears a strange tale before missing his opportunity.

Readers get Haggard's signature mix of adventure, lost kingdoms, and supernatural dread, with Quatermain's plain narration grounding the marvels. The novel appeals to fans of imperial romance and fantasy adventure, and to readers tracing Haggard's long saga of She. Its pace is brisk, its dangers are vivid, and its central mystery keeps the quest moving from camp to mountain.
5793-stories-of-red-hanrahan:
Yeats gathers the stories of Red Hanrahan, a schoolmaster and poet wandering the Irish countryside. Contents include Red Hanrahan, The Twisting of the Rope, Hanrahan and Cathleen the Daughter of Hoolihan, Red Hanrahan's Curse, Hanrahan's Vision, and The Death of Hanrahan. Yeats thanks Lady Gregory for helping him rewrite the stories, which blend folklore, love, and fate.

This introduces a hero tempted by fairy women, bound by curses, and haunted by visions, in prose that reads like poetry. The tales favor mood and myth over realistic plot, with the Irish landscape as a living presence. Lovers of Yeats, Irish folklore, and lyric short fiction will find a small, powerful collection that shows the poet as storyteller.
5983-the-institutes-of-justinian:
The Institutes of Justinian present Roman law in the emperor's own address to youth desirous of studying law. Justinian, conqueror of Goths, Franks, Vandals, and many more peoples, declares that imperial majesty should be armed with laws as well as glorified with arms, for good government in war and peace.

This English version by J. B. Moyle follows the fifth edition of 1913. The work sets out the foundations of Roman law as a teaching text, meant to train students in justice as surely as armies win victories. Its proem frames law as the ruler's second weapon, equal to the sword.
6056-the-desired-woman:
Will N. Harben opens in Atlanta, inside a gray-stone bank on a narrow asphalt street sloping toward the old passenger depot, warehouses, and hotels. Clerks and accountants bend over ponderous ledgers before opening hour, while locomotive bells clang, steam escapes, and newsboys cry the morning papers.

Jarvis Saunders, of Mostyn, Saunders and Company, bankers and brokers, comes in and hangs up his straw hat. Harben sets a southern business romance amid banks, railways, and city noise. The desired woman of the title moves through a world of ledgers, deals, and reputations, where money and longing meet.
6057-fran:
John Breckenridge Ellis opens with Fran knocking at a front door too dark for finding the bell, though she would have knocked anyway. Nobody answers at first, which surprises no one, since everybody is supposed to be at the Union Camp-meeting advertised for two months in Littleburg.
