Chapters promise a disturbing laugh, a foot-bridge, the woman who was not Mrs. Gregory, war declared, skirmishing, an ambuscade, and a new bridge at midnight. Grace captures outposts, alliances form, and a tamer of lions appears. Ellis turns a small town's secrets into a lively campaign of wit and feeling.
6125-the-making-of-an-american:
Jacob A. Riis, author of How the Other Half Lives, tells his own making as an American, insisting his papers are not made-up stories. Originally published in The Outlook, with one chapter in The Churchman and parts in Century Magazine, they trace a Danish immigrant's American life.

Chapters run from a meeting on the Long Bridge and landing in New York to going to war at last. Working and wandering follow, then going into business headlong, and becoming an editor who receives his first love letter. Elizabeth tells her story, early married life follows, and Riis writes with pride at having been in it all.
6137-the-home-of-the-blizzard-being-the-:
Douglas Mawson tells the story of the Australasian Antarctic Expedition of 1911 to 1914 in The Home of the Blizzard. It is illustrated in color and black and white with maps, 260 pictures, photogravure frontispieces, and plates from Dr. Wilson's sketches. He dedicates it to subscribers, comrades, and those who waited.

Mawson's preface aims at a connected narrative from a popular and general point of view, admitting the record is inadequate to the expedition's endeavors. Lasting reputation, he says, rests on scientific volumes to come, while Antarctic exploration history is kept to a minimum. The book brings blizzard country home.
6159-vicky-van:
Carolyn Wells introduces Vicky Van, whose full name Victoria Van Allen appears on letters and cheques, while Vicky Van signs her whole captivating personality, from dainty tossing head to dainty dancing feet. The narrator likes her from the first, though her small and earlies puzzle guests.

Chapters follow Mr. Somers, a waiter's story, Somers's real name, the Schuyler household, Vicky's ways, Ruth Schuyler, a letter box, and a social secretary. An inquest, notes from Vicky, Fleming Stone, walls with tongues, and proofs lead to truth from Ruth. Wells mixes society mystery with bright comedy.
6395-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Long disturbance ends when the Flavian family restores empire to peace and security, Suetonius says, though its descent was obscure and boasted no ancestral honours. The public had no cause to regret the elevation, except that Domitian later met the just reward of avarice and cruelty. Titus Flavius Petro of Reate, centurion or evocatus of Pompey's party, fled Pharsalia and went home, founding the line that would rule.

Vespasian himself reforms army discipline with a sharp tongue. Telling a perfumed young officer seeking thanks for a horse command that he would rather he had smelt of garlic, he revokes the commission. Fleet men travelling from Ostia and Puteoli to Rome petition late for gratuities, and the emperor answers with law and delay. Suetonius gives a plain, thrifty ruler, whose jokes and firmness steadied Rome after three violent reigns.
6397-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Born on October 24, when his father was consul elect, in Rome's sixth region at the Pomegranate, Domitian grew up in want and infamy. Suetonius says he owned not one piece of plate. Clodius Pollio, a praetorian, kept a note in Domitian's handwriting and sometimes produced it, a small evidence of a youth spent borrowing and promising. The house of his birth later became a temple of the Flavian family.

As emperor, Domitian turns savage after civil war success. He puts Helvidius the younger to death for a farce on Paris and Oenone that mocked his divorce. Flavius Sabinus, his cousin, dies because a crier blundered and proclaimed him emperor instead of consul at election. He hunts the adverse party with industry. Suetonius writes the last Flavian as a reign where a slip of the tongue could kill, and fear governed Rome.
6451-the-rover-boys-on-the-great-lakes-o:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, sends the Rover boys to the Great Lakes in the fifth volume of their series, subtitled The Secret of the Island Cave. A storm on Lake Erie opens it: Dick, Sam, and Tom Rover watch wind freshening ten minutes and wonder if they should turn back, three miles from shore. Talk turns to the Baxters, buried alive in a Colorado mountain landslide, a terrible fate the brothers are glad to be rid of.

Later, Sam and Tom insist Captain Langless hides the Baxters and Dick aboard his boat, while the captain, asked about stowaways, hears his mate answer that none were found below. It is all a riddle to him, he says. The volume is a complete story in itself, the introduction promises, with sailing, storms, and a search for a hidden cave on island waters.
646-the-coral-island-a-tale-of-the-pacif:
Robert Michael Ballantyne writes a boys' adventure in this 1884 tale of the Pacific, with illustrations by Dalziel. Ralph Rover, born at sea to a line of captains, thirsts for adventure and sails abroad, only to be wrecked on a coral island with two companions. The preface speaks straight to boys, promising pleasure, profit, and amusement.

Ballantyne writes with brisk, hearty prose, full of reefs, canoes, and island perils. The tale taught generations of boys to dream of the South Seas. It endures as a classic castaway story, where three lads learn courage, friendship, and faith on a coral shore.
6474-the-iron-woman:
Margaret Deland's The Iron Woman, dated August 12, 1911, opens with Elizabeth Ferguson commanding children to climb an apple tree and play house in the Maitland orchard. She sits on the lowest branch, swinging white stockinged legs so recklessly that the summoned children back away for safety. If you do not, she warns, looking down, perhaps, maybe, I will get mad, her foreboding tempered by a giggle and a deepening dimple.

The others know well what Elizabeth mad means, and Nannie Maitland, oldest of the group, answers helplessly, well. Nannie is always helpless with Elizabeth, as with her half brother Blair. A mid passage shows Robert Ferguson complaining of a love sick girl on his hands, trowel under arm, thinning peonies in the fall. Deland writes a strong willed heroine and the family that bends around her.
6481-personal-experience-of-a-physician:
John Ellis, M.D., writes Personal Experience of a Physician with an appeal to the medical and clerical professions, plus a review of Christ and the Temperance Question in the Christian Union. Every physician, he opens, should strive for the best education medical schools afford, since physicians hold not simply property or money but the very lives of their fellows. His chapters argue why every physician should examine homoeopathy, and warn of dangers from allopathic treatment of diseases.

Personal religious experience follows, with dawn of a new dispensation, a new day for earth, wants of the Christian church, and restraining and curing spiritual and natural diseases. A mid passage quotes Galatians: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap, urging practical doctrines uniting religion and life. Ellis writes a doctor's testimony, where medicine, faith, and temperance meet.
6609-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Puritan New England takes center stage in Skinner's fourth volume, from Evangeline to Salem witchcraft. A snoring hermit, a dead ship at Harpswell, a partridge witch, and Peter Rugg, the missing man, all pass in turn. The White Mountains, Mount Katahdin, and the Saco river give the tales their stern, pine-dark ground.

Witch lore, lost loves, and grim portraits, like that of Edward Randolph, show a people who feared both devil and neighbor. Skinner tells each story briefly, letting the place and the dread do the work. Tales of Puritan Land is a dark, rich slice of New England folk memory.
663-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words from F through G. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from F, the sixth letter, through Fa, the fourth tone in solmization, and Fabaceous, like a bean, and onward. Notes trace Latin, Greek, and Phoenician forms.

Here the dictionary moves from music and fable into the thick of G: fables, fabrics, and feudal terms yield to gardens, gems, and ghosts. The two-letter span shows how much of English sits in ordinary work and play. It is a handy shelf for settling a spelling or tracing a word's kin.
665-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words from M through N. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from M, the labio-nasal letter, through Ma, a child's word for mother, and onward through hundreds of headwords. Guide references aid pronunciation.

Spanning two letters, this slice is a wide field for browsing: mammal names, manners, and measures sit beside nautical and legal terms. A reader can watch meanings shift as M gives way to N. It keeps 1913 English in view, a useful check for anyone reading old books or tracing a word's past.
6687-from-the-caves-and-jungles-of-hindo:
Helena Blavatsky's letters from India, first sent to the Russian Messenger, were written in leisure moments more for fun than for science. She warns readers herself that facts and incidents are broadly true. Yet she grouped, colored, and dramatized them for artistic effect. She would rather be judged as a romance of travel than as a serious work. Her translator adds a like caution.

Caves, jungles, temples, and strange folk fill the letters, with wonder and wit in equal parts. Blavatsky's voice is bold, curious, and never dull. From the Caves and Jungles of Hindostan is a vivid, period travel romance, best read for its color rather than as a guidebook.
6730-observations-of-a-retired-veteran:
Henry Tinsley, writing as P. Boyzy in the Staunton Vindicator, offers essays chosen from years of weekly columns. His editor praises a winning humor joined to pathos, humor's most exquisite companion, and a shrewd, homely wit joined to deep knowledge of the human heart. Tinsley, a political journalist in his strenuous years, turns here to gentler themes.

The essays that follow mix laughter and feeling, with a Virginian's eye for character. They read like talk from a wise old friend, not like lectures. Observations of a Retired Veteran is a warm, small book of newspaper wisdom, still pleasant to dip into.
6741-memoirs-of-the-life-of-the-rt-hon-r:
Thomas Moore writes the memoirs of Richard Brinsley Sheridan, playwright and statesman, in two volumes, the first inscribed to George Bryan. Moore notes that his first four chapters were written seven years before, then set aside during a long absence from England, and only finished in the last year. Charles Sheridan, the subject's son, supplied most of the materials.

Moore thanks Charles for trust and for restraint, since, though deeply concerned, he never meddled with the work. The memoirs that follow trace Sheridan from stage triumphs to parliament and ruin. Volume one is a rich, friendly life of a wit who ruled both theatre and Commons.
7016-adventures-in-the-land-of-canaan:
Robert Lee Berry writes Adventures in the Land of Canaan from the heart, hoping to reach the hearts of others. Some lessons came through long and bitter experience, and the adventures were very real, though he hopes readers may never face some of them. The real battles, he writes, are fought within, and the struggle for mastery goes on in the soul, hidden in the mysterious depths of the spirit.

Such battles are often fought alone, while others nearby sense nothing of moment happening. Berry disclaims interest in pleasing super critical minds, writing only to bless the hearts and lives of common men and women. The book blends travel, trial, and faith into a plain spiritual memoir, grateful for help received in the writing.
7040-paula-the-waldensian:
Eva Lecomte's Paula the Waldensian, adapted and translated from the Spanish by W M Strong, hopes young readers will share the joy its author found in writing it. Paula's Saviour, Lecomte writes, wishes to be the reader's Saviour too. Paula had her faults, yet she gave God her whole heart and cared for others as for herself: an unspoiled village girl, youthful and sturdy, gentle and selfless.

Lecomte compares her to a sparkling stream in the country she loved, clean and bright, gliding silently past forget-me-nots along its flowered banks. It was by love that Paula conquered, as the tale will show. The author, living at Villar at the valley's foot, invites any reader who visits her country to call. The book is a gentle tale of Waldensian faith.
706-the-amateur-cracksman:
E. W. Hornung introduced A. J. Raffles in this first set of tales, told by his school friend Bunny Manders. Raffles is a star cricketer and a darling of London clubs by day, and a bold burglar by night. Bunny, broke and in debt, is drawn into the game and narrates each job with awe and dread.

Eight stories follow, from the Ides of March to the Gift of the Emperor, with jewel thefts, disguise, and narrow escapes. Hornung plays the crime tale as a sport: skill, nerve, and honour among thieves count for more than brute force. The book set the model for the gentleman thief, and it still reads as brisk, witty adventure.
707-raffles-further-adventures-of-the-am:
E. W. Hornung continues the tales of A. J. Raffles, the gentleman cricketer who steals by night, told by his friend Bunny Manders. In these eight stories Raffles takes a sinecure, steals a jubilee gift, chases a thief, and meets old flames, all with cool nerve and charm. The year 1897 frames the action, and London's clubs and streets form the stage.

Bunny's voice gives the tales their pull: he admires Raffles, fears the law, and cannot quit the game. Hornung keeps the plots brisk, with disguise, wit, and close escapes. The book fixed the gentleman thief in popular fiction, and it still charms readers who enjoy crime told from the thief's side, with style rather than gore.
7072-tramping-through-mexico-guatemala-a:
Harry Franck tramps through Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras in random notes of an incurable vagabond, illustrated with his own photographs. He dedicates the book to the Mexican peon, with sincere wishes for his ultimate emancipation. His foreword says the simple story of a journey southward grew up of itself, as he chose a less monotonous route than a steamship track toward a planned exploration of South America.

The narrative gives day by day rambles over bad roads into worse lodgings, the lot of all who venture afield south of the Rio Grande. It joins his five months on the Canal Zone, already published, and clears the stage for a larger South America volume to come. Franck writes a vagabond's plain, observant travel book.
7124-the-coral-island-a-tale-of-the-paci:
R M Ballantyne's Coral Island, a tale of the Pacific Ocean, opens with Ralph Rover recalling he was a boy when he lived the wonderful adventures set down. With boyish feelings strong in memory, he presents the book specially to boys, hoping they gain information, pleasure, profit, and unbounded amusement. Any boy or man who loves melancholy and cannot share kindly in fun, he warns, should shut the book and put it away, since it is not meant for him.

Contents promise early life and character, departure and a dreadful storm, the coral island itself, curious discoveries, and enchanting excursions among coral groves. An excursion inland and a horrible encounter with a shark wait beyond. Ballantyne writes a boys classic of shipwreck, island life, and high spirits.
7251-sweet-cicely-or-josiah-allen-as-a-p:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen's Wife, dedicates Sweet Cicely to sad-eyed mothers who, like Cicely, look across the cradle of their boys into a great world of temptation and danger. Her preface opens in Josiah's voice, debating whether one child may be loved more than another. Her answer, that she loves them all yet feels a special sorrow for one, sets the book's tender, comic tone.

Josiah Allen as a politician gives the tale its public frame, while Cicely gives it a mother's heart. Holley writes in the wife's own homely dialect, mixing humour with moral warning about drink and danger. The novel pleads for boys at risk through a mother's eyes, plain and warm.
7279-the-shopkeeper-turned-gentleman:
Moliere's Shopkeeper Turned Gentleman, Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme in Charles Heron Wall's English prose translation, first played before the king at Chambord on October 14, 1670, and at the Palais Royal that November. Louis XIV told Moliere he had never written anything that amused him more, and Paris agreed, as the bourgeois good-humouredly laughed at what they took for their neighbours' weaknesses.

Wall notes that the first three acts are the best, since the king hurried Moliere over the last. Yet the comedy's heart stays clear: a tradesman aping gentility, taught by masters, dressed by tailors, and fooled by flattery. The play's laughter cuts both ways, at snobbery and at those who feed it. This translation keeps its prose brisk for stage and study.
7305-memoir-and-letters-of-francis-w-new:
I. Giberne Sieveking's Memoir and Letters of Francis W. Newman follows its subject from ancestors and two brothers at school and college through a missionary journey to the East, marriage, his mother's death, and a classical tutorship at Bristol in 1834. Friendship with Dr Martineau and Newman's work as a teacher carry the story onward, with letters giving the man's voice throughout.

Sieveking dedicates the book to her mother and fronts it with a Greek motto on praising one who dares to renew the state of the many. Newman emerges as a restless, principled scholar, brother to a cardinal yet on his own road. The memoir lets letters do much of the telling, plain and intimate.
744-the-golden-mean:
An electronic text gives the golden ratio, (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2, to one million digits, opening 1.6180339887 and running on in long blocks of figures. It rests on a computation of the square root of five by Robert Nemiroff and Jerry Bonnell. There is no essay or story here: the file is the number itself, laid out for reference.

Readers use such a file to check calculations, to test programs, or to feed art and design work that draws on the ratio. Its length is its point, since a million digits far pass any need of hand reckoning. The text stands as a plain, exact record of a famous constant, kept in full for anyone who wants it at hand.
790-lady-windermere-s-fan:
Oscar Wilde wrote this play about a good woman, Lady Windermere, whose birthday fan becomes the token of a scandal. Mrs Erlynne, a woman with a past, enters London society and seems bent on stealing Lord Windermere, while Lady Windermere plans to flee with Lord Darlington. Secrets, letters, and a fan left in a man's rooms drive the plot.

Wilde's wit sparkles in every scene, yet the play turns serious on a mother's sacrifice: Mrs Erlynne is, in truth, Lady Windermere's mother, shielding her daughter at her own cost. First staged in 1892, the play made Wilde a West End force. It remains his most tender comedy of manners.
808-the-complete-plays-of-gilbert-and-su:
William S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan wrote fourteen comic operas together between 1871 and 1896, and this volume gathers their libretti. The Gondoliers, The Grand Duke, H.M.S. Pinafore, Iolanthe, The Mikado, and The Pirates of Penzance head the set, with eight more in full acts.

Gilbert's topsy-turvy plots and witty verse meet Sullivan's graceful music, though only the words appear here. Each opera turns rank, law, or love upside down, with choruses of sailors, peers, or fairies. The collection is the core library for Savoy fans, and a fine way to read the jokes that made the pair famous.
81-the-return-of-tarzan:
Tarzan sails for Europe still torn between jungle and civilization. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Return of Tarzan, second in the series, opens with intrigue aboard a liner and a duel in Paris. Countess Olga explains a plot that binds Tarzan to old enemies.

Desert fights, a dancing girl, and the valley of the Waziri follow. Tarzan becomes white chief of the Waziri and finds the lost city of Opar, with its gold vaults and priestess La. The novel ends with Tarzan choosing the wild over London. Its mix of adventure and identity made the series grow.
85-the-beasts-of-tarzan:
Tarzan's wife and child are stolen, and his revenge runs through jungle and sea. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Beasts of Tarzan, third in the series, opens with kidnapping and marooning off Africa. Tarzan escapes with the help of apes, panthers, and other beasts.

Mugambi the chieftain joins him, and the trail leads down the Ugambi River to the Kincaid. Paulvitch plots revenge while Tarzan rallies the law of the jungle. The novel pits beast loyalty against human treachery. Its pace and animal allies made it a series favorite. The beasts' loyalty contrasts with the villains' greed in nearly every chapter.
850-tom-grogan:
F. Hopkinson Smith wrote this novel about Tom Grogan, a stevedore boss on the New York waterfront. Babcock, a businessman waiting for a ferry, first senses trouble in the air, and the tale unfolds around the docks, where work, rivals, and loyalties clash. Tom runs a tough crew in a tough trade.

Smith, who knew the waterfront world, writes with vigour for its labour, its bargains, and its codes of honour. The novel turns on fair dealing against sharp practice, and on the respect Tom earns from men and rivals alike. It remains a sturdy, old-fashioned tale of American working life, told with sympathy and pace.
876-life-in-the-iron-mills-or-the-korl-w:
Rebecca Harding Davis wrote this novella of life in an iron-mill town, where the sky sinks muddy and flat before dawn and the air is thick with the breath of crowded workers. Hugh Wolfe, a mill hand, sculpts a strange figure from korl, the waste of the furnaces, a woman with a hungry, pleading face.

Davis uses Hugh's art to ask what becomes of souls crushed by labour, and whether beauty can plead for the poor. Her realism was new and shocking in its day, and the tale helped launch American social fiction. The book remains a powerful, short classic, read for its pity and its moral force.
90-the-son-of-tarzan:
Tarzan's son Jack grows up in London hearing tales of his father's jungle life. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Son of Tarzan follows Jack as he runs away to Africa and takes the ape name Korak. A strange white man on the Ugambi River sets the plot in motion.

Korak learns the jungle, befriends apes, and meets Meriem, a girl held by Arab raiders. Their youth, danger, and first love fill the novel's middle chapters. Tarzan himself returns to the story as father and judge. The book passes the series torch to a new generation.
938-good-indian:
B. M. Bower wrote this western about the Peaceful Hart Ranch and its folk, with a character called Good Indian at its heart. Chapters on old wives' tales, a Christmas angel who plays ghost, and Miss Georgie Howard, the telephone operator, mix ranch work with humour and romance. Pepajee Jim and midnight prowlers add trouble.

Bower writes the West with a light, knowing touch, praising ranch loyalty and poking fun at greenhorns and gossips. Her dialogue is brisk, and her people feel real. The book charms readers who like westerns with humour and heart, where the ranch, not the gunfight, is the centre of the tale.
946-lady-susan:
Jane Austen wrote this short novel in letters about Lady Susan Vernon, a beautiful, scheming widow who charms her way through society. In forty-one letters and a conclusion, Lady Susan writes to her brother, her friend, and her victims, plotting marriages for herself and her daughter Frederica, while hiding her true aims.

Austen's irony is sharp: Lady Susan's own letters betray her, even as she flatters her readers. The novella, written early and published after Austen's death, shows her wit at its most biting. Lady Susan remains a favourite among Austen fans, as a portrait of a villainess who almost wins.
966-maid-marian:
Thomas Love Peacock wrote this comic romance of Maid Marian, opening at Rubygill Abbey. An abbot in his alb stands at the altar with his plump, sleek, rosy friars, to marry the beautiful Matilda Fitzwater, daughter of a baron. Robin Hood's men break in, and Matilda becomes Marian of the greenwood.

Peacock retells the Robin Hood legend with wit and satire, mocking monks, lords, and law, while praising love and liberty in Sherwood. His prose is urbane, his songs are gay, and his Robin is a gentleman outlaw. The book charms readers who like the legend told with a smile, and with a poet's eye for fun.
986-master-and-man:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this tale of master and man, translated by Louise and Aylmer Maude. It happened in the seventies, in winter, on the day after St. Nicholas's Day, when Vasili Andreevich Brekhunov, a second-guild merchant and church elder, sets out with his servant Nikita through a blizzard on business.

The storm traps master and servant in the snow, and Brekhunov, who has lived for gain, must choose between self and the man he has used. Tolstoy tells the choice with stark, moral power, as the snow closes in. Master and Man is a late Tolstoy masterpiece, short, severe, and profoundly moving.
995-ballads-of-a-bohemian:
Robert W. Service wrote these ballads of a bohemian life, opening with a prelude and a first book called Spring. My Garret, Julot the Apache, L'Escargot d'Or, and It Is Later Than You Think follow, with Noctambule, Insomnia, Moon Song, and The Sewing-Girl in turn. Paris, its cafés and garrets, forms the scene.

Service, author of The Spell of the Yukon, writes here of artists, lovers, and night owls, with his usual vigour and rhyme. The ballads mix gaiety with melancholy, as bohemian youth fades into memory. The book suits readers who enjoy Service's rollicking verse, transplanted from the Yukon to the Latin Quarter.
a-mountain-woman:
Elia Wilkinson Peattie gathers tales of the American West, most first printed in magazines such as Harper's Weekly and the Cosmopolitan, as her foreword notes. The title story opens with a letter from Colorado: the writer has married a mountain woman, a remnant, he says, of the heroic ages. Eight tales follow, including Jim Lancy's Waterloo and The Three Johns.

Her people are miners, ranch families, schoolteachers, and wanderers in Colorado, Michigan, and the gulches. Peattie writes women who endure weather, loss, and rough men without losing warmth or humor. The tales mix dialect, landscape, and sentiment in the regional style her day loved, and they keep a clear eye on frontier hardship.
a-new-voyage-to-carolina-containing-the-:
John Lawson, surveyor-general of North Carolina, published his voyage account in the early seventeen hundreds, and the title page promises an exact description and natural history of the country. The first part reports his journal of a thousand miles traveled through several nations of Indians. Lawson writes as an explorer who walked the ground himself.

He describes rivers, soil, plants, beasts, and fish, then the customs, dress, food, wars, and beliefs of the native peoples he met. The second part gives the present state of the colony, its towns, trade, and prospects for settlers. Lawson's plain, curious record remains a key source for the early Carolina backcountry and its peoples.
a-people-s-man:
A People's Man is a 1914 political novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, who called himself the prince of storytellers. Oppenheim wrote some one hundred fifty novels, mainly of suspense and international intrigue. He was among the earliest writers of modern spy fiction and founded the rogue male school of adventure thrillers, and this book turns his hand to politics at home.

As its title signals, the story follows a man of the people through the world of Westminster power. Ambition, loyalty, and public pressure collide in the Edwardian political scene. The novel shows Oppenheim applying his thriller pace to Parliament and party struggle, rather than to the foreign intrigue of his better-known tales.
a-poor-wise-man:
Mary Roberts Rinehart opens in a steel city seen from the railway, blackened walls and river mist under a gray, smoke-laden sky. Through its gates come hopeful workers and men who would destroy their dreams. After the Great War, the city simmers with strikes, radicals, and fear.

Fifty-two chapters follow a rich steel family, its rebellious daughter, and Willy Cameron, the poor wise man of the title, a clerk whose plain decency steadies everyone he touches. Rinehart mixes romance with a serious look at labor unrest and revolutionary plots in America. Known for mysteries, she here writes a novel of ideas about class, loyalty, and the country's future.
adventures-in-the-land-of-canaan:
Robert Lee Berry says in his foreword that his book comes out of his heart and is meant for the hearts of others. Some of it was learned by long and bitter experience. His introductory chapter explains the plan: Israel's story, from bondage in Egypt to conquering Canaan, is a type of the Christian's path from sin to entire sanctification.

Thirteen chapters follow that path as a pilgrimage. They cover getting ready to enter, crossing the Jordan, and a memorial stone. They explore Canaan by faith. They fight Giant Accuser, Giant Mistake, and Giant Doubt. They enter the dungeon of Giant Discourager. The wine of prayer and the pilgrims of the victorious life close the course. Berry writes holiness teaching as allegory, in Bunyan's long shadow.
an-amiable-charlatan: An Amiable Charlatan is a 1916 novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, the English master of suspense and international intrigue. By this date Oppenheim was a major popular author, midway through a career of some one hundred fifty novels. The story centers on its title figure, a charming rogue whose schemes drive the tale, in the light, plot-led style that made Oppenheim a household name for thriller readers of his era.
an-iceland-fisherman:
Pierre Loti writes of the Breton fishermen who sail each year to fish off Iceland, in M. Jules Cambon's translation. A long prefatory essay praises Loti's power to carry readers into far lands with simple art. The novel itself divides between the icy sea and the Breton land, as its part titles state.

On the Iceland grounds the men work through fog and storm while the women wait at home in Brittany. A first love grows between a fisherman and a girl of his village, shadowed by orders for foreign service and the sea's long record of taking men. Loti keeps the plot spare and the feeling deep, and the ending is among the saddest in French fiction.
another-study-of-woman:
Honoré de Balzac sets his tale at a Paris ball, in a translation by Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell. When the glittering party thins out, a smaller circle stays behind for the real talk of the night. There the company falls to discussing women, marriage, and love, and one guest tells a story to prove his point.

The frame lets Balzac stage a contest of wits among fashionable men and women, each with a theory and a past. A tale within the tale, of a woman's sacrifice and a husband's blindness, gives the talk its weight. The piece shows Balzac the observer of salons at his most polished and ironic.
arms-and-the-man:
George Bernard Shaw calls his play a pleasant one and sets it in Bulgaria during and after the war with Serbia. The introduction in this edition marvels, with some irony, at orthodox critics who found Shaw ignorant of dramatic art while audiences kept coming. In a young lady's bedroom, a fleeing enemy officer climbs in through the window, more armed with chocolates than with cartridges.

Raina, the romantic heroine, hides the fugitive and slowly trades her heroic ideals for the plain truth he tells about soldiering. Her dashing fiancé Sergius and the practical servant Louka complete the upset of every romance. Three acts of wit carry Shaw's case: war is work, not glory, and sense beats swagger.
b09-luther-freedom-christian:
On the Freedom of a Christian, also called Concerning Christian Liberty, is Martin Luther's gentle tract of 1520. Where his other works of that year attack, this one consoles and teaches. It sets out his core claim: a person is made right with God by faith alone, not by works.

Luther holds two truths in tension through the tract. A Christian is a free lord of all, subject to none, and yet a ready servant of all, subject to everyone. Faith frees the soul; love then spends that freedom on the neighbor. The short work became the best known plain statement of Reformation teaching. Its calm tone still wins first-time readers.
ballads-of-a-bohemian:
Robert W Service organized Ballads of a Bohemian by seasons, spring through winter, following a poet in a Paris garret. The contents promise My Garret, The Sewing-Girl, The Absinthe Drinkers, and the death of Marie Toro, mixed with program pieces like The Philistine and the Bohemian. Service had swapped his Yukon gold rush for Montmartre.

The poems sing of models, pencil sellers, domestic tragedies, and gods in the gutter, in the swinging meters that made Service famous. A cozy middle passage, wife sewing and kettle purring, shows his gift for the sentimental scene. Readers who know only the Yukon ballads will find the same storyteller here, working Paris streets instead of frozen trails.
baree-son-of-kazan:
James Oliver Curwood's Baree, Son of Kazan is the third of his animal books, after Kazan and The Grizzly King. His preface answers hundreds of letters from readers of wild life. Americans, he confesses, have gone after nature with a gun, himself with twenty-seven of them. He has learned to know animals as they actually live.

Baree, Kazan's son by a wild she-wolf, is born in the northern forest. The pup's world is hunger, cold, and the law of claw and fang. A lynx, an owl, and a trapper's cabin shape his first year. Curwood refuses to humanize his hero, letting fact carry the romance. The story follows Baree toward his father's old haunts and man's uneasy friendship. It remains a favourite among readers of true-to-life animal tales.
bond-contract-1895-rothschild-morgan:
The House Ways and Means group sent this report to the full House on February 13, 1895. It is House Report No. 1824 of the 53rd Congress. Its theme is the great bond deal that saved the gold store of the United States that year.

The report prints the bond pact in full, with the terms the syndicate took. That group acted for N. M. Rothschild and Sons of London and for J. P. Morgan and Co. of New York. The deal is a core record of how the house lent to states at the top level.
carolinian: Sabatini set this tale in the southern colonies during America's revolt. A young hero faces love and war in old Carolina. The tale moves fast. The archive keeps the book open to all who seek it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dund: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Dundrennan describes a Cistercian house in Kirkcudbrightshire, founded in 1142 by King David the First and Fergus, Lord of Galloway, for monks from Rievaulx. Its name means 'fort of thorn-bushes', and the house commands a view over the Solway Firth. Queen Mary fled there after Langside, spending her final night on Scottish soil before sailing from Port Mary. The abbey passed to the Crown in 1587, was annexed to Stirling's chapel in 1621, and was long quarried for stone before repairs began in 1842.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-mar:
Alexander Martin Sullivan was an Irish politician, lawyer, and journalist, born at Bantry in 1830 and dead at Dublin in October 1884. He drifted into journalism in 1850, becoming the Nation's assistant editor in 1855 and then its editor and proprietor. From 1861 to 1884, with his elder brother T. D. Sullivan, he made the Nation a potent force for Irish nationality, and he also issued the Weekly News and Zozimus.

Sullivan entered Parliament in 1874 as member for Louth and later for Meath, was called to the Irish bar in 1876, and became Queen's Counsel in 1881. As a Dublin Corporation member he secured the site for the Grattan Monument, giving £400 subscribed by admirers while he was jailed for a political offence in 1868. He defended Patrick O'Donnell in his last great case in November 1883, wrote The Story of Ireland and New Ireland, and laboured as a temperance reformer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
The early history of Sodor and Man is obscure. The Scandinavian diocese covered Man and the western isles of Scotland, the Southern Hebrides. It took the name Sodor, or southern isles, against Nordr, the Orkneys and Shetland, for the northern isles. Man may have joined Sodor under Magnus Barefoot, in 1098, having earlier stood as a distinct see dependent on Dublin.

When Man became head of a kingdom under Norway, Eugenius III placed the diocese under Nidaros, or Trondhjem, in 1152, and Anastasius IV confirmed the arrangement in 1154. Man stayed under Drontheim until 1458, when Calixtus III moved it to York. Norway's rule ended in 1266, Scotland held the island till 1334, and England followed. Henry IV gave the island to the Stanleys, who held the patronage of the bishoprics, though the bishops never became spiritual lords of Parliament. The last Catholic bishop, Thomas Stanley, appointed under Mary, was recognized until 1568.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-forema:
Andrew Foreman, Scottish prelate of border family, was born at Hatton near Berwick-on-Tweed and died in 1522. His talents marked him out for promotion. Through King James IV's influence, he soon became a prothonotary Apostolic and took on important missions. The king sent him in 1497 with two envoys to conclude the truce of Aytoun with Henry VII, and later empowered him to negotiate James's marriage to Henry's daughter Margaret.

By 1502 Foreman was Bishop of Moray, exempt from Saint Andrews' jurisdiction despite the primate's protest. As ambassador to Henry VIII in 1509, he sought peace for a new crusade. Julius II intended him for the cardinalate, but Leo X made him Archbishop of Saint Andrews and legate a latere in 1514, with Dunfermline Abbey. His eight years as primate brought vigorous administration, the restoration of Dunkeld and Dunblane, and a synod showing zeal for clergy reform, learning, and solemn services.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelica-kauf:
Angelica Kauffman, painter, was born at Coire in Switzerland in 1741 and died at Rome in 1807. Her father Johann Joseph, a mediocre painter, taught her colours early. Before twelve she was summoned to Como by Bishop Nevroni to paint his portrait. Francis III of Este became her protector. Cardinal Roth commissioned his portrait.

She showed aptitude for music, but friends urged her in vain to give up painting. After Parma and Florence, she reached Rome in 1763 for Winckelmann's perspective courses. Meeting English noblemen at Venice, she moved to London in 1766. Her pictures include The Mother of the Gracchi. The Royal Academy elected her an original member. Deceived in 1767 by a stranger posing as Count de Horn, whom she married, she separated. After his death in 1781 she married Antonio Zucchi, settling at Rome, where her salon welcomed Goethe. Sentimentalism helped her vogue, but her works have since declined for weak drawing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ardbraccan:
Ardbraccan, Hill of Braccan or Brecan, is the site of an old abbey, now a parish and village in County Meath, three miles west of Navan. Its abbey was founded and ruled by St. Brecan, grandson of Carthan Finn, first Christian ruler of Thomond, and son of Eochaidh Balldearg, whom Patrick baptized. Brecan, credited with prophecy, died early in the sixth century by Petrie's dating, or after 650 by Ware's, and was buried at Templebrecan in the Great Isle of Arran.

Petrie transcribed his tombstone inscription, found early in the 19th century. The Martyrology of Donegal calls Brecan bishop of Ardbraccan, but the see's founder was St. Ultan, who followed him as abbot. Ultan, famed for charity to children, wrote lives of Brigid and Patrick and died in 657, and his successor Tirechan compiled Acts of Patrick from Ultan's own lips. Ardbraccan was often pillaged between the ninth and twelfth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-audran:
Audran was the family name of four generations of French artists from Paris and Lyons, counting eight noted engravers and two painters. Their work spans the 1600s and 1700s. Some of their plates rank among the finest work of the burin, the engraver's cutting tool. Charles Audran, born in Paris in 1594, studied in Rome, engraved in pure line, and left more than two hundred plates, including portraits and copies after Titian and the Carracci.

His brother Claude the First taught engraving at Lyons and fathered three sons, of whom Gerard became the family's most famous artist. Later Audrans kept the trade alive into the 1700s. Among them were Germain, Claude the Second, and Benoit the Younger, the last of real artistic weight. Prosper Gabriel, a grandson of Jean, gave up art for law and became professor of Hebrew at the College de France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aurelian:
Aurelian, in full Lucius Domitius Aurelianus, was Roman Emperor from 270 to 275, born near Sirmium in Pannonia in 214 of humble parents. He entered the army at twenty, rose fast through ability and bodily strength, and was proclaimed emperor by the army at Sirmium on Claudius's death. He became sole master when his rival Quintillus, the Senate's candidate, took his own life. The empire he took up was split three ways.

Gaul and Britain stood under a Gallo-Roman empire, the East under Palmyra, and Rome itself held only Italy, Africa, and a few provinces. Invaders pressed the Danube, the treasury was empty, and the coinage was ruined. Backed only by the Danube army, Aurelian restored the frontiers, rebuilt unity, and reformed the state in under five years. He was slain before he could enforce a persecution edict, and the martyr acts tied to his reign are judged unauthentic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auxentius-of-:
Auxentius of Milan was a native of Cappadocia, ordained priest in 343 by Gregory, Alexandria's intruded bishop. After Dionysius of Milan was banished in 355, Arian intrigue made Auxentius bishop of the see, though he did not know Latin. Leading Western bishops tried in vain to bring him to accept the Nicene Creed, the orthodox statement of Christ's divinity. In 359 he made many Illyricum bishops sign the Rimini creed, a compromise formula.

St Hilary of Poitiers publicly accused him at Milan in 364, and a disputation held by Emperor Valentinian's order convicted him of error. His submission was only apparent, and he stayed strong enough to force Hilary's departure from Milan. Though St Athanasius got Pope Damasus to condemn him at a Roman synod in 369, Auxentius kept his see until his death in 374. St Ambrose succeeded him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethany-beyon:
Bethany beyond the Jordan, the place of Jesus's baptism in John's Gospel, is the subject of this textual entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. John 1:28 locates the baptism at Bethany across the Jordan, but a celebrated variant reads Bethabara instead. Most ancient manuscripts of weight support Bethany, a reading approved by Lachmann, Tischendorf, and Westcott-Hort.

Other old manuscripts, the Syriac versions, and Fathers such as Origen, Jerome, Eusebius, and Chrysostom support Bethabara. Origen's commentary argues for the second name. The entry weighs manuscripts and Fathers to settle a single place-name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-betharan: Betharan was an Amorite city east of the Jordan, in its valley plain, some twelve miles from Jericho. Rebuilt by the tribe of Gad, it was later fortified by Herod Antipas, who renamed it Livias for the wife of Augustus, and Josephus calls it Julias. Burnt at Jerusalem's fall, it was restored by Christians and became a bishopric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethsan:
Bethsan, or Beth Shean, meaning place of rest, was a city within Issachar assigned to Manasseh, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Later called Scythopolis, it survives as the village of Beisan, three miles west of the Jordan. Its strength kept the Israelites from taking it at the conquest, and it likely stayed Canaanite when the Philistines hung Saul's body on its walls.

Under Solomon it became the centre of an administrative district, and about the third century BC it took its Greek name. The entry follows a strong city from Canaanite holdout to Hellenistic town, with a name that changed with each master.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boetius-egan:
Boetius Egan, Archbishop of Tuam, led Irish Catholics from penal-era hardship toward the relief of the 1790s. Born near Tuam in 1734 to a once-wealthy Galway family, he trained for the priesthood at the Irish College of Bordeaux. He returned to minister in Ireland, became Bishop of Achonry in 1785, and Archbishop of Tuam two years later.

He welcomed the Catholic Relief Act of 1793 with gratitude to George III. He served as a trustee when Maynooth College opened in 1795. One of his last acts signed an address to Lord Camden condemning revolutionary associations, praising the king as the best of kings. He died near Tuam in 1798.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-dolma:
Charles Dolman was a publisher and bookseller born at Monmouth in 1807 and dead at Paris in 1863. The only son of a Monmouth surgeon and Mary Frances Booker, daughter of a London Catholic publisher, he was educated at St. Gregory's, Downside, near Bath. He gave it up when the Bookers, publishers into whose family his father had married, invited him to London.

When Joseph Booker died in 1837, Dolman kept the firm going with his aunt Mary Booker and cousin Thomas Booker. The firm became Booker and Dolman in 1840 and finally continued under his name alone. His periodical career began in 1838 with a new series of The Catholic Magazine. His many attempts to lift the Catholic press to a higher standard came to nothing. Disheartened and ill, he withdrew to Paris and died there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-patri:
An entry on Charles Patrick Meehan, an Irish priest, historian, and translator who spent his life in Dublin parish work and historical writing. Born in Dublin in 1812 to parents from Ballymahon, County Longford, he was sent to the Irish College at Rome. Ordained in 1834, he came home soon after Catholic Emancipation lifted legal penalties on Catholics. After a posting at Rathdrum in Wicklow, he moved to Sts. Michael and John's parish, staying there until his death in 1890.

Meehan wrote histories of the O'Tooles of Powerscourt, the Confederation of Kilkenny, and the Geraldines, and a study of the fate of the Earls of Tyrone and Tyrconnell. He translated Manzoni's tale of a nun, a Latin life of Bishop Kirwan, and an Italian history of Dominican painters. Most of his books went through several revised editions, and he also wrote graceful verse and tales for the young.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-mus:
An entry on the Christian Museum of the Lateran, founded by Pius the Ninth in 1854 in the Lateran palace built by Sixtus the Fifth. Gregory the Sixteenth had founded a profane Lateran museum in 1843 and mooted a Christian collection. Nothing of consequence happened until Pius entrusted the work to Father Marchi and Giovanni Battista de Rossi. Marchi took sculpture, De Rossi took inscriptions, and a third section held copies of catacomb frescoes.

Much material came from the Vatican Library hall set apart by Benedict the Fourteenth in 1750 and from the Capitoline Museum. More came from convents, chapels, sacristies, and private collections, with plaster casts where originals could not move. The epigraphy section, ordered by De Rossi, runs from basilica and baptistery inscriptions through Damasan texts, consular dates, dogma, hierarchy, and civil matters, to symbols such as anchor, dove, and monogram. Its prize piece holds the epitaph of Abercius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christine-de-:
An entry on Christine de Pisan, a French poet and historian born at Venice in 1363. Brought to Paris at five with her father, astrologer and secretary to Charles the Fifth, she was reared at court and learned the ancient languages. At fourteen she married Etienne du Castel of Picardy, and widowed at twenty-five with three children, she refused invitations from Henry the Fourth of England and Galeazzo Visconti of Milan.

Christine chose to earn her living with her pen in France, and her prose and verse soon won renown. Her contemporaries likened her eloquence to Cicero. In six years, from 1397 to 1403, she wrote fifteen important books, including a biography of Charles the Fifth, a treatise on educating princes, and the Treasury of the City of Ladies. Her long poems include the Book of the Mutations of Fortune and the Book of a Hundred Tales of Troy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clean-and-unc: The distinction between legal and ceremonial cleanness and uncleanness, as opposed to moral cleanness and uncleanness, stands out prominently in Mosaic legislation. Legal cleanness concerns ritual fitness under the Law, while moral cleanness concerns right conduct. The Law treats ritual states and moral states by different measures, and confusing the two misses the legislation's own division.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantino-c:
Thomas Shahan's entry follows Constantino Cajetan, Benedictine savant born at Syracuse, Sicily, in 1560, died at Rome on 17 September 1650. While brothers Ottavio and Alfonso joined the Society of Jesus, Constantino became a Benedictine on 29 October 1586 at San Nicolò d'Arena in Catania. Clement VIII soon called him to Rome, entrusting an edition of Saint Peter Damian's works, completed in four folio volumes at Rome in 1606 and after.

Constant, successful research in Roman archives won Cardinal Baronius's friendship. Through Baronius he became titular Abbot of San Baronzio in Pistoia diocese and Custodian of the Vatican Library, holding the latter office under four popes until death. Baronius owed much to him in composing the Annales Ecclesiastici, praising more than once his thorough knowledge of Roman archives. His labours later earned nomination as first consultor of the new college, the College of Propaganda, closing a life spent among archives, editions, and papal service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cormac-maccui:
James MacCaffrey's entry treats Cormac MacCuilenan, 836 to 908, Irish bishop and King of Cashel. In 900, by descent, he became King of Cashel, combining spiritual and temporal rule over Leth Moga.

The high king, Flann, assisted by Leinster's king, led forces into the Southern Province in 906, meeting Munstermen under Cormac at Moylena, Tullamore, and losing heavily. In 908 Flann returned with Ceorbhall of Leinster and Cathal of Connaught. Cormac, instigated by Flaherty, Abbot of Inniscathay, had claimed Leinster tribute and signified intent to assume the high kingship. At present-day Ballymoon the Munstermen suffered complete defeat, and Cormac was killed. His Irish Glossary, Sanas Chormaic, explains over 1,400 Irish words. Said to form only part of the Saltair Chaisil, also attributed to Cormac, that work has disappeared, or was at best a collection of transcripts by different writers. John O'Donovan translated and annotated Sanas Chormaic, edited by W. Stokes at Calcutta in 1868.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dan:
A scriptural entry untangles the name Dan, which covers a person, a tribe, and places. Dan was Jacob's fifth son, elder son of Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid, and his name, from a root meaning to rule or judge, is read as God's judgment in Rachel's favour. The Bible says little of Dan himself beyond his birth and a single son, Husim, likely a clan name.

Most passages use Dan for the tribe, whose territory and history are then traced, including its northern sanctuary. A second Dan was a city, and a third sense covers other biblical uses. The entry closes with the tribe's most notorious act: Jeroboam's golden calf at Dan, set up to draw northern Israelites from Jerusalem's sanctuary, a lasting symbol of schism in Israel's story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dean:
An office entry defines the dean, from the Greek for ten, as one of a diocese's principal administrative officials. The term first meant a military officer over ten soldiers. It then meant an imperial household official, and in Anglo-Saxon England a local judge for trials of first instance. Saint Benedict's Rule uses it for a monk set over ten others to oversee work and observance.

Monastic usage soon shaped diocesan life. Distant communities gained priest or deacon assistants to the bishop, known by the early fourth century as chorepiscopi. They were subject to the city bishop and able to confer only minor orders. Sections cover rural deans, with delegated jurisdiction set by statutes, custom, or mandate. They also cover deans of chapters, first dignitaries who take precedence in choir, processions, and deliberations and celebrate Mass when the bishop is absent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-detroit-michi:
A diocesan history of Detroit, established 8 March 1838 across the lower peninsula of Michigan south of Ottawa, Kent, and neighbouring counties, an area of 18,558 miles. Its story, as a suffragan of Cincinnati, opens with Jesuit missions. Jogues and Raynbaut reached the Sault in 1642. Menard followed in 1660, martyred the following year. Marquette's 1671 mission at Michilimackinac raised Michigan's first chapel for white settlers.

Cadillac's post of 1700 grew around Saint Anne's church, dedicated in 1701 as the mother church of the region. John Frederic Reze became first bishop in 1833, and later pages list bishops, religious orders, and statistics, from 237 priests and 146 churches to seminaries, colleges, and academies. A Monroe congregation of sisters, founded in 1845 by Louis Gillet, stands out among the orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocletian:
Diocletian, a Roman emperor who persecuted the Church, was born near Salona in Dalmatia about 245. His parents had been slaves, yet he rose through the army to govern Moesia, hold the consulship, and command the palace guards. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how the army chose him emperor in 284 after the murder of Numerian. Diocletian slew the murderer Aper with his own hand.

His reign, ending in 305, opened a new era in the empire's military and political story. The entry gives only a summary of his secular career, since its concern is the Church. It ends with the great persecution that bears his name and with his death at Salona in 313, after his abdication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domitian:
Domitian, full name Titus Flavius Domitianus, was a Roman emperor and persecutor of the Church. Son of Vespasian and younger brother of Titus, he was born on 24 October 51 and reigned from 81 to 96. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that, despite private vices, he posed as a reformer of morals and religion. He was the first emperor to deify himself in life, taking the title Lord and God.

After the revolt of Saturninus in 93 he launched bloody proscriptions against wealthy and noble houses. A conspiracy joined by his own wife ended him, murdered on 18 September 96. When Nero's acts were reversed after death, the persecution of Christians was kept in force, and a Jewish revolt soon brought fresh unpopularity on the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-bailey:
Edmund Bailey O'Callaghan was an Irish-born doctor, writer, and historian who lived from 1797 to 1880. After study in Paris he settled at Montreal, edited the Vindicator, sat in parliament, and took part in the failed rising of 1837, which drove him into exile in the United States. At Albany he went back to medicine and to editing.

Learning Dutch, he mined the neglected old Dutch records of New York and put out the first volume of his History of New Netherland in 1846. As keeper of New York's historical papers for twenty-two years he edited eleven volumes of colonial records from London, Paris, and The Hague. He also drew wide notice to the Jesuit Relations, the reports that later filled a great seventy-three volume set.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-colema:
Edward Coleman was a Catholic controversialist and secretary to the Duchess of York, executed at Tyburn in 1678 as a victim of the Titus Oates Plot. Son of a Suffolk clergyman and a Cambridge man, he became Catholic and sought French money for the Catholic cause. He took payments from three French ambassadors in return for daily news of Parliament.

When Oates named him a plotter, Coleman, sure of his innocence, let his papers be seized and gave himself up. Tried on 28 November 1678, he said he had only sought liberty of conscience through Parliament and denied any plan to kill the king. His letters showed an intriguer, but nothing tied him to murder. On the false word of Oates and Bedloe he was still found guilty and put to death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emmanuel-maig:
Emmanuel Maignan was a French physicist and theologian, born at Toulouse in 1601 and dead there in 1676. His father was dean of the city's chancery, and his mother's father taught medicine at Toulouse University. Schooled by the Jesuits, he joined the Minims at eighteen. His philosophy teacher followed Aristotle, but Maignan soon disputed what seemed false in Aristotle, above all in physics, and preferred Plato.

He mastered the mathematics of his day almost unaided, and his superiors soon put him in charge of novices. In 1636 the general of his order called him to Rome to teach mathematics at Trinita dei Monti. There he spent fourteen years in mathematics and experiments. He published on sundials and perspective. Back at Toulouse in 1650 he became provincial, then gladly returned to study. Louis XIV, who had seen his machines at Toulouse, invited him to Paris in 1669, but Maignan begged to stay in his convent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-father-abram-:
Abram Ryan was a poet-priest of the American South, born in Norfolk in 1839. Ordained just before the Civil War, he served as a Confederate chaplain throughout it. His poem Conquered Banner, sung in Southern homes, made his fame. Its measure, he said, came from a Gregorian hymn.

After the war Ryan ministered in New Orleans and edited a Catholic weekly. He started the Banner of the South in Augusta, then retired to Mobile. In 1880 he gave lectures in several Northern cities to warm and attentive audiences. His poems, patriotic, religious, and miscellaneous, reached dozens of printings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-mag:
Ferdinand Magellan was the first man to undertake the circumnavigation of the world. Born in Portugal about 1480, he learned astronomy and the nautical sciences. After Portuguese service in India, Malacca, and Morocco, he turned to Spain. Charles I backed his westward search for the Spice Islands.

His fleet of five ships sailed from Spain in September 1519 with 234 men. Through the straits that bear his name, he reached the vast Pacific Ocean. He died at Mactan in April 1521 before reaching his Moluccan goal. Only the Victoria returned to Spain, laden with cloves that repaid the voyage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernando-pere:
Fernando Perez de Guzman was a Spanish historian and poet. Born in 1376, he belonged to a family distinguished for rank and letters. His uncle, Lopez de Ayala, served as Grand Chancellor of Castile, historian, and poet. His nephew, the Marquis of Santillana, ranked among the leading authors of Juan II's time.

His Generaciones e Semblanzas paints thirty-six portraits of contemporary personages. It forms the third part of his large Mar de historias. No physical trait escaped his sharp observation of character and station. His prose ranks among the finest examples of character painting in Spanish literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-firmilian:
Firmilian was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia and died about 269. A disciple of Origen with Gregory the Wonder-Worker, he later invited Origen to Cappadocia. He ranked among the most eminent bishops of his day, beside Dionysius and Cyprian. He opposed the antipope Novatian and backed a synod at Antioch against his heresy.

His one surviving writing is a long letter to Cyprian on the baptismal controversy. He argued that heretics outside the Church, lacking the Holy Spirit, cannot give what they lack. The letter attacks Pope Stephen for accepting heretical baptism on the Trinitarian formula alone. It also claims Cappadocia had rebaptized from the beginning, setting tradition against tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-kerna:
Francis Kernan, born in Steuben County, New York, on 14 January 1816 and dead at Utica on 7 September 1892, was a lawyer and statesman of the old school. Son of General William Kernan, an Irish immigrant from County Cavan, he attended Georgetown College from 1833 to 1836. He studied law in Utica under Joshua Spencer and became his partner, winning fame against the leading advocates of the New York bar.

His public service ranged widely. He was school commissioner of Utica, manager of the state hospital, reporter of the Court of Appeals, and member of the constitutional convention of 1867. He was regent of the state university, assemblyman, congressman from 1863 to 1865, and United States senator from 1876 to 1882. He spoke extemporaneously with clearness, fairness, and fidelity to conviction, and his old age was calm, genial, and contented, a model, the entry says, of the Catholic lawyer and statesman.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-moyla:
Francis Moylan, born at Cork in 1739 and dead in 1815, was Bishop of Cork in the penal-law age, when Catholics could not easily be educated at home. Son of a rich merchant, he was sent to Paris for schooling, and though his father wanted him in trade, his vocation was religious. Delicate health barred the Carthusians. After a doctorate in theology at Toulouse he was ordained in 1761, laboured in Paris, then returned to Cork as pastor of St. Finbarr's until he became Bishop of Kerry in 1775.

Transferred to Cork in 1787, he ruled that diocese until his death. He helped found Maynooth College as one of its first trustees and supported the Union. He agreed to the veto in 1799, then regretted being tricked by Pitt and Castlereagh and opposed it when revived in 1814.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-patri:
Francis Patrick Cardinal Moran, born at Leighlinbridge in Ireland on 16 September 1830 and dead at Manly, Sydney, on 16 August 1911. He was the third Archbishop of Sydney and a commanding figure in Australian Catholicism. Orphaned before eleven, the only son of Patrick Moran and Alice Cullen, sister of Cardinal Cullen, he left Ireland in 1842 to study at Rome. His public defence in universal theology won him the doctorate by acclamation, impressing the future Leo XIII among his examiners.

 As coadjutor Bishop of Ossory he ruled a divided diocese with a firm yet benign hand. As Archbishop of Sydney from 1884 he built churches, schools, and institutions, writing widely on history, labour, federation, and the Church, from the Apostolate of St. Patrick to the Discovery of Australia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-tregi:
Francis Tregian, born in Cornwall in 1548 and dead at Lisbon on 25 September 1608, was an English Catholic confessor who suffered twenty-eight years in prison for his faith. Son of Thomas Tregian of Wolveden and Catherine Arundell, he inherited land worth three thousand pounds a year, all confiscated by Elizabeth because he had harboured Blessed Cuthbert Mayne. He had lived at court to help persecuted Catholics, and his biographer says he earned the queen's displeasure by rejecting her improper advances.

Imprisoned at Windsor and in various London prisons, he was freed by James I, who banished him instead. After visiting Douai he withdrew to Madrid, where the King of Spain gave him a pension. He married Mary, daughter of Lord Stourton, and had eighteen children. Seventeen years after his death his body was found uncorrupted, and miracles were reported through his intercession, sealing his memory as a steadfast witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-zur:
Francisco Zurbaran, born at Fuente de Cantos in Estremadura in November 1598 and dead probably at Madrid about 1662. He was a Spanish painter of monks, saints, and still lifes, famed for serenity, strength, and nobility. His peasant parents encouraged his drawing, and as a boy he joined the studio of Juan de las Roelas, becoming a favourite pupil.

The Marquess of Malagon then commissioned the retable of San Pedro in Seville Cathedral, where his powerful, individual manner already shines. For the Mercedarian convent at Seville he painted five or six of twelve scenes of St. Peter Nolasco, founder of the Order of Mercy. Two of them hang in the Prado: the Vision of St. Peter Nolasco and the Apparition of the Crucified to him. His vigorous manner aimed at fidelity of expression, painting drapery, flesh, and shadow with austere truth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gelasius-o-cu:
Gelasius O'Cullenan, a Cistercian abbot of Boyle in Ireland, was hanged as a martyr outside Dublin in November 1580. Born near Assaroe Abbey in Donegal, he was eldest of five brothers, three more abbots and one a bishop. He studied at Salamanca, took his doctorate at the Sorbonne in Paris, and was made abbot of Boyle in Roscommon.

Boyle had been seized and granted to Cusack, sheriff of Meath, yet Irish regulars still named superiors to suppressed houses. O'Cullenan went at once to Ireland and is said to have won his abbey back. Seized at Dublin with Eugene O'Mulkeeran of Holy Trinity, he refused to conform, was tortured, and was hanged with his fellow abbot. Friends saved his body from mutilation, and his clothes passed as relics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-michae:
George Michael Wittman, bishop-elect of Ratisbon, formed over fifteen hundred priests across forty-five seminary years. Born near Pleistein in Bavaria in 1760, he studied with Jesuits and Benedictines at Amberg and at Heidelberg, and was ordained in December 1782. After parish work he became professor and subregent at Ratisbon's seminary in 1788, regent in 1802, and cathedral pastor in 1804.

Wittman became auxiliary bishop in 1829 and vicar-general under Sailer in 1830. Nominated bishop of Ratisbon in July 1832, he died before preconization in March 1833. His zeal, charity, and exemplary life won universal affection, and his monument stands in Ratisbon cathedral. His writings include Catholic Principles on Sacred Scripture and notes on the Pentateuch, plus a New Testament translation made with Feneberg, which he stopped spreading through London's Protestant Bible Society in 1820.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerard-schnee:
Gerard Schneeman, a Jesuit scholar born at Wesel in 1829, edited the voices that shaped Catholic debate after 1870. After three years of law he entered Münster seminary, was ordained subdeacon in 1850, joined the Society in 1851, and was ordained priest in 1856. He taught philosophy at Bonn and Aachen, then church history and canon law at Maria Laach.

His Studies on the Honorius Question of 1864 refuted Döllinger. From 1865 to 1870 he wrote timely dissertations for the Pius IX encyclical and council series that became Voices from Maria Laach. When the Stimmen turned monthly in 1871 he edited it six years. He chiefly promoted the Collection Lacensis of recent councils' acts and decrees, dying at Kerkrade in 1885 while preparing Vatican Council documents for its seventh and final volume. His 1881 work on grace and free will renewed controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-card:
Girolamo Cardan, also called Cardano or Cardanus, was an Italian physician and mathematician born at Pavia in 1501, who died at Rome in 1576. Educated at Pavia and Padua, he lectured on medicine at Milan in 1543 and at Pavia in 1544, then taught at Bologna from 1562. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an eccentric whose fame rests on algebra.

His Ars Magna of 1545 gave the solution of the cubic equation, since named after him, and drew him into a long dispute with Tartaglia. Cardan had obtained the solution from Tartaglia under a promise of strict secrecy. He published it after his pupil Ferrari solved the biquadratic by means of the cubic. His philosophy, leaning toward magic and astrology, holds little weight in history, yet his collected works filled ten volumes at Lyons in 1663.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-godfrey-goodm:
Godfrey Goodman was Anglican Bishop of Gloucester, born at Ruthin in Denbighshire on 28 February 1582-3, who died at Westminster on 19 January 1656. He passed all his public life in the Protestant Church, though his sympathies inclined to the old faith, and late in life, when misfortune and ruin overtook him, he entered its fold. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a court preacher at war with Laud.

Educated at Westminster School and Trinity College, Cambridge, he rose through rectories and prebends. He became Dean of Rochester and Bishop of Gloucester. His leanings drew royal reprimands for court sermons and blame for a crucifix at Windsor. They brought a clash with Laud over the seventeen Articles of 1640, which he refused, then signed after five weeks in prison. Impeached with Laud, he spent four months more in prison before his fortunes collapsed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gordian:
Gordian is the name of three Roman emperors who reigned between A.D. 237 and 244, all of whom met violent deaths. The elder Marcus Antonius Africanus Gordianus, descended from the Gracchi on his father's side and Trajan on his mother's, was chosen emperor in Africa against the usurper Maximin. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a family the Church could welcome after a persecutor.

Father and son reigned only thirty-six days. The son fell in battle to Maximin's lieutenant Capellianus, and the father took his own life in July 237. The grandson, made Caesar at thirteen under Maximus and Balbinus, became sole emperor when the Praetorians massacred them in 238. He married the daughter of his teacher Misitheus, marched against the Persians, and was slain by mutinous soldiers in 244 at Philip's instigation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gran:
Gran, in Hungarian Esztergom and Latin Strigonium, is an archdiocese in Hungary whose archbishop is Primate of Hungary. From the eighth century to the early eleventh, the diocese embraced most of Hungary, though later foundations shrank it. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a see that stayed the most important despite its losses.

Today it covers fourteen counties, with Latin suffragans Neutra, Veszprém, Waitzen, Steinamanger, Stuhlweissenburg, Raab, Fünfkirchen, and Neusohl, plus the Greek Ruthenian dioceses of Eperies and Munkács. It holds three chapters, three vicariates at Gran, Tyrnau, and Budapest, eight archdeaneries, and forty-six deaneries. Its parishes once numbered over a thousand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gratian:
Gratian was a Roman emperor, son of Valentinian I, born at Sirmium in 359, who died at Lyons in 383. Before nine he received the purple robe and diadem as Augustus. On his father's death in 375 he became Emperor of the West, with his infant half-brother Valentinian II associated in the title. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a reign that marks the empire's passage from paganism to Christianity.

He fixed his residence at Trier and routed the Alamanni at Colmar in 378. After Valens fell at Adrianople the same year, he gave the East to Theodosius I. At Ambrose's instance he removed the statue of Victory from the Senate house in 382, abolished pagan pontiffs' privileges and grants, and undid Valens's persecution. A rebellion under Maximus drove him from Paris to Lyons, where he was treacherously slain on 25 August 383.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-ren:
French cardinal Guillaume-René Meignan, born at Chauvigné in 1817, made Scripture study his weapon against Ernest Renan and the critics of his age. Ordained in 1840, he learned from Görres and Döllinger at Munich and Neander and Schelling at Berlin. He took a theology doctorate at the Sapienza in 1846 and took up the Sacred Scripture professorship at the Sorbonne in 1861.

Bishop of Châlons in 1864, of Arras in 1882, and Archbishop of Tours in 1884. He wrote for lay readers on Messianic prophecy, the Gospels, and the prophets from Daniel to John the Baptist. He answered Renan with German rationalist critics themselves. Leo XIII raised him to the cardinalate in December 1892, and he died at Tours in 1896.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gustave-xavie:
Bayonne Jesuit Gustave Xavier Lacroix de Ravignan, born in 1795, gave up a rising legal career for the priesthood and became France's most admired pulpit orator. A king's counsel and deputy attorney-general by 1821, he entered the seminary at Issy in 1822, joined the Jesuits that November, and was ordained in 1828 after teaching dogmatic theology.

His Notre Dame conferences on God, Christ, and the Church made him, in the entry's phrase, virtue preaching truth. His 1844 defence of the Jesuits sold 25,000 copies in a year amid fierce anti-Jesuit campaigns. He preached across France, Rome, Belgium, and London, and advised firm but lawful resistance during the order's partial disbanding. He closed his life in retreats, confessions, and a two-volume study of Clement XIII and Clement XIV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hadrian:
Martyr Hadrian, dead about 306, was honoured at Constantinople as a victim of Diocletian's persecution, though his story reaches us only through legendary Greek and Latin records. An officer in Emperor Galerius's bodyguard, he watched the trial and torment of twenty-two Christians at Nicomedia, declared himself a Christian on the spot, and was thrown into prison with them.

His wife Natalia, secretly a Christian herself, cheered and served the prisoners. The Acts deck the tale with poetic detail before the martyrs' limbs were broken and their bodies given to the flames. Natalia is said to have carried her husband's remains to Constantinople, and his church on the Roman forum, S. Adriano, still stands, with his chief feast on 8 September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-fitzala:
Henry Fitzalan, twelfth Earl of Arundel, was born about 1511, educated in Henry VIII's palace as the king's godson, and governed Calais from 1540 before succeeding to the earldom in 1543. He took Boulogne in 1544 and was rewarded with the lord chamberlainship. He opposed Protector Somerset under Edward VI, and on Edward's death abandoned Lady Jane Grey to proclaim Mary queen, serving her as lord steward on much diplomatic business.

Under Elizabeth, Fitzalan at first kept his offices and was even considered a possible consort for the widowed queen. Disgrace in 1564 and his leadership of the Catholic party drew him toward the scheme of marrying Mary, Queen of Scots, to his son-in-law, the Duke of Norfolk. Cautious enough to survive the northern rebellion of 1569, he was confined after the Ridolfi conspiracy of 1571 and lived out his life in retirement, dying in London in 1580.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-glarean:
Henry Glarean, born Heinrich Loriti at Mollis near Glarus in 1488, was the most distinguished of Swiss humanists, working as poet, philosopher, geographer, mathematician, and musician. Educated at Rottweil and Cologne, he was crowned poet laureate by Maximilian I in 1512, taught at Basle and Paris, and counted Erasmus among his devoted friends. Early sympathy with Luther's writings and friendship with Zwingli gave way to disillusion, and in 1529 he left Basle for Freiburg-im-Breisgau, where he taught until his death in 1563.

Glarean produced editions and commentaries on Livy, Horace, Ovid, Caesar, Sallust, and many other ancient writers. His Dodekachordon of 1547, fruit of twenty years' study of ancient and church music, introduced twelve tones where only eight had been known. As geographer he described Switzerland in verse and wrote a forty-chapter study of mathematical geography, while a manuscript world map of 1510 already named the new continent Terra America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herbert-vaugh:
Herbert Vaughan, cardinal and third Archbishop of Westminster, was born at Gloucester in 1832 into a family that had kept the Catholic faith through persecution. It had suffered fines and imprisonment, and had fought for Charles I and at Culloden. His mother, a convert, prayed daily that her children serve God; of her eight sons, six took priestly orders, three became bishops. Herbert, the eldest, studied at Stonyhurst, Brugelette. Downside, reached Rome in 1851, and was ordained at Lucca in 1854 at twenty-two.

Hoping to mission in Wales, Vaughan instead became vice-president of St. Edmund's College, Ware, where his Oblate ties entangled him in Wiseman's quarrel with his chapter. Disappointment turned him to foreign missions. After begging in the Americas from 1863 and defying Panama's ban on Mass during a smallpox epidemic, he conceived a great missionary college sending missioners abroad. That dream shaped the rest of his life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herman-schaep:
Herman Schaepman, an orator, poet, and statesman born at Tubbergen in 1844, studied at Oldenzaal, Kuilenberg, and Ryzenburg, was ordained at Utrecht, and took his doctorate at Rome. Teaching church history at Ryzenburg from 1870, he worked on De Tyd and founded De Wachter with Nuyens in 1871. His poem De Paus of 1866 was a literary event, and his masterwork Aya Sofia of 1886, joined later poems on Napoleon. His prose, collected as Menschen en Boeken, was incisive, its authorship recognizable at a glance.

Schaepman was long the nation's first orator, from his Park speech at Amsterdam in 1871 and in speeches on Pius IX and Vondel. As the first priest elected to the States-General he fought for Catholic emancipation and formulated an 1883 programme declaring Catholics a political personality demanding liberty. He later built with Kuyper the coalition of Catholics and anti-revolutionists that gave Holland three ministries. Leo XIII made him domestic prelate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-oldman:
Hugh Oldman was bishop of Exeter, born in Lancashire, either at Crumpsall or Oldham, and dead on 25 June 1519. A short Oxford spell preceded his entry to Queen's College, Cambridge. Once ordained, he served as chaplain to the Countess of Richmond and gathered many benefices, including the deanery of Wimborne and the archdeaconry of Exeter, plus prebends at London, Lincoln, and York.

Henry VII honoured him as a layer of his chapel's foundation stone in 1503, and in 1504 a papal bull made him bishop of Exeter. Though not learned himself, he encouraged learning, founding and endowing Manchester Grammar School in 1515. His friend Bishop Foxe of Winchester founded Corpus Christi College, Oxford, for secular clergy, with Oldman's six thousand marks added to the foundation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hyderabad-dec:
Hyderabad-Deccan, also called Bhagnagar, was the capital of the Nizam's dominions; Mohammed Kuli, king of Golconda, founded it in 1589. Its mission was cut from the vicariate of Madras by Pius IX in 1851 and became a diocese in 1886.
