Bounded by the Bay of Bengal, the Godavari, the Bombay frontier, and the Tungabhadra and Kistna, it lies partly in the Nizam's kingdom and partly in British territory.

Of the region's early history, little is known. Documents place Christians at Moodgul under Ibrahim Adil Shah I, and Franciscans arriving in 1502 likely made the first conversions. Christians at Raichur and Chitapur were visited by priests from Goa, and Urban VIII sent Theatines to Bijapur in 1637, founding the vicariate of the Great Mogul under Father Mateo de Castro.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ispahan:
Ispahan, a Catholic Armenian and Latin see, began as Aspandana, once a chief town of Media. Christianity reached it early: a bishop named Aphraat appears in 424, with Abraham in 497, another Abraham in 554, Ahron in 576, and further bishops in 987 and 1111. The town owes its later glory to Shah Abbas I of the Safavid line, who made it his capital late in the sixteenth century.

Abbas drew merchants, artists, artisans, and farmers from all quarters. He raised fine buildings. He stretched the town to about six miles round with nearly 600,000 people. It counted among the finest and richest towns on earth. Julfa, the Armenian quarter he founded, still stood apart from Ispahan proper. The entry moves from an ancient Median town to a Safavid showcase city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-andrew-:
Theologian, editor, and Orientalist James Andrew Corcoran was born at Charleston, South Carolina, on 30 March 1820. He died at Philadelphia on 16 July 1889. At fourteen he was sent to Rome's College of Propaganda. There he made a brilliant course and was ordained priest on 21 December 1842. He was the first Carolina native to receive priestly orders. He stayed a further year in Rome to finish studies and earn a doctorate in sacred theology.

He read Western and Northern European literatures and dialects with ease. He spoke Latin as fluently as his native tongue. He mastered the idiom that marks the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore's text. He was also a profound Semitic scholar, with special love for Syriac. On Bishop England's death in 1842 he was recalled to Charleston. There he taught in the seminary and did parish work. The entry presents an American scholar-priest of rare linguistic range.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-clarenc:
Irish poet James Clarence Mangan was born in Dublin on 1 May 1803. He died there on 20 June 1849. His father James was a grocer, and his mother was Catherine Smith. He attended school in Saul's Court, but while still young he had to work to support his family. For seven years he served as a scrivener's clerk. For three years he earned meagre wages in an attorney's office.

Mitchel accepts Mangan's own story of an unhappy love affair. It infused a bitter and mocking note into his later verses. It even drove him to intemperance that clouded his remaining days. O'Donoghue doubts that story, however. In 1831 Mangan joined the Comet Club and contributed verses and first German translations to its journal. His Dublin University Magazine connection ended because his habits barred regular work. The entry presents a gifted, troubled translator-poet of Young Ireland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-macgeog:
James MacGeoghegan was born at Uisneach, Westmeath, Ireland, in 1702. He died at Paris in 1763. He came from a family long settled in Westmeath and long high among Leinster chiefs. He was related to the MacGeoghegan who heroically defended Dunboy Castle against Carew. He was also related to Connell MacGeoghegan, translator of the Annals of Clonmacnoise. Early in the eighteenth century penal laws barred Catholic education except in Protestant schools.

Young MacGeoghegan therefore went abroad for schooling at the Irish, then Lombard, College in Paris. In due course he was ordained priest. For five years he served as vicar at Possy in the Chartres diocese, attending choir, hearing confessions, and giving sacraments in laudable and edifying manner. In 1734 he was elected one of the Irish College's officials at Paris. The entry presents an exile priest-historian of penal Ireland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-japan:
Japan, called Nihon or Nippon in its own language, meaning Land of the Rising Sun, lies northwest of the Pacific and east of Asia. It consists of six large islands: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, Hokkaido, Taiwan, and southern Karafuto. About six hundred small islands join them, including Sado, Oki, Tsushima, Iki, Awaji, and the Pescadores, Kurile, Bonin, and Okinawa groups. Japan proper excludes Formosa and Karafuto from the collective name.

Its total area amounts to 162,655 square miles. On 31 March 1908 its population stood at 49,092,000, with Formosa adding over three million more. From that geography the entry moves through history, government, peoples, and religions, with extended treatment of Catholic missions from Xavier onward. Readers get a whole empire in one survey, written when Japan's modern rise was still fresh news.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste-Alphonse Lusignan, a French-Canadian writer born in 1843 on the Richelieu and dead in 1893, first aimed at the priesthood, then turned to law and letters. After three years of theology he studied law at Saint-Hyacinthe and Laval, practised briefly, and edited Le Pays, the French-Canadian Liberal organ, from 1865 to 1868.

Lusignan's paper often clashed with church authority over clerical sway in politics. His later fame rested on mastery of French: a digest of reported cases, essays, and criticism that guarded the tongue's purity. Fellow Canadians hailed his grasp of grammar and phrase as unrivalled, and in 1885 he joined the Royal Society of Canada.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-buridan:
Jean Buridan, a fourteenth-century French philosopher born at Béthune late in the thirteenth century. He taught at Paris under William of Ockham's influence and rose to rector of the university in 1327. He also served as procurator of the Picard nation and in 1345 went as envoy to the papal court at Avignon.

Buridan belonged to Ockham's nominalist school, holding fast despite repeated condemnation, and shared its doubt that reason alone can settle the highest questions. His Compendium of Logic developed at length the art of finding a syllogism's middle term, and his commentaries on Aristotle, above all on the Politics, were reprinted for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-pierre-c:
Jean-Pierre Claris de Florian, a French writer born at Florian in 1755 and died at Sceaux in 1794. He lost his parents young, was raised by his grandfather, and at ten was taken to Voltaire's Ferney by an uncle. Sent as page to the duke of Penthièvre in 1768, he gained a patron who guided his reading and bade him write only with reserve and decency.

Florian left the dragoons for letters, joined the French Academy in 1788, and was arrested at Sceaux in 1793, surviving the Terror only briefly after Robespierre's fall. Today he lives by pretty fables for the young, but his age also praised pastoral novels Galatée and Estelle. Critics called him the Boucher and Watteau of letters for grace and delicacy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeanne-louise:
Jeanne-Louise-Henriette Campan, née Genest, was a French educator born in Paris in 1752 and dead at Mantes in 1822. Raised by her father, a head clerk at Foreign Affairs, she met writers like Duclos and Marmontel at home, spoke English and Italian by fifteen. She became reader to Louis XV's daughters.

Married to Campan, she served Marie Antoinette as first lady of the bedchamber from 1770 until June 1792, even asking to share the queen's prison lot. Left poor with a son and a debt-laden husband, she opened a girls' boarding school at Saint-Germain with a nun, counting Hortense de Beauharnais among pupils. Napoleon then made her head of the Ecouen school for officers' daughters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-gratia:
Jerome Gratian, Saint Teresa's spiritual director and the Discalced Carmelites' first provincial, was born at Valladolid in 1545 and died at Brussels in 1614. Son of a secretary to Charles V and Philip II, he studied at Madrid and Alcalá and was ordained in 1569.

Drawn by Teresian nuns, Gratian took the Discalced habit at Pastrana in 1572 and almost at once directed souls and ran convents. As pro-vicar for Andalusia's Calced Carmelites he faced stubborn resistance, yet founded a Discalced house at Seville and approved others for friars and nuns. His closeness to Teresa shaped the reform's early years and its later quarrels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-philip:
Johann Philipp Roothaan, twenty-first General of the Society of Jesus, was born at Amsterdam in 1785 into a family that had moved from Frankfurt and become Catholic. A gifted pupil, he finished the gymnasium before sixteen and studied classics at the athenaeum under Jakob van Lennep. In 1804 he set out for the Jesuit novitiate at Dunaburg in White Russia, where the order still survived.

Gifted with languages, he mastered Polish and French alongside Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, taught at Dunaburg, studied philosophy and theology at Polotsk, and was ordained in 1812. He taught rhetoric through the Franco-Russian War. He welcomed the order's restoration by Pius VII in 1814. After the Jesuits were banished from Russia in 1820, he carried his work into exile in Switzerland. There he taught and joined popular missions before rising to lead the whole society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-cusp:
Johannes Cuspinian, properly Spieshaym, was a humanist scholar and diplomat at the court of Emperor Maximilian. Born at Schweinfurt in 1473, he studied at Leipzig and Vienna, edited Prudentius while still young, lectured on Virgil, Horace, Sallust, and Cicero, and was crowned poet laureate in 1493. He became doctor of medicine, rector of Vienna's university in 1500, and Maximilian's confidential councillor.

As lifelong curator of the university and chief librarian of the imperial library, he shaped Vienna's intellectual life and, with Conrad Celtes, led the Danubian literary society. Maximilian and later Charles V sent him on missions to Hungary, Bohemia, and Poland, where he settled a disputed succession and escorted a royal bride to Cracow. His editions of Florus, Marbodius, and Otto of Freising, and his collecting of manuscripts, made him a notable editor of ancient and medieval texts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-grat:
Johannes Gratian was the twelfth-century monk whose great compilation founded the science of canon law, the Church's system of law. His birthplace was Italy, perhaps Chiusi in Tuscany, and he became a Camaldolese monk and taught at Bologna's monastery of Saints Felix and Nabor. Little else about his life is certain. The entry warns that stories making him a bishop, or a brother of Peter Lombard and Peter Comestor, are medieval inventions.

His work, the Concordance of Discordant Canons, usually called the Decretum Gratiani, gathered Church decrees into an ordered whole. It cannot predate 1139, since it includes decrees of that year's Second Lateran Council. Scholars now favor about 1140 over the older date of 1151. Peter Lombard already used it, and Gratian died before the Third Lateran Council of 1179, honored at Bologna with a monument in St. Petronius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-baptist-:
John Baptist Hogan, better known as Abbe Hogan, was an Irish Sulpician who taught theology in Paris and founded seminaries in America. Born near Ennis in County Clare in 1829, he was brought to France at fifteen by a priest uncle. He mastered French at the Bordeaux seminary while keeping his English and Irish temper, and entered the Sulpicians at Issy, being ordained in 1852.

At twenty-two he took the chair of dogmatic theology at Saint-Sulpice in Paris, later holding moral theology from 1863 to 1884 alongside sacred liturgy for thirteen years. After thirty-two years teaching there, he crossed to America as first president of Boston's new theological seminary in 1884. He then led the graduate seminary at the Catholic University in Washington, before returning to Saint-Sulpice, where he died in 1901.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-brugman:
John Brugman was a renowned Franciscan preacher of the Low Countries and a poet of his day. Born at Kempen near the end of the fourteenth century, he became lector of theology and vicar-provincial. He helped found the Cologne province of the Observant Friars. For twenty years he stood as the region's most illustrious preacher, dying at Nimwegen in 1473.

At his suggestion his friend Denis the Carthusian wrote on Christian doctrine and rules of life, dedicating it to Brugman. He also defended the Brothers of the Common Life in two surviving letters when they faced persecution. His two lives of Saint Lidwina, the first printed at Cologne in 1433, were gathered by the Bollandists. His devout Life of Jesus and poems such as O Ewich is so lanc kept his name among the best poets of the fifteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-cassian:
John Cassian was a monk and ascetic writer who first brought the rules of Eastern monasticism into the West. Born probably in Provence about 360, he visited the holy places of Palestine as a youth with his friend Germanus. He took monastic vows at Bethlehem. He then spent years among the solitaries of the Egyptian desert, collecting the material for his two chief works.

His Institutes and Conferences set out Egyptian monastic practice for Western readers. From Egypt he went to Constantinople, where St. John Chrysostom made him deacon and keeper of his cathedral treasures. After Chrysostom's expulsion he carried the Constantinople clergy's appeal to Pope Innocent I at Rome, where he was likely ordained priest. About 415 he settled at Marseilles and founded two monasteries, one for men above the tomb of St. Victor, shaping Western monastic life until his death about 435.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-colgan:
John Colgan was an Irish Franciscan hagiographer who gathered the lives of Ireland's saints at Louvain. Born in County Donegal early in the seventeenth century, he joined the Franciscans, studied at the Irish college of St. Anthony at Louvain, and left a professor's chair to pursue Irish studies, taking up the great history of Irish saints projected by Hugh Ward.

Ward had sent Michael O'Clery and others to Ireland to collect materials, and Colgan, master of the Irish language, inherited a manuscript collection unmatched in Irish hagiology. His planned six-volume work yielded the Acta Sanctorum Hiberniae in 1645, covering saints of January through March, and the Trias Thaumaturga in 1647, gathering ancient lives of Patrick, Brigid, and Columba. Long the chief source on St. Patrick, it remains indispensable even after later editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-henry-ne:
John Henry Newman was the cardinal, philosopher, and man of letters who led the Oxford Movement into the Catholic Church. Born in London in 1801, eldest of six children of a banker father and a Huguenot mother, he grew up in a modified Calvinism at his mother's knee. He became guide, philosopher, and martyr of the great religious revival at Oxford.

His Apologia, a classic from its completion, remains the chief authority for his early thought and for the movement he led. His immense correspondence shows originality amounting to genius joined to a deep spiritual temper, expressed in language of perfect poise and rhythm. The entry traces a life of energy that might have created sects or churches, from Anglican leader to Catholic cardinal. He died at Edgbaston, Birmingham, in 1890, the most illustrious of English converts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-lanigan:
John Lanigan was an Irish church historian whose Ecclesiastical History of Ireland became a standard work. Born at Cashel in 1758, eldest son of a schoolmaster, his father trained him, as did a private Protestant classical school, since Catholic schools were forbidden. He then went to the Irish College at Rome in 1776 and was ordained after a brilliant course.

On Tamburini's advice he took the chair of church history and Hebrew at Padua, refusing in 1786 to join the Synod of Pistoia. He published a learned biblical introduction at Pavia in 1793. Returning destitute to Ireland after the Napoleonic invasion, he was suspected of Jansenism and failed at Maynooth over a test formula he would not sign. He became assistant librarian of the Royal Dublin Society in 1799, where he labored on his great history of Irish Christianity to the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-o-donova:
John O'Donovan was the Irish scholar who, with Eugene O'Curry, became supreme authority on the Irish language and antiquities. Born in County Kilkenny in 1806, he came to Dublin in 1823 to prepare for Maynooth. Finding no vocation for the priesthood, he turned to Irish, which he had studied since age nine. Employed by Hardiman to transcribe manuscripts, he met Petrie, and their friendship joined Petrie's antiquarian accuracy to O'Donovan's native learning.

Together with Ferguson they destroyed the fanciful theories of Betham and Vallancey. O'Donovan's edition of the Charter of Newry in 1832 showed his method. The government Ordnance Survey gave him his great chance. Sent into the field by Larcom, he wrote the letters on antiquities and traditions now collected in 103 volumes at the Royal Irish Academy, lively with humor and anecdote. He became the mainstay of Ireland's archaeological societies and journals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-o-dugan:
John O'Dugan was a fourteenth-century Irish hereditary historian whose topographical poem maps pre-Norman Ireland. Died at Roscommon in 1372, his family had served for centuries as historians to the O'Kellys of Ui Maine. His chief work is a verse compilation naming the tribes, territories, and chiefs of Ireland before the Normans.

He gives 152 lines to Meath, 354 to Ulster, 328 to Connacht, and only 56 to Leinster, leaving the poem evidently unfinished at his death, when his contemporary O'Huidhrin completed it. No similar work throws more light on ancient Irish names and territories, and Lynch in Cambrensis Eversus called it the best source on Irish families before the English. O'Dugan also wrote mnemonic poems on Ireland's kings and rules for movable feasts, valuable chiefly for their facts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-o-hagan:
John O'Hagan was an Irish lawyer, judge, and man of letters who led the Land Commission. Born at Newry in 1822, he was educated by the Dublin Jesuits and at Trinity College, graduating in 1842. He always advocated Catholic university education, arguing in the Dublin Review that Trinity was no place for Catholics. Called to the bar in 1842, he joined the Munster circuit.

Made Commissioner of National Education in 1861 and Queen's Counsel in 1865, he was chosen by Gladstone after the Land Act as first judicial head of the Irish Land Commission. He was raised to the High Court for the purpose, a tribute to his legal standing and his countrymen's esteem. An earnest Catholic, he wrote the Children's Ballad Rosary and youthful poems for the Nation such as Dear Land. He also made the first English translation of the Song of Roland, which Longfellow praised as admirably well done.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jonathan:
Jonathan is the name of several Old Testament figures, above all Saul's eldest son and David's beloved friend. The entry also notes Jonathan son of Gershom, the young Levite who left Bethlehem and became priest of Micah's idol on Mount Ephraim. He followed the Danites to Laish, where he and his descendants served the stolen idol until the Captivity.

Jonathan son of Saul first appears fighting Philistines beside his father, commanding a thousand men at Gibeah and routing a Philistine garrison. That victory was completed by what seemed miraculous intervention. Ignorant of Saul's rash oath against eating, he tasted wild honey and was saved from death only by the people's intervention. After David's victory over Goliath, a deep and loyal friendship bound them. Jonathan more than once saved David from Saul's envious wrath before falling with his father on Mount Gilboa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-francisc:
José Francisco de Paula Señan was a Spanish Franciscan missionary in California who lived from 1760 to 1823. Born in Barcelona, he joined the Franciscan order in 1774 and reached California in 1787. He served at San Carlos before settling at Mission San Buenaventura in 1798, where he stayed until his death.

Twice chosen presidente, or head, of the California missions, Señan also acted as vicar for the Bishop of Sonora in Upper California. He knew the local Indian languages well, and his mission reports were praised for exact detail and fine handwriting. Fellow friars nicknamed him Padre Calma, since he loved a quiet life and disliked giving orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-autran:
Joseph Autran was a French poet of the nineteenth century, born at Marseilles in 1813 and dead there in 1877. Family losses forced him to earn his living as a teacher in a religious school. An ode on Lamartine's departure for the Holy Land first drew notice, and his sea poems of 1835 and 1852 won praise for vivid description and musical verse.

Autran also wrote an epic on the French conquest of Algiers and a tragedy, La Fille d'Achille, which shared the French Academy's Monthyon prize in 1848. Elected to the Academy itself in 1868, he later went blind. The entry values his pure expression, his love of nature, and his steady religious feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-spillm:
Joseph Spillman was a Swiss Jesuit author beloved for stories for the young. Born at Zug in 1842, he left school for his father's business over weak health, resumed study at Feldkirch at sixteen, and joined the Jesuit novitiate in 1862. Ordained in 1874, he worked on the periodicals Stimmen aus Maria-Laach and Katholische Missionen.

From his youth supplements grew seventy volumes of travel pictures and twenty-one booklets from distant lands, tales prized in many editions and translations. He also wrote a five-volume history of Catholic persecution in England from 1535 to 1681 and seven longer novels in the manner of Scott and Dickens. An eighth novel stayed unfinished at his death in 1905.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kiang-nan:
Kiang-Nan is a vicariate apostolic, a missionary district under a titular bishop, covering the Chinese provinces of Kiang-su and Ngan-hwei. This entry covers a rich and crowded region of over 60,000,000 people, where Jesuit Matteo Ricci first brought Catholic teaching at the end of the sixteenth century.

Ricci's ally, the minister and scholar Paul Siu, baptized at Nanking in 1603, spread the faith from Shanghai, and Jesuits soon built churches at Soochow, Nanking, and Yangchow. A vicariate was set up in 1660, and persecution from 1664 to 1671 sent twenty Jesuits into exile at Macao, until Father Verbiest won their release. In 1690 Alexander VIII raised the Diocese of Nanking, placed under the Archbishop of Goa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-koran:
The Koran is the sacred book of the Muslims, held as God's revelation and, with the Hadith traditions, the ground of Islam in dogma, law, worship, ethics, and daily conduct. Its name, from Arabic qara'a, to read or recite, means the Reading, the Book above all books.

It holds 114 suras, or chapters, from near Genesis length to two or three sentences, smaller than the New Testament, with no chronological or logical order. Contents mix dogma, legend, history, law, prayer, threats, liturgy, and visions of heaven, hell, judgment, and resurrection. The article follows Sir William Muir's chronology through the Meccan periods, from early rhapsodies to preaching, opposition, and the growing conflict with the Koreish tribe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laban:
Laban, son of Bathuel the Syrian and brother of Rebecca, is Jacob's uncle and father-in-law in Genesis. His home stood at Haran, the city of Nahor in Syrian Mesopotamia, where Nahor stayed when Abraham and Lot moved to Canaan.

Laban first appears welcoming Abraham's servant and consenting to Rebecca's marriage to Isaac. Jacob's story then intertwines with his: welcomed to Haran, Jacob agreed to work seven years for Rachel, Laban's younger daughter, but at the feast received elder Leah instead. After Jacob's protest, Laban gave Rachel too, for seven more years of service. Kept on again for profit, Jacob at last outwitted his uncle's terms, and father, sons, and nephew parted in tension.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-llancarvan:
Llancarvan, in Glamorganshire, Wales, was an early college and monastery whose founding date is disputed. Welsh writers tie it to Germanus's visit to Britain in 447, with Dubric as first head and Cadoc after him.

Yet the Life of Germanus, written about fifty years after his death, says nothing of a school he founded in Britain or of his presence in Wales. Lives of Cadoc instead credit Cadoc himself, which would push the founding a century later. Those lives mix up two or three saints of one name, so the entry leaves the date open, noting abbots as witnesses from the later sixth century onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-de-sabr:
Louis de Sabran was an English Jesuit, born in Paris in 1652 and dead at Rome in 1732. His father served the French embassy in London, his mother was English, and Louis trained at St. Omer before joining the English Jesuits.

He became a royal chaplain to James II in 1685, preached widely, and disputed with Dean Sherlock and Edward Gee. Revolution in 1688 sent him to Portsmouth with the infant Prince of Wales, then through mob seizures and escapes to France. Later he led the Neapolitan Jesuits, headed the Liege seminary against Jansenist attack, served as provincial, and ended as spiritual director at the English College in Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucas-alaman:
Lucas Alaman was a Mexican statesman and historian, born at Guanajuato in 1792 and dead at Mexico City in 1853. Of Spanish parents, he studied in Mexico City, travelled to Spain and France in 1814, and returned to America in 1815.

Secretary of State in 1824, this moderate republican hid a full year in 1834 from extremist foes. After 1836 he gave himself to history until Santa Anna recalled him as Secretary of State in 1851. His Disertaciones of 1844 and his History of Mexico of 1849, tracing independence from 1808 to his own day, remain standard works, save for outdated views of early Indian life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maine-de-bira:
Maine de Biran was a French philosopher born near Bergerac in 1766. He died at Paris in 1824. After schooling at Perigueux and a short army career, he entered politics. He sat in the Council of Five Hundred in 1797. Royalist leanings drew the Directory's hostility, and he withdrew to Grateloup.

There he turned to philosophy. He won an Institut prize for his essay on habit in 1802. Later works in 1805, 1807, and 1811 broke with the ideologists. His thought moved in three stages. Sensation ruled up to 1804, following Condillac. Will ruled from 1804 to 1818, as effort meeting resistance taught the self to tell ego from non-ego. Religion ruled after 1818, adding love and union with God to representation and volition. Cousin ranked him the greatest French metaphysician since Malebranche, though fame came only after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-man:
Man, in the School definition, is a rational animal, a single substance formed when a human soul shapes matter. This long philosophical entry asks three things in turn. What is man's nature, where did he come from, and toward what end does he move? Scripture, theology, and philosophy each get a hearing.

On nature, the entry defends soul and body as one person against Descartes, who split them in the sixteenth century and strained the unity of consciousness. It rejects metempsychosis, argues for bodily resurrection, and treats the soul's direct creation as a corollary. On origin, revelation and scholastic reason agree in the main. On ends, man's nature tends toward its natural goal, while a further, supernatural end crowns it in fact. Grand theories of limitless human progress are weighed and found wanting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maphrian:
Maphrian was a Syriac title meaning one who fructifies, a consecrator. It named the prelate second only to the patriarch among Jacobite Syrians. The dignity reaches at least to the seventh century, perhaps to the late sixth. Its roots lie in Persia's church struggles, when the school at Edessa closed under Nonnus and then Cyrus, and Nestorianism triumphed under the Sassanids.

Persian Monophysites fled into exile, and Tagrit alone held out as their mission centre in the early sixth century. James Baradaeus ordained a bishop for the Persians, Ahudemmeh, and the office grew from there. Persian armies invading Roman lands brought home crowds of captives, swelling the flock. Relations between maphrian and Jacobite Patriarch of Antioch, despite several schisms, stayed largely harmonious. Assemani and Bar Hebraeus supply the chief sources for the office and its holders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcian:
Marcian was Roman Emperor at Constantinople, born in Thrace about 390 and dead in January 457. He rose as a soldier, poor at first, reaching the capital with only borrowed gold. He served under Ardaburius and his son Aspar, winning note against Persians and Huns. Aspar, a foreign Arian kingmaker, could not take the throne himself and raised Marcian instead.

Pulcheria, sister of Theodosius II, had long steered the state. On her brother's death she was chosen empress, then made a nominal marriage with Marcian to firm her place. He cut court and treasury costs, scrapped a hated property tax, eased the crushing praetorship burden, and refused Attila the tribute Theodosius had paid. His chief act was the Council of Chalcedon in 451, where some 600 bishops met at St Euphemia's and Marcian spoke at the sixth session. Attila died in 453, Pulcheria too, and Marcian followed four years later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-margaret-hall:
Margaret Hallahan founded the Dominican Congregation of St Catherine of Siena, born in London on 23 January 1803 and dead on 10 May 1868. Her parents were poor Irish Catholics who died when she was nine. She spent two years in a Somers Town orphanage, then went into service at eleven and stayed in it nearly thirty years.

In 1826 she followed her employers to Bruges and tried a week as lay sister with English Augustinian nuns, convinced God meant her for other work. She became a Dominican tertiary in 1842 and worked at Coventry under Dr Ullathorne among factory girls. She framed constitutions from first and second order rules, since third order rules fit life in the world, not community life. First professions came in 1845 and papal approval in 1851. Stone in Staffordshire became mother house in 1852, with a church and a hospital for incurables, plus houses at Stoke, Bow, and Torquay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-becan:
Martin Becan, born Verbreck or van der Breck, was a controversialist, born at Hilvarenbeck in Brabant in 1563 and dead at Vienna in 1624. He joined the Jesuits in 1583, taught theology twenty-two years at Wurzburg, Mainz, and Vienna, and served as Emperor Ferdinand II's confessor from 1620 to his death. 

His writings aimed chiefly at Calvin, Luther, and Anabaptists. His Manuale Controversarium of 1623, on predestination, free will, the Eucharist, and church infallibility, ran through several editions. His four-volume Summa Theologiae Scholasticae of 1612 largely condensed Suarez's commentary on St Thomas. The Index condemned his Controversia Anglicana in January 1613 until corrected, less for its exaggerations than to stop Paris theology faculty condemning it with anti-papal declarations. Corrected, it appeared dedicated to Paul V. His 1608 Aphorismi, drawn from Calvinist books, words, and deeds, sparked a long dispute over whether one aphorism quoted Calvin or drew a logical conclusion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-juliana-:
Mary Juliana Hardman, known in religion as Sister Mary, was born 26 April 1813 and died 24 March 1884. Daughter of John Hardman senior, a rich Birmingham manufacturer, and Lydia Waring, she came from a staunch old Catholic family generous to the Church. She was schooled at Caverswall's Benedictine convent, and at nineteen her father founded Handsworth's Our Lady of Mercy convent at a cost over five thousand pounds.

In 1840 she and three friends offered themselves to Bishop Walsh to form a new community. By his advice they made novitiate at Dublin under Mother McAuley, foundress of the Sisters of Mercy. Professed 19 August 1841, they were received at Handsworth by Bishop, later Cardinal, Wiseman, and Sister Mary Juliana became first prioress, holding office off and on for thirty-five years. Deeds not words was her motto.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximilian:
Maximilian is the name of several martyrs, and this entry treats three of them. Maximilian of Antioch, a soldier martyred there in January 353 with his fellow standard-bearer Bonosus, refused to strip the chrismon, the monogram of Christ, from the standard at Julian the Apostate's order. Count Julian had them tortured and beheaded, though the martyrdom dates in the calendars, 21 August and 21 September, both clash with the Acts.

Maximilian of Celeia, whose thirteenth-century Acts are unreliable, is said to have journeyed to Rome, preached in Noricum, become Archbishop of Laureacum, and died under Numerianus. What stands sure is that he preached in Noricum in the late third century, founded the church of Lorch, and was martyred. His cult reaches back at least to the eighth century, when St. Rupert built him a church at Bischofshofen and moved his relics there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metropolitan:
Metropolitan, in church language, refers to whatever concerns the metropolis, the chief city or see of an ecclesiastical province: a metropolitan church, chapter, official, and so on. The word alone means the bishop of the metropolitan see, now usually styled archbishop. The whole body of rights and duties canon law gives the metropolitan, not for his own diocese but for his suffragans and province, is called the metropoliticum.

Metropolitans' real power over their provinces has slowly shrunk across the centuries, and they now wield even less than Trent allowed them. The metropolitan's jurisdiction over suffragan dioceses is ordinary, set by law, but mediate and limited to canon law's objects. Since Trent his rights have narrowed to the following: he calls and chairs the provincial council, which all suffragans must attend, saving lawful excuse, and which must meet regularly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-augus:
Michael Augustine Corrigan, third Archbishop of New York, was born at Newark, New Jersey, on 13 August 1839 and died at New York on 5 May 1900. After graduating at Mt. St. Mary's College, Emmittsburg, in 1859, he entered Rome's College of the Propaganda, and was among the twelve students with whom the North American College opened there on 8 December 1859. 

Returning to his native diocese in September 1864, he served in turn as professor of dogmatic theology and Scripture, vice-president and president of Seton Hall College and Seminary. He was vicar-general until 1873. On 4 May that year he was consecrated Bishop of Newark. His seven years there were marked by tireless, successful efforts. He brought the diocese's spiritual and temporal affairs into strict accord with the plenary council of the American Church held just before his accession. As Cardinal McCloskey's health failed, Corrigan was named coadjutor in 1880 and succeeded in New York in 1885.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-corco:
Michael Corcoran, a soldier born at Carrowkeel, County Sligo, Ireland, on 21 September 1827, died at Fairfax Court House, Virginia, on 22 December 1863. His father was an army pensioner, and Corcoran joined the Royal Irish Constabulary at nineteen. He gave it up after three years and sailed for New York in August 1849.

He signed on as a private with the Sixty-Ninth Regiment of the State Militia, a body of Catholics of Irish birth or descent. He climbed rank by rank until chosen colonel on 25 August 1859. The next year brought the Prince of Wales, later Edward VII, to New York, and at his parade Colonel Corcoran would not order the Sixty-Ninth to march. The trial stirred the country, his Irish countrymen backing his course, and the case was still open when the Civil War broke out. Proceedings were dropped at once, and the Sixty-Ninth marched on 23 April 1861 to defend the Union.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-egan:
Michael Egan, first bishop of Philadelphia, was born in Ireland, most probably in Galway, in 1761 and died at Philadelphia on 22 July 1814. In his twenty-sixth year he became guardian of St. Isidore's, the Irish Franciscans' house at Rome, holding the post three years before transfer to Ireland. 

Though lacking the constitution that pioneer age's pastoral duties demanded, and often sick, Father Egan's priestly zeal and pulpit eloquence won universal praise. In April 1803 Bishop Carroll named him a pastor of St. Mary's in Philadelphia. On 8 April 1808 Pius VII raised the city to an episcopal see, with Egan as first bishop. Archbishop Carroll praised him to Rome as a man near fifty, gifted with all episcopal qualities except robust health, greater experience, and firmer temper. He was a learned, modest, humble priest who kept his Order's spirit in all his conduct.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-john-:
Michael John Brenan, an ecclesiastical historian born in Kilkenny, Ireland, in 1780, died at Dublin in February 1847. Son of a stonemason, he won swift fame as a preacher after ordination, but vanity and pride clashed him with his bishop, and he was suspended. He then left the Church, became a Protestant, and was billed to preach at St. George's Church, Dublin, under the Priests' Protection Society.

 Resolved to make public reparation, he climbed the pulpit of St. George's on the Sunday in 1809 when he was billed to open his campaign against the Church. He crossed himself with deep reverence and, to his hearers' relief, lifted the Bible and declared, This is the Word of God. Pausing briefly, he went on with slow gravity: I swear by all it holds that every word I have spoken against the Catholic Church is false. At once he left the building.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michigan:
Michigan, a state of the American Union, is bounded on the north by Lake Superior, on the east by Canada, Lake Huron, and Lake St. Clair, on the south by Ohio and Indiana, and on the west by Lake Michigan and Wisconsin. It covers 58,915 square miles and consists of two peninsulas divided by the Strait of Mackinac. The Lower Peninsula holds rich farmland, including a thirty-mile Fruit Belt along Lake Michigan, while the Upper Peninsula, mountainous and rocky, yields iron and copper.

The 1904 state census counted 2,530,016 people. French pioneers came first, aided by Jesuits Allouez and Marquette, and Detroit was settled by Cadillac in 1701. Michigan passed from Quebec's jurisdiction to Baltimore in 1789, then to Bardstown and Cincinnati. Its Catholic population, largely Irish with Germans, Poles, and French Canadians, numbered 489,451.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michoacan:
Michoacan, a Mexican archdiocese, was erected as a diocese in 1536 by Paul III at Emperor Charles V's instance, its bounds matching the ancient Kingdom of Michoacan. In 1863 it became an archdiocese, with Leon, Queretaro, and Zamora as suffragans, its territory greatly reduced at the same time. About a million people lived within it, chiefly in Morelia, Zitacuaro, Maravatio, Patzcuaro, Puruandiro, and Piedad.

Its first bishop, the Spaniard Vasco de Quiroga (1538-65), ranked among Mexico's greatest missionaries to the native peoples. Later bishops famed for learning and virtue included Ramirez del Prado, Sanchez de Tagle, who founded the diocesan seminary in 1770, and Fray Antonio de San Miguel, builder of Morelia's great aqueduct. Only two bishops of Michoacan, Portugal and Munguia, were natives of Mexico.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-milan:
Milan, in Lombardy in northern Italy, stands on the Olona River. Its three canals, the Naviglio Grande, the Naviglio Martesana, and the Naviglio di Pavia, carry the commerce of this great industrial centre, called the moral capital of Italy. Its soil is fertile, with extensive cattle raising and manufacturing through the province. The name probably comes from the Celtic words meaning in the middle of the plain.

Founded in 396 B.C. by the Insubres on the site of ruined Melpum, Milan became the chief centre of the Cisalpine Gauls. Its church claims St. Anathalon, a disciple of Barnabas, as first bishop, though a diocese can hardly predate 200. Martyrs suffered there under Diocletian, and its medieval archbishops, Ansperto and Ariberto among them, wielded power rivalling counts and kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montauban:
Montauban, a suffragan of Toulouse covering the whole department of Tarn-et-Garonne, grew from a Benedictine abbey founded in 820 as Montauriol under Saint Martin's patronage. Count Alphonse Jourdan of Toulouse took abbey lands above the Tarn in 1144 and founded the city there, settling it with abbey folk and serfs after an agreement in 1149.

Despite suffering in the Albigensian wars the town grew fast, and John XXII made it a bishopric in 1317 with Bertrand de Puy, abbot of Montauriol, as its first bishop. Later bishops included Cardinal Georges d'Amboise, minister of Louis XII. Suppressed in 1802 and split among Toulouse, Agen and Cahors, it returned by the concordat of 1817 and was filled again in 1824.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-narcisco-dura:
Narcisco Duran, born 16 December 1776 at Castellon de Ampurias in Catalonia, Spain, died 1 June 1846. He entered the Franciscan Order at Gerona on 3 May 1792, volunteered for the Indian missions, joined the Missionary College of San Fernando in Mexico City, and came to California in 1806. He was posted to Mission San Jose, working there among the Indians until April 1833, then withdrew to Mission Santa Barbara.

As early as 1817 Father Sarria recommended Duran for higher office, and Father Payeras did the same in 1820. Late in 1824 the College of San Fernando elected him presidente of the missions, a post he held with one break until 1838, and again from 1844 until his death. From 1837 to 1843 he was also comisario prefecto of the Fernandinos. During secularisation and sale of the missions he fought the pillagers step by step, though in vain, and his letters to the government are masterpieces of close reasoning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nathan:
Nathan, meaning God-given, is the name of several Old Testament Israelites, chief among them the prophet who succeeded Samuel in David's and Solomon's times. His origin is not given. He first appears when David plans a house for the Lord. Nathan assures the king of divine support and an everlasting kingdom, yet dissuades him from building the temple, an honour reserved for his son.

Nathan later reproaches David for adultery and murder, after the parable of the poor man's ewe lamb, with the words Thou art the man. He declares the Lord's anger and punishments, yet, on David's repentance, pronounces his sin forgiven. Nathan next secures Solomon's succession against Adonijah's attempt, backed by Joab and Abiathar, and the entry follows the prophet through David's court, his writings, and the other Nathans of Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-card:
Nicholas Wiseman, Cardinal and first Archbishop of Westminster, was born at Seville on 2 August 1802 and died in London on 15 February 1865. Younger son of James Wiseman, an Irish-family merchant resident in Seville, by his second wife Xaviera Strange, he was taken to Ireland after his father's 1805 death. After two years at Waterford school, he entered Ushaw College, Durham, where historian John Lingard, his lifelong friend, was vice-president.

At Ushaw he resolved on priesthood, and in 1818 he joined the first batch of students for Rome's revived English College. Pius VII received him in audience with five fellow students. Six years of hard, regular study followed, with distinction in natural sciences and dogmatic and scholastic theology. In July 1824 he took his Doctor of Divinity degree after a public disputation before learned men including a future pope, and was ordained priest on 19 March 1825.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-of-g:
Nicholas of Gorran, or Gorrain, was a medieval preacher and scriptural commentator, born in 1232 at Gorron, France, and dead about 1295. He joined the Dominican Order at his native town's convent and grew into one of its most renowned former pupils. His talents won him special schooling, and he was sent to Paris's famous Saint James convent, where he later held the prior's office for several terms.

His devout life and shrewd judgment caught the eye of Philip IV of France, whom he served as both confessor and adviser. In most ecclesiastical studies he did not notably excel, but in preaching and Scripture interpretation no contemporary surpassed him. His scriptural writings cover every Old and New Testament book with more than ordinary merit, and Paris's doctors esteemed them so highly they called him excellens postulator. His Pauline commentary is remarkably well done, and his Apocalypse gloss won the highest commendation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oran:
Oran, a diocese in Algeria separated from Algiers in 1866, carries a Christian past older than Islam in North Africa. Early Mauretania counted 123 dioceses, Tlemcen's Victor sat at Carthage in 411, and Honoratus suffered exile in 484 for denying Arianism.

Arabs destroyed many churches after 708, yet Christians and churches remained at Tlemcen in 963. Spain took Oran in 1509 and ruled until 1792, France occupied it in 1830, and the pilgrimage to Notre-Dame du Salut at Santa Cruz began in 1849. Christian troops served Moorish kings of Tlemcen until 1254, by the entry’s account. Spaniards ruled Oran to 1708, then again from 1732 to 1792, before French occupation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-the-:
The Order of the Swan, a pious confraternity indulgenced by the pope, arose in Brandenburg in 1440 to honor the Virgin. Elector Frederick led thirty gentlemen and seven ladies who wore a medal of Mary with a swan attached, its meaning read several ways.

By 1464 the confraternity counted about 330 members, with branches in Ansbach and Teutonic Prussia, but Protestant suppression of Marian devotion ended its reason for being. Frederick William IV dreamed of reviving it in 1843, yet the plan stayed a project. Elector Frederick headed thirty gentlemen and seven ladies in the original confraternity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-organ:
The organ, from Greek organon for instrument, sounds through sets of pipes, each giving one tone, blown and played by mechanism. Its ancestor is Pan's syrinx, pipes of differing length tied in a row, and Ctesibius of Alexandria about 300 BC added pumps and a wind reservoir that kept air at steady pressure.

Vitruvius and Heron describe that ancient organ as a marvel unmatched until the eighteenth century. The entry follows the instrument from Byzantine and medieval churches through stops, keyboards, and pedals to the great Romantic organs and their builders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palawan: Palawan is a Prefecture Apostolic in the Philippine Islands, covering Palawan, Cuyo, Culion, Twahig, and the Calamian Islands. It was cut from the Diocese of Jaro on 11 April 1910 and entrusted to the Augustinians. Its first prefect apostolic is Fernando Hermand y d'Arenas, who lives at Puerto Princesa. Jesuits and Sisters of Saint Paul keep houses on Culion, where a government-run leper settlement stands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-john-:
Patrick John Ryan was sixth Bishop and second Archbishop of Philadelphia, born at Thurles in County Tipperary on 20 February 1831 and dead at Philadelphia on 11 February 1911. Schooled by Thurles Christian Brothers, he entered Naughton's Dublin school at twelve for classical studies. In 1844, still a pupil, he headed a student delegation addressing Daniel O'Connell in Richmond prison, and the Liberator praised the young speaker and foretold a bright future.

Adopted for Saint Louis by Archbishop Kenrick in 1847, he studied at Carlow, finished in 1852, and, too young for priesthood, sailed with Patrick Feehan to teach at Carondelet seminary. Kenrick let the young deacon preach often in the cathedral, where his eloquence drew crowds of all denominations. Later pages follow his Saint Louis years, his Philadelphia archbishopric, and his work for schools, churches, and clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrizius-wit:
Patrizius Wittman was a Catholic journalist born at Ellwangen in Wuerttemberg on 4 January 1818 and dead at Munich on 3 October 1883. Son of stonemason Johann Wittmann, he won free scholarships at Ehingen and Tuebingen's Wilhelmsstift through school standing. At Tuebingen from 1838 to 1840 he studied theology and philosophy, won three prizes, and passed a brilliant examination.

Strict orthodoxy clashed with prevailing liberal currents, and he was dismissed from the Wilhelmsstift. Through Riffel of Giessen he joined Augsburg's Sion journal under Herbst, and Doellinger prompted his Glory of the Church in Her Missions Since the Schism of 1841, warmly received. Taking his philosophy doctorate in 1841, he settled at Augsburg, edited Sion as chief, grew its circulation, and laboured there over thirty years after marrying the wealthy widow Caroline Munding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perpignan:
Perpignan was a French diocese formed from the ancient see of Elne, French Cerdagne, and fragments of Alet and Narbonne. Joined to Carcassonne in 1802, it gained its own bishop again under the Concordat of 1817, seated at Perpignan, where Elne's bishops had lived since 1601. Elne itself had shifted allegiance often, from Narbonne to Rome to Tarragona and back.

Its bishops run from Dominus, named in 571, through Renaissance cardinals like Sforza, Borgia, and Doria to Olympe Gerbet in the nineteenth century. The entry admires Elne's eleventh-century cathedral and cloister, notes Roussillon's late medieval slave deeds under Roman law, and honours the diocese's martyrs: Vincent of Collioure and the virgins Eulalia and Julia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-john-su:
Peter John Sullivan was an Irish-born American soldier, lawyer, and diplomat, born at Cork in 1821. His parents carried him to Philadelphia at two, and he studied at the University of Pennsylvania. He won a major's commission for merit in the Mexican War, then served as an official stenographer of the United States Senate. In 1848 he settled at Cincinnati and joined the bar.

There he stood out as an opponent of the Know-Nothing movement. In the Civil War he helped raise several volunteer regiments and led the 48th Ohio as colonel, winning a brevet brigadier-generalship in March 1865. Soon after he became United States minister to Colombia, holding the post until 1869, then returned to his Cincinnati law practice. He died there in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-henry-:
Philip Henry Sheridan was a Union general of the Civil War, born at Albany in 1831. His family joined Ohio's Catholic pioneers at Somerset, and he entered West Point in 1848, graduating in 1853. Service in Texas and Oregon against Indian troubles won him credit before the war made him Halleck's chief quartermaster, then colonel of the Second Michigan Cavalry in May 1862. Brigadier-general followed in July.

Commanding the Army of the Potomac's cavalry from April 1864, he became one of Grant's chief reliances against Lee in Virginia. His famous ride from Winchester to Cedar Creek on 19 October 1864 turned a Union retreat into complete victory over Early, and Grant called him one of the ablest of generals. A regular major-generalship followed that November, and his 1865 raids cut Lee's supply lines. He died at Nonquitt in 1888.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-the-ar:
Philip the Arabian was Roman emperor from 244 to 249, son of an Arab sheikh, born at Bosra. He rose through the army to high office, and when Gordian III's able father-in-law Timesitheus died in 243, the boy emperor named Philip his successor. By starving the troops of provisions Philip turned them against Gordian, had him secretly executed, then deified him and raised his monument to fool the Senate.

He gave up Timesitheus's Persian gains, pulled troops from Dacia, Raetia, and Britain to guard Italy, and beat the Carpi on the Danube, earning the name Carpicus Maximus on coins. Kin given high office abused it, his seven-year-old son became co-ruler, and Rome's thousandth birthday was celebrated in April 248. Rival emperors rose, Decius marched on Italy, and Philip and his son were killed near Verona in 249.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-politian:
Politian, born Angelo Ambrosini at Montepulciano in 1454, was an Italian humanist and master of Greek and Latin letters. He went to Florence at ten and studied under Landino, Argyropoulos, Callistus, and Ficino. In 1477 he became tutor to the children of Lorenzo the Magnificent and joined Lorenzo's academy with Ficino, Pico della Mirandola, and Barbarus.

From 1480 he taught Greek and Latin literature at Florence, counting Grocyn, Linacre, and Reuchlin among his pupils. At eighteen he translated five books of the Iliad and won the name Homericus juvenis. His Miscellanea of 1489 treated scholarly puzzles from Greek breathings to the spelling of Virgil, and his care for manuscripts helped fix the texts of many Latin authors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-popayan:
Popayán is a Colombian archdiocese covering the whole department of Cauca and parts of Nariño and Valle. Since the decree of July 1910 its bounds run from the Diocese of Cali in the north and west to Pasto in the south and Garzón in the east. The diocese was established by Paul III in September 1546, though the see was not erected until September 1547.

Its first bishop, Juan del Valle, performed the erection ceremony by apostolic delegation at Aranda del Duero in Spain. Popayán served as suffragan to Lima until 1573, then to Bogotá, and became an archdiocese in June 1900 with Pasto, Garzón, and Cali as suffragans. Among its bishops, Agustín de la Coruña suffered banishment defending the Indians, and Carlos Bermúdez restored the seminary while defending church rights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-joan:
Pope Joan names a fabled woman pope, first heard of around the middle of the thirteenth century. Jean de Mailly, a Dominican chronicler, tells the earliest version, which Etienne de Bourbon took into his Seven Gifts of the Holy Ghost. There the supposed popess belongs about 1100, still without a name.

The tale has a gifted woman donning men's dress, rising to Curia notary, then cardinal, then pope. Out riding one day, she bore a son, whereupon the crowd tied her to a horse's tail, dragged her through the streets, stoned her, and buried her on the spot. Martin of Troppau's chronicle gives a second version, setting her after Leo IV as John of Mainz, with a reign of two years, seven months, and four days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-fa:
Fabian was pope from 236 to 250. Eusebius tells the strange story of his election. After Anterus died, Fabian had come to Rome from his farm. While illustrious names were weighed, a dove landed on his head. The crowd recalled the Spirit descending on the Saviour and chose him with joyous unanimity.

His fourteen years brought a lull in persecution. Little else is known. The Liber Pontificalis says he split Rome into seven districts, each under a deacon, and set seven subdeacons to gather martyrs' trial records. Tradition credits him with the four minor orders and work in the catacombs. He moved Pope Pontianus's body from Sardinia to the Catacomb of Callistus. He is also said to have sent seven bishops as missionaries to Gaul in 245, among them Denys of Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-ponti:
Pontian was made pope on 21 July 230 and reigned until 235. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Roman, son of Calpurnius. With him begins the brief third-century chronicle of Roman bishops that the Liberian list later used, giving more exact data. The Hippolytus schism ran through his reign, but toward its end the schismatics reconciled with Rome's bishop.

After Alexandria condemned Origen in 231 or 232, a Roman synod under Pontian concurred. In 235 Maximinus the Thracian opened a persecution aimed at church heads. Pontian and Hippolytus were banished to unhealthy Sardinia. To allow a new election, Pontian resigned on 28 September 235, and Anteros succeeded him. Hippolytus, banished with him, soon reconciled with Rome, ending his schism. How long Pontian endured Sardinia's mines is unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-vital:
Vitalian reigned from 657 to 672 and died on 27 January 672. Nothing is known of his life before the papacy. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a native of Segni, son of Anastasius. After Eugene I died in June 657, Vitalian was elected and enthroned on 30 July. Like his predecessor, he pursued friendly ties with Constantinople and an end to the Monothelite controversy.

He sent letters announcing his elevation to Constans II and Patriarch Peter, who leaned to Monothelitism. The emperor confirmed Rome's privileges and sent St Peter a gold-covered Gospel codex set with gems. Peter answered vaguely, seeming to agree, and intercourse resumed on that mutual reserve. Vitalian's name entered Byzantium's diptychs. In England he backed Rome's Easter and tonsure at Whitby, where Oswy chose Roman practice. After his death, the Monothelite patriarch Theodore struck his name from the diptychs, and the Sixth Council of 681 restored it when Monothelitism was suppressed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prudentius-ma:
Prudentius Maran, learned Benedictine of the Maurist congregation, was born at Sézanne in the Marne on 14 October 1683. He died at Paris on 2 April 1762. After schooling in the humanities at Paris, he took the Benedictine habit at Saint Faron near Meaux in January 1703. He went on studying at Saint Denis. Sent to Saint Germain-des-Prés, he worked with his confrère Touttée on an edition of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem.

Trouble came in 1734, when Cardinal Bissy had him removed from Saint Germain-des-Prés. Bissy suspected Maran of holding his brethren back from accepting the Bull Unigenitus. After a year at Orbais and a stay at Saint Martin de Pontoise, he moved in 1737 to Blancs-Manteaux. There he spent the rest of his life. His wide knowledge of theology and the Church Fathers marks the scholarly works listed at the entry's close.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-publican:
In the Gospels, a publican is a member or servant of the Roman companies that farmed the taxes. This encyclopedia entry traces the word from the publicanus of the Vulgate. From republican times Rome spared itself the trouble of gathering provincial taxes directly. It auctioned each province's taxes in a lump sum, and the highest bidder won the right to wring that sum from the province. The system invited rapacious exactions, and abuses were often intolerable.

Jews who profited by serving foreign rulers in this way drew their countrymen's execration, sharpened by hatred of Roman supremacy. In Gospel stories publicans appear as a class habitually coupled with sinners, the very picture of collaboration. Yet the twelve apostles include Levi, also called Matthew the Publican. Maas, Dietrich and Thibault supply the entry's sources on the tax companies and Roman customs houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-publius-aeliu:
Publius Aelius Hadrian, Emperor of the Romans, was born at Rome on 24 January 76 and died on 10 July 138. He reigned from 118 to 138, having married Julia Sabina, his cousin and ward and Trajan's grand-niece. He gave up Armenia, Mesopotamia and Assyria, lands his predecessor had hoped to hold after conquering the Parthians, and bent his efforts to developing the Province of Arabia.

Favours to the Senate, including the remission of fifteen years of tax arrears, strengthened his standing, and imperial power under him reached heights never seen before. A conspiracy by distinguished officers on a campaign in Moesia was crushed, its four ringleaders executed. Later pages follow his travels. They tell of his favourite Antinous, drowned in the Nile in 130 and then deified. They also tell of the Jewish revolt of 132, after he planted the colony Aelia Capitolina on Jerusalem's ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-verst:
Richard Verstegan, born Rowlands, was a Catholic publisher and antiquary who worked from exile in Antwerp. Born in London about 1548 to a family from Guelderland, he entered Christ Church, Oxford, in 1565 under the name Rowlands. As a Catholic he could not take a degree, so he returned to Antwerp and resumed his family name.

His first major book, a 1583 illustrated account of Catholic martyrdoms in England, was seized and destroyed in France after the English ambassador called it a libel on Elizabeth. Arrested and nearly extradited, he was freed through Cardinal Allen and the papal nuncio. From Antwerp he issued Catholic devotional manuals and primers, acted as a correspondence agent for Allen and the Jesuits, and wrote political tracts. His later antiquarian work, A Restitution of Decayed Intelligence, traced English customs and words to Anglo-Saxon roots. He died at Antwerp in 1636.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-fabyan:
Robert Fabyan was a London clothier and alderman whose chronicle remains a key source for the city's history. He died on 28 February 1513. A member of the Drapers' Company, he held several responsible civic posts but resigned his aldermanship in 1502, probably to escape the heavy costs of the mayoralty.

Fabyan ranks among the city chroniclers, writers chiefly concerned with municipal life, yet he first tried joining London's story to the nation's. His Concordance of Histories runs from Brutus to the death of Richard III, yet his attempt to harmonize earlier chroniclers shows little art or judgment. The work's value lies chiefly in its London material. Its second edition of 1533 adds pithy notes on municipal affairs under Henry VII, thought to abridge a lost chronicle of that reign. The best edition is Ellis's of 1811.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roch-amboise-:
Roch-Ambroise-Auguste Bebian was a pioneer in the education of the deaf in France. Born at Pointe-a-Pitre in Guadeloupe in 1789, he was sent to France under the care of the Abbe Sicard, famed educator of the deaf. Sicard placed him with the Abbe Jauffret. After the Lycee Charlemagne in Paris, Bebian gave himself to studying deaf education. He followed Sicard's courses and attended to Laurent Clerc, later of Hartford.

As prefect of studies at the Paris institution, he sought the signs best fitted to express deaf pupils' ideas. His Essai sur les sourds-muets of 1817, Mimographie of 1822, and Manuel of 1827 set the principles used at Paris. After leaving the school he wrote, refused schools at St Petersburg and New York, and founded an institution in Montparnasse. He directed Rouen's school, then returned to Guadeloupe, where he founded a school for black children. He died there in 1839.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-william:
Roger William Vaughan, known as Bede, was the second Archbishop of Sydney. Born at Courtfield in Herefordshire in 1834, second son of Colonel John Vaughan, he was the younger brother of Cardinal Vaughan of Westminster. Delicate in health, he was schooled at home under his saintly mother until seventeen, then went to Downside and became a Benedictine. After his novitiate he studied at St Paul Outside the Walls in Rome from 1855 and was ordained in 1859.

Back at Downside he ran the mission, taught philosophy from 1861, and served as cathedral prior at Belmont from 1862 to 1872. Chosen coadjutor to Archbishop Polding of Sydney in 1872, he was consecrated at Liverpool and sailed for Australia. On Polding's death in 1877 he succeeded as archbishop. He founded Catholic schools, pressed primary education, and opened his completed cathedral. He lived as simply as a monk and died suddenly in Lancashire in 1883 while visiting England for his health.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacristan:
A sacristan looks after the sacristy, the church, and all in them. In old times doorkeepers did much of this work, later mansionarii and treasurers. Gregory IX's Decretals call it an honoured post tied to a benefice. Nowadays he is chosen or paid.

Church rules said that in cathedrals the sacristan should be a priest. It lists work for the sacristy, Eucharist, font, oils, relics, and church decor. It also covers prep for rites, bell ringing, and order in church. The under-sacristan, or custos, helped him, under the archdeacon, with much the same work. Now the post is hardly ever tied to a benefice but is usually paid. Trent wished clerics to hold such posts, but in most churches laymen do much of this work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-la:
Saint John Lateran is the oldest of Rome's four patriarchal basilicas, standing where the palace of the Laterani family stood. Plautius Lateranus, consul designate under Nero, was accused of conspiracy and his goods confiscated. Traces of the palace appear in the walls and in a hall found within the basilica. The palace passed to Constantine through his wife Fausta, giving it the name Domus Fausta, and Constantine gave it to the Church by 311.

A council against the Donatists met within its walls in 313, and it was the centre of Christian life, the popes' residence and the city's cathedral. It holds the cathedral rank, with the title of mother and head of all churches of the city and the world. The first church there was probably an adapted palace hall rather than a new building. It was dedicated to the Saviour, with the dedication to Saint John coming later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-lawrenc:
Lawrence Justinian, bishop and first patriarch of Venice, was born in 1381 into the Giustiniani, a Venetian patrician family counting several saints. He died on 8 January 1456. His pious mother planted a devout life in him young. In 1400, at about nineteen, he entered the monastery of the Augustinian Canons Regular on the island of Alga near Venice.

Ordained in 1406, he soon became prior and then general of the congregation, gave it its constitution, and spread it so widely that he counts as its founder. Raised to the bishopric of Castello in 1433, he restored churches, set up parishes in Venice, and reformed the canons, while giving all he could raise to the poor. In 1451 Nicholas V joined Castello to the patriarchate of Grado and moved the see to Venice, naming Lawrence its first patriarch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-loman:
Loman, bishop of Trim in Ireland and nephew of Saint Patrick, was the first man Patrick placed over an Irish see, in the year 433. He had converted Fortchern, prince of Trim and grandson of Laeghaire, king of Meath, together with Fortchern's father Foidilmid, and Trim was given to him as his see.

Some say he was already a bishop before reaching Ireland, but this seems unlikely, since he would not accept Trim unless Patrick came to ratify the gift. The Tripartite Life and Tirechan state plainly that he was only a simple priest whom Patrick consecrated for Trim. He did not long survive his promotion, and after visiting his brother Broccaid in Connacht, he resigned the see to Fortchern with Patrick's permission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-ninian:
Ninian, bishop and confessor who died about 432, counts as the first preacher of Christianity to the southern Picts of Scotland. Almost everything known about him comes from a short passage in Bede's church history, which calls him a Briton trained at Rome. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia builds on that passage and tests the fuller tales that came later.

Bede places his see at Candida Casa, the White House, named for a stone church he built in honour of Martin of Tours, a rarity among the Britons. A twelfth-century Life by Aelred adds much detail, claiming older sources, but the entry shows how little of it can be checked. Readers meet a shadowy founder whose stone church and mission to the Picts outlived the man himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saints-kieran:
Kieran is a name shared by many Irish saints, and this entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sorts them out. Most celebrated is Kieran of Clonmacnoise, treated under that place, but Kieran of Seir-Kieran and Kieran of Disert-Kieran stand next in fame. The note serves as a guide to a crowded calendar, not a single biography.

Seir-Kieran's founder, active through much of the fifth century from about 450, also founded the see of Ossory and is honoured in England, Brittany, Wales, and Scotland on 5 March. Disert-Kieran's Kieran, called the Devout by Irish annalists, wrote a Life of Patrick and died in 775, kept on 14 June. Two lesser Kierans follow, of Clonsost on 30 April and son of Colga on 19 May.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-severian:
Severian, Bishop of Gabala in Syria, flourished in the fourth and fifth centuries and was known as a good preacher and writer of biblical commentaries and sermons. Nothing survives about his life before his consecration. This entry remembers him chiefly for the regrettable part he played in the deposition and banishment of Saint John Chrysostom. Drawn to Constantinople about 400 by the success of his fellow Syrian Antiochus, he won hearers despite a strong Syrian accent.

Chrysostom invited him to preach and, leaving for Asia in 401, made him his deputy for liturgical functions. Severian used the absence to quarrel openly with Serapion, the archdeacon and administrator. Swayed by personal interest amid the strained relations between Chrysostom and Empress Eudoxia, he sided against Chrysostom and helped bring about his fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-dominic-c:
Dominic Corrigan, physician born in Dublin in 1802, died there in 1880, won distinction for original observations in heart disease, with a special pulse type named after him. Son of a poor shopkeeper, he was schooled at Maynooth. Drawn to medicine by the attending physician, he took his medical degree at Edinburgh in 1825.

Back in Dublin he became physician to Jervis Street Hospital, then holding only six medical beds. Over four years he recast teaching on aortic valve disease. His paper on permanent patency of the aortic valves appeared in Edinburgh's Medical and Surgical Journal in April 1832. A gifted teacher, he won a London diploma in 1842 and a Dublin honorary doctorate in 1849. His work in the famine fever years made him famous, and Trousseau proposed calling aortic heart disease Corrigan's disease.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
The Sisters of the Good Samaritan, Tertiaries Regular of Saint Benedict, began at Sydney, Australia, on 2 February 1857. A second community followed at Windsor in 1859, and foundations multiplied until the Archdiocese of Sydney alone counted 21 houses with 202 members, and all Australia 29 communities.

Houses followed at Gawler in 1902, Northcote in 1904, and South Yarra, with boarding and day schools in Port Augusta, Rockhampton, and Cooktown. At Tempe, Arncliffe, the sisters established Saint Magdalen's Retreat, a home for penitent women of all creeds, supported by voluntary gifts and the inmates' labour. About 130 women lived there in 1909, encouraged to remain at least two years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-son-of-man:
Son of Man is a phrase with a long biblical career. This entry follows it from Hebrew poetry to the Gospels. In the Old Testament it serves as a poetic synonym for man, or for ideal man. God addresses the prophet Ezekiel by it more than ninety times. That usage is found elsewhere only once, in Daniel.

Daniel's night vision of one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven gave the phrase its apocalyptic weight. The entry shows how the New Testament takes it up as Christ's own chosen self-designation. Tracing each occurrence, it explains why a humble-sounding title became one of the richest names in Christian speech.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-adamnan-eu:
St. Adamnan, also called Eunan, was abbot of Iona, born at Drumhome in County Donegal about 624 and dead at Iona in 704. This entry follows a boy schooled by Columban monks at home who became a novice at Iona in 650, rose to the abbacy in 679. And presided over all Columban houses in Ireland.

Three long visits to Ireland marked his rule, one remembered for winning acceptance of the Roman date of Easter. And on his third, in 697, he stood at the Synod of Tara when the Cain Adamnain, his canon, was adopted, freeing women and children from being killed or captured in war. The entry also notes his possible rule of Mayo, and his memory remains inseparable from Iona.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aileran:
St. Aileran, generally known as Sapiens, the Wise, was one of the most distinguished teachers at Clonard in seventh-century Ireland. This entry places him at the great school through the fame of St. Finian and his disciples, rector of that celebrated seat of learning about 650. And dead of the Yellow Plague, his death recorded in the Annals of Ulster on 29 December 664.

As a classical scholar he had almost no rival in his day, and his command of Origen, Philo, Jerome, and Augustine marks him as a master of Latin and Greek. Colgan credits him with many works, including a Fourth Life of St. Patrick and lives of Brigid and Fechin, while the Latin-Irish Litany is scarcely doubted as his, and the entry presents a scholar-saint of the Irish golden age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alban:
St. Alban was the first martyr of Britain, suffering about 304, and this entry retells the account known since Bede's Ecclesiastical History. A pagan living at Verulamium, now St. Albans in Hertfordshire, he sheltered a cleric fleeing persecution, and after some days, moved by his guest's example, received baptism himself.

When the governor's men came to search the house, Alban put on his guest's cloak and gave himself up in his place, was dragged before the judge, scourged. And, refusing to deny his faith, condemned to death. On the road to execution he held back a river's waters so the party crossed dry-shod. And a fountain sprang on the hilltop, wonders the entry reports as Bede told them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aphian:
St. Aphian, or Apian, was an illustrious martyr under Emperor Maximian, about 306. This entry follows a youth of only eighteen who entered the temple at Caesarea while the prefect Urbanus offered sacrifice. Seizing the outstretched hand that presented the incense, he reproached the magistrate for idolatry. Guards fell on him furiously, tortured him cruelly, and flung him into a dungeon.

On the following day the prefect had him torn with iron claws, beaten with clubs, and burned over a slow fire. Then he was sent back to confinement. After three days he was taken from prison again and cast into the sea, stones tied to his feet. Eusebius, who saw it, declares that an earthquake shook the city at that moment, and the sea flung his corpse onto the shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-brendan:
St. Brendan of Ardfert and Clonfert — Brendan the Voyager, as he is also known — was born in 484 in Ciarraighe Luachra, near present-day Tralee in County Kerry, Ireland. He died at Enachduin, now Annaghdown, in 577. This entry follows a boy baptized at Tubrid near Ardfert by Bishop Erc. For five years St. Ita, the Brigid of Munster, educated him; St. Erc finished his studies and ordained him priest in 512.

Between 512 and 530 Brendan set up monastic cells at Ardfert and at Shanakeel, or Baalynevinoorach, below Brandon Hill. From there he sailed on his famous voyage to the Land of Delight. The old Irish calendars mark a special feast for the Egressio familiae S. Brendani on 22 March. In his litany from the close of the eighth century, St. Aengus the Culdee invokes the sixty who accompanied Brendan on his quest for the Land of Promise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-brogan:
St. Brogan flourished in the sixth or seventh century, and this entry follows a name borne by several persons in repute for holiness. The name is written Brogan, Broccan, Bracan, and even Bearchan and Bearchanus. Two of those persons are commemorated in the Irish Martyrology of Aengus, whose early date, about 800, is now generally admitted. There, under 8 July, we read that Brocan the scribe gained a noble triumph without any fall.

Under 17 September we read that Brocan of Ross Tuirc thou shouldst declare. Colgan seems inclined to identify both persons as the author of an Irish hymn upon St. Brigid. The Aengus glosses and the Martyrology of Gorman, while seemingly treating them as distinct, prove the matter admits of no certainty. Some modern hagiographers regard the Brogan of 8 July as the amanuensis and possibly the nephew of St. Patrick, styling him bishop and locating him at Ross Tuirc.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cajetan:
St. Cajetan, or Gaetano, was founder of the Theatines, born in October 1480 at Vicenza in Venetian territory. He died at Naples in 1547. This entry follows a boy raised by a pious mother, studious and exemplary in youth. He took his law doctorate at Padua in his twenty-fourth year. In 1506 he became a prothonotary apostolic at Rome in Julius II's court.

He took an important share in reconciling the Republic of Venice with that pontiff. On Julius's death in 1523 he withdrew from court. Shortly after, he is credited with founding the Oratory of Divine Love, an association of pious priests and prelates that spread to other Italian towns. Though remarkable for intense love of God, he did not reach the priesthood till 1516. Recalled to Vicenza in 1517 by his mother's death, he founded a hospital for incurables there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-conan:
St. Conan, bishop of the Isle of Man, died in January 684. This Irish missionary was also known as Mochonna. This entry follows a man easily confused with St. Conindrius — said to have been a disciple of St. Patrick who lived to a very advanced age, dying 17 November 560. The Bollandists count Conan among Man's early bishops, and Colgan recounts his life and labours.

Unfortunately, fifth- and sixth-century Isle of Man history is very obscure, and definite facts are hard to get at. Yet Conan, or Mochonna, also called Bishop of Inis-Patrick, left a clear mark of his zeal for souls in Manxland. Some authorities give his death date as 26 January, but Colgan, quoting the ancient Irish martyrologies, gives 13 January, the day Conan's feast is observed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-corbinian:
Freising in Bavaria had him as bishop, and Chatres near Melun in France was where he was born, about 680. He died 8 September 730, the date also kept as his feast; 20 November marks his translation, and a bear is his emblem. Of his early years, nothing survives in the record. Waldekiso, his father, had died before his birth, and after his mother Corbiniana died, he withdrew to a solitary life at the Saint-Germain church in Chatres.

With some disciples he went to Rome in 716, or 709 by another reckoning. There he was consecrated bishop and given the pallium, then sent to preach, with great success near his former home.
