The contents start with Boone's birth, school pranks, first hunts, and a brush with a panther. The family moves to North Carolina, and Boone grows into a hunter famed for fire hunting by night. A near-fatal blunder in that sport and his marriage close the first chapter's list. Flint, an early western writer, shaped Boone into the model of the backwoods pathfinder for a wide young readership.
the-foreigner-a-tale-of-saskatchewan:
Ralph Connor wrote The Foreigner as a tale of Saskatchewan, signed from Winnipeg in 1909 with a preface on the making of Canada. Many breeds, he says, are being made into one people there.

The contents open with a city on the plain where East meets West, then turn to the marriage of Anka, an unbidden guest, and the grip of British law. Kalman finds a mine and fights for it in the later chapters. Connor pleads for fair dealing and kind faith to bind Saxon, Slav, Celt, and Gaul into one Canadian people, and his tale tests that plea in love and law.
the-foundations-of-japan: The Foundations of Japan is present here only in front matter. Two pictures show life in a farm school. A list gives the author's past books on the Far East and on farming. The title page then begins. It gives the book's ground in a few lines. The notes were made on journeys of six thousand miles through the rural districts. The author's name does not stand in what can be read here. No chapter text is present. So the book's findings cannot be judged from the front pages alone.
the-going-of-the-white-swan:
Gilbert Parker wrote The Going of the White Swan. D. Appleton and Company printed it in New York in 1912. Earlier copyrights are dated 1895 and 1898. The tale opens in a northern cabin. A hurt child lies under a wolfskin robe. He asks his father why his mother does not come back.

The father shakes his head. He fumbles with the robe and says nothing. The child insists she would come if she knew he was hurt. The father nods, then turns to the door. He acts as if he still waits and hopes. A picture caption shows a priest in the tale. The priest says: No, no — this! The spare opening sets a story of loss and faith. It is also a story of a child's longing in the far north.
the-golden-mean:
The Golden Mean gives the golden ratio to one million digits. The ratio is written as (1 plus the square root of 5) over 2. A short head note gives the basis. It rests on a square root of 5 by Robert Nemiroff and Jerry Bonnell. No author, story, or argument is present. The work is the number itself, printed out in full.

The digits begin 1.6180339887498948482045868343656381177203091798057. They run on, block after block. They show no repeat and no end in sight. Such a list serves math readers. They need the constant to great depth for tests of machines. They need it for checks of methods. They need it for study of the ratio in geometry, growth, and art. Its value lies in its length and exactness.
the-goldfish-being-the-confessions-af-a-: Arthur Train edited The Goldfish. Its subtitle is Being the Confessions of a Successful Man. The book is dated 1921. Only front matter is present here: the title page, a contents list, and two quotes. The contents split the confessions into Myself, My Friends, My Children, My Mind, My Morals, and My Future. A line likens the rich to goldfish in a bowl: they can look out dimly, but cannot get out. A quote from William James calls the fear of poverty the worst moral disease of the age.
the-great-prince-shan:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Great Prince Shan. It is dated 1922. Chapter I opens in the card room of the St. Philip's Club. Prince Karschoff looks through a cloud of tobacco smoke. The room is spacious but almost deserted. He calls it a club for diplomats and gentlemen. Yet, he says, a decent rubber of bridge seems impossible to get.

Sir Daniel Harker answers him. Harker is a retired plenipotentiary to one of the smaller Powers. He has concluded that the club's reason for being is passing. There is no diplomacy nowadays, he says. Every man who pays his taxes is a gentleman. The Honourable Nigel Kingley is told to ransack the club for a fourth. The idle talk of three men in a fading club opens the tale. Behind it stand the new powers of the postwar world.
the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-dicti:
This record is the F to G section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary. The C. and G. Merriam Company published the version of 1913 at Springfield, Massachusetts. Noah Porter directed the work. The section begins on page 535 with the letter F. F is defined as the sixth letter of the English alphabet, and a nonvocal consonant. Its form came from the Latin, which took it from the Greek digamma, and that from the Phoenician.

The entries give pronunciation, derivation, and senses in the Merriam manner. Fa is the fourth tone in solmization. Fabaceous means having the nature of a bean. Fabian means cautious and dilatory, after the Roman general Fabius Maximus. His policy of delays and cautions foiled Hannibal. Fable is a feigned story meant to instruct or amuse. The section serves readers who need exact meanings and word histories from F into G.

This record is the M to N section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary. The C. and G. Merriam Company published the version of 1913 at Springfield, Massachusetts. Noah Porter directed the work. The section opens with the letter M. M is defined as the thirteenth letter of the English alphabet, and a vocal consonant. From its formation, it is called the labio-nasal consonant. Its form came from the Greek, through the Latin, and behind that the Phoenician and the Egyptian.

The entry gives M's further uses. As a numeral, M stands for one thousand, in English and in Latin. In printing, an em is a square quadrat, the unit for measuring type. In law, an M was a brand for a manslaughter convict admitted to benefit of clergy. The entries that follow run in the same full manner, for words from M into N.
the-henchman:
Mark Lee Luther wrote The Henchman. The Macmillan Company published it in New York in 1902. The copyright is dated 1901. Luther is named as the author of The Favor of Princes. A note before book one addresses knowing readers, who will spot the Tuscarora Stories from western New York history. Luther adapted them from Judge Arad Thomas's county history.

Chapter one opens with old geography lessons for children. Italy was likened to a boot in those lessons. France was likened to a coffee-pot. New York state figured as a couchant lion. Its head was thrust high in the North Country. Luther uses the playful image to place his tale.
the-highwayman: H. C. Bailey wrote The Highwayman. The contents list nineteen chapters. Early titles include The Complete Hero and The House of Waverton. Later titles include A Man of Many Worlds. One chapter is called A Gentleman's Purse. Another is called The World's a Miracle. Later titles include Harry Is Not Grateful. The list ends with Alison Finds Friends. No text past the front matter is present here. The novel itself does not appear.
the-hillman:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Hillman, copyright 1917 by Little, Brown, and Company. He is named as the author of The Kingdom of the Blind and Mr. Grex of Monte Carlo, and a frontispiece by George Avison is noted. Chapter one opens with Louise leaning back among the cushions of a motionless car.

Louise feels self-engrossed yet pleasantly apart from the troubles of the moment. Her eyes travel past a dim hillside of wall-enclosed fields, up to leaning clouds and unseen heights lost in mist. Oppenheim begins with stillness, wealth, and distance from the world below, before the calm of the scene is set to break.
the-home-of-the-blizzard-being-the-story:
Sir Douglas Mawson, D.Sc., B.E., wrote The Home of the Blizzard, the story of the Australasian Antarctic Expedition, 1911-1914. The title page promises maps and 260 illustrations by Dr. E. A. Wilson and other members of the expedition, plus plates in facsimile from Wilson's sketches. An author's preface states the object of the book.

Mawson aims to give one linked, plain account of the expedition for general readers, while granting that any such account falls short of the endeavor. Lasting reputation, he says, rests on the scientific volumes to come. History of Antarctic exploration is kept to a minimum, reports from sledging leaders were cut for balance, and a glossary helps readers with the terms.
the-hoosier-schoolmaster-a-story-of-back:
Edward Eggleston wrote The Hoosier Schoolmaster, subtitled a story of backwoods life in Indiana, dated 1871. A revised library edition carries an introduction and notes on the district by the author, character sketches by F. Opper, and other illustrations by W. E. B. Starkweather. Eggleston inscribes the edition to the memory of James Russell Lowell.

A preface to the library edition, called the history of a story, explains the occasion. Eggleston dates the writing and printing to the autumn of 1871. That made the book about twenty-one years old at the new edition. The publishers mean to mark its coming of age, and Eggleston uses the chance to revise the text and tell how the book began.
the-hunted-woman:
James Oliver Curwood wrote this northern adventure. His earlier novel Kazan is named on the title page. Frank B. Hoffman drew the illustrations. Curwood dedicated the book to his wife. He added their comrades of the trail. It appeared in 1915. Chapter I follows a woman in a pearl-gray veil. She has ridden eighteen hours into the mountains. A rushing crowd surrounds her. A voice behind her calls it the horde.

The illustrations list promises her story's shape. One caption quotes a man drawn north by a grave, not gold. Another shows a woman beside a huge brown bear. A third gives a tunnel sealing shut. Forty-five minutes of air remain in that scene. Curwood frames the gold-rush migration grandly. Such crowds made the flesh-and-blood foundation of nations. One frightened, watchful woman rides inside it.
the-institutes-of-justinian:
J. B. Moyle, barrister of Lincoln's Inn and fellow of New College, Oxford, translated Justinian's Institutes into English; the copy here is the fifth edition of 1913. The work opens with the emperor's own prologue, addressed to the youth desirous of studying the law. Justinian declares that majesty should carry laws as proudly as arms. Rome's ruler should be as careful in justice as in triumph over his foes.

He recounts the codification: inconsistencies removed from the sacred constitutions, the immense volumes of older jurisprudence crossed like a mid-ocean, and Tribonian, Theophilus, and Dorotheus commissioned to compose the Institutes. Where students once waited four years to read the constitutions, beginners may now learn their first lessons in law directly from the emperor's mouth. Moyle's translation keeps that proud voice intact for English law students.
the-iron-woman:
Margaret Deland wrote this novel. She dedicated it to Lorin Deland on August 12, 1911. He was her patient, ruthless, inspiring critic, she says. A text from Ezekiel fronts the book. It names fulness of bread and abundance of idleness as sin. Chapter I opens years earlier in an orchard. Elizabeth Ferguson has climbed an apple-tree there. She commands three children to climb up and play house. Her white-stockinged legs swing recklessly above them.

Her threat is gentle and frightening at once. She is afraid, perhaps, maybe, she will get mad. A giggle and a dimple soften nothing. All three children know what Elizabeth mad means. Nannie Maitland answers helplessly, as she always does. Deland begins with a child tyrant of charm and will. That child grows toward the iron woman of the title.
the-koran-al-qur-an:
George Sale's English Koran was made from the original Arabic. Notes from the most approved commentators explain it. A preliminary discourse opens the work. Sale dedicates it to John, Lord Carteret. He expects to need an apology. Founders of states and givers of laws are usually honored, he writes. Arabia's lawgiver has fared very differently at their hands. All who deny his divine mission treat him so. Christians especially do.

Sale argues the Arab conquests cannot alone explain the hatred. Calamity charges apply to all conquerors alike. The difference is that Mohammed gave a new religion. Sale's version was the first English Koran made directly from Arabic. It held the field for two centuries. Its long preliminary discourse made it a work of scholarship too. Scripture and scholarship stand together in it.
the-last-man:
Mary Shelley wrote this vast tale of the last man on earth in 1826. She had by then lost her husband and most of her dear kin and friends. The book is the first great work of its kind, the tale of the end of mankind.

A plague spreads year by year through the world and leaves Lionel Verney alone at last. He roams a Rome of tombs and writes his tale for no reader who may come. The book founds the whole line of tales of the end of the world in print.
the-later-works-of-titian: Claude Phillips, keeper of the Wallace Collection, published his study of Titian later paintings in 1898. Only the title page and list of illustrations are present here, naming copper plates of a self portrait, La Bella, Titian daughter Lavinia, and the Cornaro family. Sepia plates and text images from galleries in Florence, Berlin, London, and Paris also appear in the list. The critical text on the Venetian painter late style does not appear in this record.
the-leopard-woman: Stewart Edward White published his African adventure novel in 1916, illustrated by W. H. D. Koerner. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing thirty-two chapters on a march, a rhinoceros, a stranger, a water hole, thirst, an ivory stockade, a murder, and a trial. Kingozi and a woman called the Leopard Woman drive the later chapter titles. The safari narrative itself cannot be seen in this record beyond those chapter headings.
the-life-and-opinions-of-tristram-shandy:
Laurence Sterne presents his comic novel through a dedication to the Right Honourable Mr. Pitt. He writes from a retired thatched house in a far corner of the kingdom. Mirth, he says, forms his defense against ill health and the other evils of life.

Sterne begs Pitt to carry the book into the country and hopes it may win a smile or ease a moment of pain. That playful plea sets the tone for Tristram own wandering account of his life and opinions. Digression, jokes, and family oddity rule a novel famous for refusing a straight line.
the-life-of-john-bunyan:
Edmund Venables wrote his life of John Bunyan for an 1888 Walter Scott edition. Chapter one places Bunyan birth at Elstow in Bedfordshire late in 1628, with baptism on the last day of November. His book, Venables says, likely leads all English books in editions, readers, and translations.

The birth year also brought the Petition of Right and a growing struggle between Charles I and Parliament. Venables sets a tinker preacher life against civil war politics and church pressure. Grace Abounding and The Pilgrim Progress grew from that pressure, and the life traces both faith and jail time.
the-little-red-chimney-being-the-love-st: Mary Finley Leonard wrote The Little Red Chimney, subtitled The Love Story of a Candy Man, published by Duffield and Company in 1914 with silhouette pictures by Katharine Gassaway. What is present stops at the title page and part of the contents; the story itself does not appear. The chapter summaries are playful. The curtain rises on the Candy Wagon. The Candy Man walks abroad in citizen's clothes and is mistaken for a man of wealth. The Little Red Chimney appears on the horizon without a clue to its importance.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-1:
Volume ten of Suetonius's Lives, in the Thomson translation revised by T. Forester, turns to Titus Flavius Vespasianus Augustus. Suetonius says the empire, long unsettled after its last three rulers rebelled and died violently, was restored to peace by the Flavian family. That family was obscure and boasted no ancestral honors, yet he adds that the public had no cause to regret its rise.

He traces the line to Titus Flavius Petro of Reate, who fled the battle of Pharsalia and later collected money at public auctions. Petro's son Sabinus never served as a soldier and instead farmed the tax of the fortieth penny in Asia. An emperor from tax collectors and auction rooms makes the volume a study in unlikely origins.

Domitian, the last of the Twelve Caesars, closes Suetonius's set in volume twelve, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester. He was born on October 24 at a place called the Pomegranate in Rome, in a house he later turned into a temple of the Flavian family. Suetonius reports hostile stories about his youth: great want, no silver plate of his own, and shameful bargains alleged by his enemies.

During the war with Vitellius, Domitian fled into the Capitol with his uncle Sabinus. When the temple burned, he hid all night with the sacristan, then escaped across the Tiber disguised as a worshipper of Isis among her priests. Suetonius mixes documented danger with scandal, inviting readers to judge which parts deserve belief.
the-lookout-man: B. M. Bower's The Lookout Man was published by Little, Brown of Boston in August 1917, with a frontispiece by H. Weston Taylor. Only the title pages, a list of Bower's novels, and the start of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters include Some Time!, Thanks for the Car, and To the Feather River Country and Freedom. They hint at a car and an escape into Sierra country. Bower's listed books include Good Indian and The Heritage of the Sioux.
the-magician:
W. Somerset Maugham's The Magician, dated 1908, is printed together with a fragment of his autobiography. In that fragment Maugham recalls qualifying as a doctor at St Thomas's Hospital in 1897 after five years of study. While still a student he had published a novel, Liza of Lambeth, which caused a mild sensation. On its strength he rashly abandoned doctoring to earn his living as a writer, and set out for Spain, spending the best part of a year in Seville.

He amused himself hugely and wrote a bad novel, he admits. Back in London he shared a small flat near Victoria Station and spent six years writing novels and plays that mostly failed. One play, A Man of Honour, at last reached the Stage Society. Sixteen chapters of The Magician follow, but the fragment itself is the candid draw here.
the-make-believe-man:
Richard Harding Davis's The Make-Believe Man is told by a twenty-five-year-old stenographer at Joyce and Carboy's, woollen manufacturers, who has always wished for adventures that avoid him. His friend Kinney, a clerk a year older, sits next to him at work and rooms at the same boarding-house. Adventures find Kinney constantly: he helps people down fire-escapes, befriends noblemen and actors, and is pursued by beautiful women in taxicabs calling for assistance.

The narrator, raised in the pretty harbor of Fairport, studies law at night hoping to reach the bar. For vacation he plans to seek adventures at last, and Kinney arranges that they go together, pointing out that no better guide exists. The narrator half suspects Kinney invents his exploits, and the trip is set up as a test of the make-believe man.
the-making-of-an-american:
Jacob A. Riis, author of How the Other Half Lives, wrote The Making of an American as his autobiography. A note to the reader, dated from Richmond Hill, New York, in October 1901, explains that the papers first appeared in The Outlook, with parts in The Churchman and The Century Magazine. To readers asking whether the stories are made up, Riis answers that they are not, and that he is glad to have lived every part of it.

The contents begin the arc in chapter titles: The Meeting on the Long Bridge and I Land in New York and Take a Hand in the Game. I Go to War at Last, Working and Wandering, and I Go into Business Headlong follow. A chapter in which he becomes an editor and receives his first love letter closes the list. Readers get a reporter's life told as an American success story.
the-man:
Bram Stoker, author of Dracula, wrote The Man, shown here in the 1897 Robert Hayes edition from London. A short opening called Fore-Glimpse sets a young man and a young girl on a low tombstone in an old churchyard. Through a hawthorn tree they overhear two children talking, and one child's sentence stops them cold: "I would rather be an angel than God!" They sit as still as mice to listen.

Stoker pauses over the scene like a painter. The low, square-towered church has long mullioned windows and yellow-grey stone roughened with lichens. Tombstones tilt in all directions, gnarled yews line the back, and laburnum, lilac, hawthorn, and meadowsweet mingle their sweetness over a lazy stream in June sunlight. The foreglimpse promises a story seeded by a child's remark about ambition and heaven.
the-martyrdom-of-man:
Winwood Reade published The Martyrdom of Man in 1872, a sweeping work shaped by his travels and his religious skepticism. An opening note gives his life in brief: born near Crieff in 1838, nephew of the novelist Charles Reade, and educated at Oxford. He traveled in Africa in 1862, returned in 1868, and later reported the Ashanti War for The Times.

Reade's own preface explains that a London merchant, Andrew Swanzy, financed his second African journey and left him free to choose his route. He spent two years traveling, in 1868 to 1870, studying religion and morality among the peoples he met. The note also traces his other books, from Savage Africa to The Outcast, a novel about persecution for unbelief. Readers meet a Victorian explorer whose field experience fed a bold, questioning history of mankind.
the-master-christian:
Marie Corelli's novel The Master-Christian carries a dedication to all churches who quarrel in the name of Christ. Corelli, author of Thelma and Ardath, opens her story in Rouen as the Angelus bells ring at sunset. Market women cross themselves on the road home, and a bargeman on the Seine mutters a prayer from habit. Schoolchildren hesitate over whether the old formula still belongs in their modern, secular schooling.

A visitor gives the evening its charge: a cardinal-archbishop famed for purity of heart has come to Rouen that day. His own diocese regards him almost as a saint. Corelli sets the scene amid grey towers, river light, and a France that has pushed God out of its national institutions. Readers enter a tale about living faith set against church quarrels and public unbelief. Corelli's Rouen glows while her questions sharpen.
the-measure-of-a-man: Amelia E. Barr published The Measure of a Man with D. Appleton and Company in 1915, with illustrations by Frank T. Merrill. Only the title page, the dedication, and the opening contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Barr dedicated the book, with sincere esteem, to Mrs. Arthur Roberts of Evanston, Illinois. The contents begin with The Great Sea Waters and The People of the Story, then turn to love venturing in, brothers, a hearth fire, and love's young dream.
the-middle-class-gentleman:
Moliere's comedy-ballet The Middle Class Gentleman, in a translation by Philip Dwight Jones, was first presented at Chambord for the king's entertainment in October 1670. Jones also produced the text. The cast centers on Monsieur Jourdain, a bourgeois, with his wife, their daughter Lucile, and her suitor Cleonte. A count, Dorante, and a marchioness, Dorimene, supply the aristocracy Jourdain longs to join. Masters of music, dancing, fencing, and philosophy crowd the household staff.

Act One opens in Jourdain's Paris house, where the Music Master's pupil sits composing a serenade Jourdain has ordered. The Music Master and Dancing Master settle their performers on either side of the stage to wait for their patron. Their patience frames the joke of the whole play: artists, tutors, and tradesmen all live off one rich man's vanity. Readers meet the machinery of flattery assembled before its victim even enters.
the-miracle-man: Frank L. Packard published The Miracle Man with Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1914. Only the title page, a dedication 'to nearly everybody,' and the opening contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The contents open with The Roost, then promise A New Cult, a character called Needley, and the Patriarch. Later chapters bring the Patriarch's grand niece, a pilgrimage, and the miracle itself, with the bait nibbled along the way.
the-motor-maids-in-fair-japan:
Katherine Stokes's The Motor Maids in Fair Japan, dated 1913, is present here only in title page and contents, so the Japanese tour does not appear. Stokes is billed as author of The Motor Maids' School Days, The Motor Maids by Palm and Pine, and The Motor Maids Across the Continent, among other volumes in the series.

Eighteen chapters are listed. Off for Japan opens the book, followed by Tea in the Garden and Shopping in Jinrikshas, the hand-pulled carts of Japan. Cherry blossoms, a birthday party, a theatre party, and a letter that came though it was never sent fill the middle headings. The Ancient City of Sleep, The Storm King, and The Magnet and the Silver Churn close the list.
the-naturewoman:
Upton Sinclair's play The Naturewoman opens with a cast list and a plan of its four acts. Oceana, the Naturewoman herself, heads the characters. Around her stands the Masterson family of Beacon Street, Boston: Mrs. Sophronia Masterson, her husband Dr. Quincy Masterson, their son Freddy, and their daughters Ethel and the married Letitia Selden. Remson, a butler, completes the household.

Act I is set in the Masterson drawing room on a winter afternoon, and Act II in the same room the next day. Act III moves to a portion of the parlour used as a stage that evening, while Act IV shifts to Henry Selden's camp in the White Mountains a week later. The curtain rises on Ethel, a frail girl of sixteen, opening a framed photograph and crying Oceana's name in rapture.
the-new-frontiers-of-freedom-from-the-al:
E. Alexander Powell's The New Frontiers of Freedom, subtitled From the Alps to the Aegean, was published in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in April 1920. Only a list of Powell's books, title page, dedication, and the heading of an acknowledgment are present here, so the travel narrative does not appear. A caption shows the Queen of Rumania telling Major Powell how much she enjoys being a queen.

Powell's earlier war books head the list printed on the facing page: Fighting in Flanders, The Road to Glory, Vive la France! and Italy at War. The volume is dedicated to Major J. Stanley Moore of the Department of State, called a real and lifelong friend. The acknowledgment begins by citing the disturbed conditions prevailing across most of the region.
the-night-horseman:
Max Brand's The Night Horseman, dated 1920, is present here only in a series list, title page, and contents, so the western itself does not appear. The facing list names three Brand books in the set: The Untamed, Trailin', and The Night Horseman itself. Eighteen chapters are listed, each with a short title.

The Scholar opens the book, followed by Words and Bullets and The Doctor Rides. The Chain, The Waiting, and The Mission Starts build toward Jerry Strann and The Gift-Horse. Battle Light, a chapter titled Sweet Adeline, The Buzzard, and Music for Old Nick fill the middle list. Buck Makes His Get-Away and Doctor Byrne Analyses close what is shown.
the-patrician: John Galsworthy wrote the novel The Patrician, dated 1911 in the header. Only the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters are numbered without titles. Part I alone runs to eighteen numbered chapters in the list shown. Nothing in the pages present names the characters or the setting. The record offers only the book's bare frame, the plan of a long first part with no word of its people or places.
the-perpetuation-of-living-beings-heredi:
Thomas Henry Huxley lectured on The Perpetuation of Living Beings, hereditary transmission, and variation. He begins by setting aside the origin of life, on which, he says, we know nothing historically or experimentally. The question for the night is narrower: given living forms, how are they reproduced, perpetuated, and modified?

On that question our knowledge is large. Huxley divides perpetuation into asexual and sexual kinds. Gardeners know the first from cuttings: a geranium cutting, given light, warmth, and nourishment, grows into a plant with all its parent's properties. Sexual perpetuation, by the action of two individuals, is far more common among animals. The lecture lays out heredity in plain terms.
the-pharisee-and-the-publican:
The Pharisee and the Publican appears here in the 1845 Thomas Nelson edition of the Works of the Puritan Divines (Bunyan). The text opens with the parable from Luke, chapter eighteen. Two men went up into the temple to pray. The Pharisee thanked God he was not as other men. The publican smote his breast and asked for mercy.

Bunyan first recalls the earlier parable of the unjust judge and the widow. That parable teaches men to pray and not faint. If urging moved an unjust judge, he argues, God's people will prevail with a loving Father all the more. He then turns to his text with two aims. He means to convict the proud Pharisee. He also means to raise up the cast-down publican.
the-poor-gentleman:
Hendrik Conscience's The Poor Gentleman, translated expressly for this American edition, closes a series of tales about women in positions of trial. The preface explains the design. In The Village Innkeeper the heroine is torn between propriety and foolish ambition for high life. In The Conscript the heroine of humble life shows uncorrupted virtue and courage against authority. Here the heroine comes from the educated classes of Conscience's own countrymen.

The tale's hero, the perplexed De Vlierbeck, is praised as a character who engraves himself on the memory. The French critic Pontmartin is quoted calling these simple stories pearls set in Flemish gold. At not more than a hundred and fifty pages, the book is credited with a photographic minuteness of detail. That detail never loses motion or picturesque effect. The preface withholds plot summary on purpose, so as not to anticipate the author.
the-return-of-tarzan:
Edgar Rice Burroughs lists twenty-six chapters for Tarzan's return. The list opens with an affair on a liner. Paris streets and a countess's explanation follow. A duel and a desert fight come next. A wreck leads back to the primitive. Treasure vaults of Opar close the contents. Chapter one opens aboard ship instead. The Countess de Coude murmurs admiration under her breath.

Her husband asks what is magnificent. She covers a flush with a quick excuse. She was only recalling wit, she claims. Shipboard manners hide jungle loyalties in the exchange. The contents promise a wide arc for Tarzan. He will pass from drawing rooms to apes. Waziri warriors and a city of gold await him.
the-revolt-of-man:
Walter Besant explains in a preface dated December 1896 that his satire first appeared anonymously fourteen years earlier and stood ignored for six weeks until a strong review drew readers. Many editions followed, and he thanks two ladies who heard chapters read aloud during a summer holiday.

Their key advice shaped the ending: keep the revolt bloodless rather than closing with a real battle. Contents then open in Park Lane with an earl, a chancellor, and a great duchess. The preface alone tells readers to expect a role-reversal comedy handled with wit rather than violence.
the-river-war-an-account-of-the-reconque:
Winston S. Churchill recounts the reconquest of the Sudan. A 1902 edition carries his account here. Contents run from the Mahdi's rebellion onward. A Dervish empire and years of preparation follow. Firket and the Dongola recovery mark the advance. A desert railway transforms the campaign's supply lines. Abu Hamed and Berber fall in sequence.

The Atbara battle and the grand advance follow. Operations of the first of September precede Omdurman. The city's fall and the Fashoda incident come next. The Khalifa's end closes the contents list. Only the title page is present on these pages. The contents list and a campaign map appear with it. The campaign narrative itself does not appear here.
the-riverman:
Stewart Edward White sets his logging novel in 1872. A river bend above a pond holds the scene. A dam ends the pond at its lower reach. A two-story mill stands on the flat below it. Stump-dotted clearing surrounds the mill on every side. Dense forest covers all the land beyond it. Hardwoods crowd the bottom-lands along the stream. Their branches spray out in first spring green.

White pine and hemlock crown the higher lands behind. Norway pine and spruce stand sturdy among them there. Wind riffles the pond in fan-shaped cat's-paws overhead. Wavelets lap against a barrier of floating logs below. More logs carpet the inlet as far as sight reaches. A man could walk down that river like a highway. White builds a working river world before its rivermen.
the-rover-boys-on-the-great-lakes-or-the:
The fifth Rover Boys volume, The Rover Boys on the Great Lakes, is introduced by Arthur M. Winfield, identified as Edward Stratemeyer. He admits he first planned only three or four volumes. Reader demand kept extending the line. A frontispiece shows a blaze revealing a mass of lumber on turbulent waters.

The tale moves Dick, Tom and Sam from Putnam Hall to a pleasure tour of the Great Lakes. On Lake Erie they meet an old enemy. He schemes to kidnap Dick after the boy falls overboard from his yacht in a storm. The subtitle points to the secret of the island cave.
the-scarlet-gown-being-verses-by-a-st-an:
The Scarlet Gown gathers verses by a St. Andrews man. No name is given for the poet. The edition transcribed here was published in 1891. Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton and Company issued it in London. An epigraph from Andrew Lang calls St. Andrews a haunted town. Lang names its college of the scarlet gown and its northern sea.

The first poem, The Voice That Sings, asks who can hear a voice across the night. It carries echoes of long forgotten days and things. Faded eyes brim over at the sound, the poem says. The next piece, The Best Pipe, turns comic. The speaker rejects a cutty clay pipe, however fervently praised. A twelvemonth smoked, it smells of rank decay, he complains. He asks instead for a finely seasoned briar.
the-second-story-man:
Upton Sinclair's play The Second-Story Man has three characters. Jim Faraday is the second-story man of the title. Harvey Austin is a lawyer, and Helen Austin is his wife. The scene is the library of the Austin home. The time is two in the morning. Stage directions show a luxuriously furnished room. A lamp stands on a central table, and a cabinet of curios fills one corner.

At rise, the room is dark except for firelight. Sounds of breaking wood come from the window. Jim enters through it, a roughly dressed young fellow with a patch over one eye. He flashes a dark lantern and pockets a silver cup from the mantel. Austin then enters at the front door in evening dress. A crash offstage sends him to a drawer for a revolver.
the-secret-history-of-the-court-of-justi: Procopius's Secret History of the Court of Justinian is presented as literally and completely translated from the Greek for the first time. The Athenian Society privately printed it at Athens in 1896. The pages shown give a contents list with long chapter summaries. No chapter text itself follows. The first summary treats Antonina, wife of Belisarius. Her passion for the Thracian Theodosius fills much of it. The second summary follows Belisarius to war against Chosroes of Persia. The downfall of John the Cappadocian is also promised.
the-secret-memoirs-of-the-courts-of-euro:
Mme. la Marquise de Fontenoy wrote Secret Memoirs of the Courts of Europe, issued in two volumes in 1900. This first volume treats William the Second of Germany and Francis Joseph of Austria Hungary. A frontispiece shows William the Second, emperor of Germany, from life. A publishers' note opens the book.

That note sets out the qualifications for such a work. An author needs actual acquaintance with the persons mentioned, the publishers say. Intimate knowledge of their daily lives is also required. The Marquise de Fontenoy is a nom de plume, the note explains. Its bearer is a lady of high birth and title, the note explains. Her work rests largely on her own reminiscences, the publishers add. It offers a panoramic view of court life and its striking features.
the-secrets-of-the-princesse-de-cadignan:
Honoré de Balzac dedicated The Secrets of the Princesse de Cadignan to Théophile Gautier. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the work. Its first chapter is called The Last Word of Two Great Coquettes. The scene opens after the revolution of July. That revolution destroyed many aristocratic fortunes tied to the court, Balzac writes.

The Princesse de Cadignan blamed political events for her ruin. Her own extravagance had really caused it, the narrator says. The prince left France with the royal family and never returned. His absence protected her, since their debts could only be recovered through him. She had been celebrated as the Duchesse de Maufrigneuse. Now she wisely lived in retirement and sought to be forgotten. Under her new name she became a stranger in her own city, Balzac writes.
the-seventh-man:
Max Brand's The Seventh Man opens with a chapter called Spring. Vic Gregg was past the danger side of thirty, Brand writes. He had lived alone in the mountains all winter. Marriage to Betty Neal was his aim, but marriage takes money. So he contracted fifteen hundred dollars' worth of mining work for the Duncans. He took no partner and went after the stake single-handed.

Gregg finished assessment work on fourteen claims and nearly finished a fifteenth. The acid loneliness ate into him, though. His drills became wife and child to him, Brand writes. The clang of the single-jack on drill heads was his conversation. Evenings after supper hurt him most, since a man needs talk as well as tobacco. He spent himself daily to fall straight from supper into sleep.
the-shopkeeper-turned-gentleman:
Molière's The Shopkeeper Turned Gentleman, Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme, is translated into English prose by Charles Heron Wall. His edition carries short introductions and explanatory notes. A note before the cast gives the play's first performances. It was acted before the King at Chambord on October 14, 1670. On November 28 it played at the Palais Royal.

Louis the Fourteenth told Molière the play amused him more than anything before it, the note reports. Its Paris success was still greater. Bourgeois audiences laughed good-humouredly at what they deemed their neighbours' weaknesses, Wall writes. The first three acts are the best, he judges. The King hurried Molière over the last acts, and they degenerated into burlesque. Molière himself acted Mr. Jourdain, the note adds.
the-son-of-tarzan:
Edgar Rice Burroughs continues the Tarzan story in a novel dedicated to Hulbert Burroughs and divided into twenty-seven numbered chapters. The action starts far from England, aboard a long boat drifting down the broad Ugambi River toward the waiting ship Marjorie W., three miles below.

The crew rests on the ebb tide, done with the hard rowing upstream, until every man's attention turns to the northern bank. A thin stranger stands on the bank, screaming to them in a high, cracked voice, his skinny arms stretched wide. That startling appeal launches the adventure that brings Tarzan's son into the African world his father knew.
the-sorrows-of-satan:
Marie Corelli wrote this Faust tale in 1895, and it was the best seller of her long run of hits. Corelli was the most read novelist of her day in Britain, though the critics oft scorned her. The tale's name plays on the old line that Satan grieves for his fall.

A poor author, Geoffrey Tempest, meets a rich, fair prince named Lucio, who is the devil in man's form. Fame and cash flow to him at once, and the price is the old price of such tales. The book was the most hot occult romance of the 1890s, by a vast count.
the-story-of-ab-a-tale-of-the-time-of-th:
Stanley Waterloo published this tale of the cave man in 1905. Ab is a Stone Age man. He lived too long ago to date closely. He loved and fought well, Waterloo says. Waterloo thanks learned searchers on two continents who helped him reconstruct prehistoric life, then states the one point where he departs from accepted scientific theory.

No catastrophe or new race is needed, he argues. The change from chipped to polished stone tools needs no sudden break. Growth, trial, adaptation, and discovery suffice. The steady forces of evolution did the work. Ab, Lightfoot, and the other cave people, hungry and cold among fierce beasts, are shown as Waterloo believes they truly were.
the-story-of-manhattan: Charles Hemstreet wrote this history of New York, published there in 1901. Only the title page and an index to chapters are present here. The index shows how the narrative runs. It begins with Henry Hudson's adventures from 1609. The first traders follow. Then come the Dutch governors Minuit, Van Twiller, Kieft, and Stuyvesant. The stirring times and sad end of Jacob Leisler close the list. Hemstreet's chapters themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-the-other-wise-man:
Henry Van Dyke tells of a fourth pilgrim. The man saw the star in its rising. He did not arrive with his brethren at the manger-cradle in Bethlehem. A contents list names four parts. They are the sign in the sky and the waters of Babylon. The hidden way of sorrow and a pearl of great price follow. Motto verses give a warning. A man who seeks heaven only to save his own soul may keep the path and still miss the goal.

Van Dyke promises the tale as he has heard it. It tells of the Other Wise Man's great desire. The desire was denied, yet fulfilled in the denial. It tells of his many wanderings. It tells of his long seeking. It ends with his strange finding of the One he sought.
the-submarine-boys-and-the-middies-or-th: Victor G. Durham's submarine boys adventure at Annapolis was issued by the Saalfield Publishing Company, illustrated, in an edition of twenty chapters and a conclusion. Only the title pages and that contents list appear in this record. The titles promise a prize detail. Eph flirts with science in one. Truax sulks in another. A young captain stands in tatters. The Pollard goes lame. A lieutenant commander gives a verdict. The middies' cruise itself does not appear. A companion record of the same book lists twenty-four chapters instead.
the-tale-of-the-pie-and-the-patty-pan:
Beatrix Potter's Pie and the Patty-Pan was first published by Frederick Warne in 1905; this record shows its 1985 Penguin impression. Ribby the pussy-cat invites Duchess, a little dog, to tea. Her letter promises something very nice baked in a pie-dish. An old rhyme about Pussy by the fire opens the tale with a teasing, polite tone.

Behind the invitation sits a social problem, since Ribby and Duchess each worry about what the other will serve. Potter builds the comedy from party manners, secret dishes, and two hostesses trying not to offend each other. Small readers get a story about pride and politeness told through cats, dogs, and one disputed pie.
the-talisman:
Sir Walter Scott's Talisman, a tale of the Crusaders, opens here with Scott's own later introduction explaining how the novel came to be written. Friends had complained that its companion story, The Betrothed, did not match the Crusaders title. They wanted Eastern manners and romantic conflicts of the period brought directly in. Scott admits he knew almost nothing of the East beyond early reading of the Arabian Nights.

He jokes that every traveller who had thrown his shoe over Edom could claim the right to correct him. Writers such as the authors of Anastasius and Hadji Baba, plus Southey, Moore, and Byron, had already handled Eastern themes with skill. His introduction is a candid, funny account of a novelist daring to write about a world he had never seen.
the-titan: Theodore Dreiser's Titan is presented here through a long contents list, with no chapter text attached. The headings trace Frank Cowperwood's move to a new city: A Chicago Evening, Peter Laughlin and Company, Chicago Gas, and street-railways at last. Later entries promise Aileen's revenge, the coming of Stephanie Platow, a political agreement, an election, and an hour of defeat. Dreiser's sequel to The Financier can be followed move by move in this skeleton of some forty chapters, while his dense, documentary prose remains outside the pages present.
the-trade-union-woman: Alice Henry's Trade Union Woman (1915), dedicated to the trade union women of the United States and Canada, is shown here by title page and contents. Henry was a member of the Office Employés' Association of Chicago and former editor of Life and Labor. Her chapters move from early unions among women and the Knights of Labor to the Women's Trade Union League, the huge strikes, the immigrant woman, and the woman organizer. Later chapters take up vocations, marriage, and the vote. Her argument begins past these pages.
the-tremendous-adventures-of-major-gahag:
William Makepeace Thackeray's Tremendous Adventures of Major Gahagan introduces its hero by his visiting card: Major Goliah O'Grady Gahagan, H.E.I.C.S., commanding a battalion of irregular horse at Ahmednuggar. Gahagan insists on the card because the world keeps mistaking him. The Morning Post ranked his poems among the sweetest flowrets of the season under the name Miss Gahagan, and the Quarterly Review called him Doctor Gahagan for a work on Euclid. An exalted personage at Paris urged the remedy upon him.

The contents promise Allyghur and Laswaree, famine in the garrison, an escape, a captive, and the surprise of Futtygurh. Thackeray's blustering Irish major, a cousin to Barry Lyndon in boasting, narrates Indian campaigns in which he is always the hero. The comedy lies in the gap between Gahagan's card and Gahagan's credibility, which the reader must judge alone.
the-trumpeter-swan: Temple Bailey's Trumpeter Swan was published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1920. Alice Barber Stephens illustrated it. A Latin motto on the title page means a sound from the clouds shall call thee from this earth. This record gives the title page and contents only. Eleven chapters move from A Major and Two Minors through stuffed birds, a wolf in the forest, and Mademoiselle Midas, ending with Wanted, a Pedestal. Bailey's postwar romance is charted here, while Randy waits beyond these pages.
the-turtles-of-tasman:
Jack London's Turtles of Tasman, published by Grosset and Dunlap in September 1916, opens its title story on Frederick Travers, whose face law, order, and restraint have carved. It is a strong, firm face, the face of a man accustomed to wielding power wisely. Clean living made the healthy skin, and the lines in it are honest lines left by hard, devoted work. Every feature tells the same story, from clear blue eyes to the full head of light brown hair touched with grey.

The contents gather seven more pieces. They include The Eternity of Forms, Told in the Drooling Ward, The Hobo and the Fairy, The Prodigal Father, and The First Poet. Finis and The End of the Story close the book. London's late stories turn from Yukon gold to brothers, memory, and decay, with Travers's ordered life about to meet the brother who lived by turtles and chance.
the-two-gun-man: Charles Alden Seltzer's Two-Gun Man, copyrighted in 1911 by the Outing Publishing Company and reprinted by A. L. Burt, is shown here through its contents list. Twenty-two chapters open with the stranger at Dry Bottom, who then shoots, finds a cabin in the flat, and meets a 'different girl.' Later headings promise an orphan found and lost, a shot in the dark, love and a rifle, and a promise kept. Seltzer's Western is mapped in these titles, while his stranger's story begins beyond them.
the-unspeakable-gentleman:
J. P. Marquand published The Unspeakable Gentleman in 1922, telling the story as a son's memoir of his father. The narrator, Henry, worries that his pages may sound fanciful once the French royalist plot of 1805 is forgotten. His father's peculiar part in that affair is what he means to explain.

Henry learns of his father's return to America while visiting his Uncle Jason's counting house. Jason, kindly and thoughtful, sighs over the quarrel between the brothers and his own failed efforts to help. He warns Henry not to judge too hard, since respect is owed a father. A clerk's inventory of French goods waits forgotten while family history takes over the scene.
the-verse-book-of-a-homely-woman: Fay Inchfawn, identified on the contents page by her real name, Elizabeth Rebecca Ward, gathered her poems as The Verse-Book of a Homely Woman. The record here holds the title and a contents list for part one, called Indoors, so the poems themselves do not appear. Titles keep close to the house: The Long View, Within My House, The Housewife, The Little House, and The House-Mother. Others mark a woman in hospital, convalescence, homesickness, and washing day.
the-way-of-a-man: Emerson Hough's Way of a Man was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1907, in an edition illustrated with scenes from a Pathé photoplay. An illustration caption shows Grace displaying a lack of sympathy. The pages present here give the title page and contents, so the novel itself does not appear. Twenty-one chapters begin with the kissing of Miss Grace Sheraton and the meeting of Gordon Orme. Wars and rumours of war, a wreck on the river, and adventures in new lands follow.
the-way-of-an-indian:
Frederic Remington wrote and illustrated The Way of an Indian, first published in February 1906. Contents list eight chapters following White Otter through his own shadow, a brown bat's mischief among the Yellow-Eyes, a new lodge, pony-soldiers, and the medicine fight of the Chis-chis-chash. Chapter one finds White Otter with a bad heart, sitting alone on the rim-rocks above a sunlit valley.

Below him, variegated lodges dot the plain near the creek timber, and pony herds wave their tails against the flies. Remington calls it a day of peace such as comes only between nature's fierce troubles: no enemy, no famine, no bad gods in the white midsummer light. The peace sits over a warrior whose story will not keep it.
the-white-mr-longfellow-from-literary-fr:
William Dean Howells recalls house-hunting in Cambridge in the spring of 1866 in The White Mr. Longfellow, drawn from his Literary Friends and Acquaintances. Boston was only a stop until a house turned up in Old Cambridge, but lettings were few, falling below pride or above purse. Friends backed their faith in the Howellses' future with their credit, and on May 1, 1866, the couple moved in.

Their mortgaged house was a carpenter's box hidden by an arbor-vitae hedge, with pears, grapes, and currants planted around it. Howells dug a kitchen garden at once and calculated the whole earth's latitude and longitude from the spot. Cambridge life, refined, intelligent, and gracefully simple, delighted them more than the house, and the memoir turns toward its poets.
the-wife-of-his-youth-and-other-stories-:
Charles W. Chesnutt collects stories of the color line in The Wife of His Youth, first published in 1899. Contents list nine stories, from the title piece through Her Virginia Mammy, The Sheriff's Children, A Matter of Principle, Cicely's Dream, and The Passing of Grandison. An appendix adds three essays on the color line, dated 1889, 1900, and 1903 in the list.

The title story opens with Mr. Ryder preparing to give a ball. Ryder might aptly be called, the narrator says, the dean of the Blue Veins. That little society of coloured persons organised in a northern city shortly after the war, and its standards of colour and standing govern Ryder's world. Chesnutt begins inside the community's own hierarchies before testing them.
the-wishing-ring-man: Margaret Widdemer's novel The Wishing-Ring Man is shown here through its title page, dedication, and chapter list only. Widdemer dedicates the book to her grandfather, E. S. W. Fifteen chapters are listed. Their titles mention Joy in amber satin, a wishing ring, and a rescued princess. The story chapters themselves are not present in the pages shown.
the-woman-with-the-fan: Robert Hichens's The Woman with the Fan, dated 1904 in its heading, is shown here only as a chapter list. Nineteen chapters are numbered without titles or text. No scene, character, or line of the novel follows the list. A companion record under the same title does carry the opening chapter. From these pages alone, nothing more of the story can be told.
the-writings-of-thomas-paine-volume-1-17: Moncure Daniel Conway collected and edited The Writings of Thomas Paine, and volume one covers 1774 to 1779. A partial table of contents for The American Crisis is what appears here. Thirteen Crisis papers are listed in order. Several address British commanders, including Lord Howe and Sir William Howe. One speaks to the people of England, another to its king's speech. The pamphlets themselves do not appear in the pages present.
theodicy-essays-on-the-goodness-of-god-t: G. W. Leibniz's Theodicy, essays on God's goodness, human freedom, and the origin of evil, appears in E. M. Huggard's translation. Austin Farrer edited the volume and wrote its introduction. Open Court published this printing, first issued by Routledge in 1951. Cataloguing details give Leibniz's dates and the source edition by C. J. Gerhardt. What is present here is the edition's front matter and publication history, so Leibniz's arguments themselves do not appear.
to-the-last-man:
Zane Grey's foreword explains why his romantic histories of the West finally reached a feud story. He had steered clear of that rock for years, he says, but chronicling pioneer days required it. Remote western corners still show lives marked by a fighting past.

Grey argues truth about pioneering cannot omit struggle and blood, and a stirring novel needs sensation. Romance, for him, is idealism, and ideals are desperately needed in a materialistic age. He cites Scott, Hugo, Kipling, Hawthorne, and Stevenson as fellow romancers. Readers get a western novel whose author defends dreaming as the engine of work.
tom-grogan:
F. Hopkinson Smith opens his novel with Babcock pacing a ferry slip, snapping his watch open and shut. After years of steady service, Tom Grogan has failed him for once. A scow of stone for a Lighthouse Department sea-wall has sat three days at the government dock, untouched.

Grogan's unloading once ran like grist through a mill, exact tonnage delivered within a day without supervision. Now Babcock's concrete mixers have two hours of material, divers may surface idle, and winter penalties threaten. Indian summer calm mocks his anxiety. Readers get a waterfront novel about reliability, labour, and a contractor whose reputation suddenly slips.
tramping-through-mexico-guatemala-and-ho:
Harry A. Franck walked south from the United States toward South America, and his foreword explains the route he chose. Rather than sail, he crossed Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras on foot and by local roads. The journey joined an earlier five months in the Canal Zone. His book, dated at New York in May 1916, calls itself the random notes of an incurable vagabond.

Chapters cover entering the cooler south, tramping the byways, work in a Mexican mine, and the country around Lake Chapala. The trail then leads into Michoacan. Franck promises a plain, day-by-day record of bad roads and worse lodgings. Photographs by the author illustrate the route. Readers get ground-level travel writing from before paved highways crossed the region.
un-doc-implementation-of-the-npt-safegua:
The International Atomic Energy Agency sent this report on Iran's nuclear work to its board and to the Security Council in April 2006. The agency's board had called on Iran that February to freeze all enrichment work. It also wanted the inspection pact signed and fully used. The file had just been passed to the Council.

The report lists the open questions one by one. Traces of enriched uranium need a clear source. Iran will not hand over a 1987 offer paper from a foreign sales network. A second paper tells how to cast uranium metal into half-spheres. Work on two centrifuge types and small plutonium tests stays murky. Tehran had stopped using the added inspection rules that February.
unbeaten-tracks-in-japan: Isabella L. Bird's Unbeaten Tracks in Japan appears in the 1911 John Murray edition, reprinted from 1905. Her subtitle promises travels in the interior, visits to the aborigines of Yezo, and the shrine of Nikko. Bird dedicates the volume to the memory of Lady Parkes, whose kindness she counts among her most treasured remembrances of Japan. Only the title page, printing history, and dedication are present here, so the travel letters themselves do not appear.
us-and-the-bottle-man:
Edith Ballinger Price wrote and drew the pictures for Us and the Bottle Man, published in 1920. Chapter one begins at a picnic on Wecanicut. Jerry finishes the last olives, to his brother Greg's disgust. An empty olive bottle on a water picnic has one natural use, the narrator says. You seal a message inside, as a shipwrecked sailor would. Then you throw it as far out to sea as you can.

The party includes Mother, Aunt Ailsa, Jerry, Greg, and the girl who tells the tale. They have a fire beside a fallen slab that looks like the mouth of a pirate cave. The olives were a fancy extra, bought while running for the ferry. The bottle they launch carries a letter, and the hope that its finder will write back. Readers get a seaside adventure about three children and the stranger their message reaches.
vicky-van: Carolyn Wells, a prolific writer of mystery tales, wrote Vicky Van. Pages present here give the title page, contents, and the first line of chapter one, so the story itself is not shown. Contents promise twenty chapters: a waiter tells his story, Somers's real name comes out, the Schuyler household appears, an inquest is held, and Fleming Stone, Wells's detective, enters at chapter thirteen. Chapter one begins by saying that Victoria Van Allen was the name the heroine signed to her letters.
vitruvius-ten-books-architecture-morgan:
Morris H. Morgan translated Vitruvius's Ten Books on Architecture in 1914. Vitruvius wrote De Architectura around 25 BCE under the emperor Augustus. It is the only Roman architectural treatise to survive complete.

Temples, the classical orders, and the proportions of the human body fill early books. Machines, water supply, astronomy, and siege engines follow in later ones. His famous ideal links a well-built man to a well-built temple. Every Renaissance builder, from Alberti to Palladio, learned from these books. Morgan's Harvard translation remains a standard English Vitruvius. Architects still cite his triad of firmness, commodity, and delight.
when-a-man-s-a-man: Harold Bell Wright's front pages for When a Man's a Man hold a dedication and a long note of thanks, but no story text. Wright gave the story of manhood to his sons Gilbert and Paul Norman in 1916. His thanks go to friends in Williamson Valley, Arizona, who made the tale possible. He names ranch hosts, guides, and cowboys of the Pot-Hook-S and Cross-Triangle ranches. He rode with them at rodeos and after outlaw cattle. The note is dated near Tucson, April 29, 1916.
when-buffalo-ran:
George Bird Grinnell wrote When Buffalo Ran, first published by Yale University Press in 1920. The book looks back about seventy years to Plains Indian life. Grinnell's opening chapter paints wide rolling prairie that meets the sky on every side. Spring made it green and bright with wild flowers.

The contents follow a boy's growth: an attack on the camp, lessons of the prairie, and a buffalo horse. Later chapters bring the medicine circle, enemy lodges, marriage, and a warrior ready to die. Pictures show lodges, hunts, and a grandmother at home. Readers get a warm account of a world already passing when Grinnell wrote.
with-kitchener-in-the-soudan-a-story-of-: The pages here give a chapter list and the first line of a preface for G. A. Henty's With Kitchener in the Soudan, with the tale itself not begun. The contents open with a disinherited hero and a rising in Alexandria. Chapters name a march south, life among the Dervishes, and a prisoner. The battle of Atbara comes at chapter twelve. Omdurman, Khartoum, and a crowning victory close the list. The preface calls the reconquest of the Soudan a hard and successful enterprise.
woman-s-institute-library-of-cookery-vol: Volume Two of the Woman's Institute Library of Cookery covers milk, butter, cheese, eggs, and vegetables. Pages present here show a contents list, and the lessons themselves stay absent. Listed topics include grades of clean milk, butter substitutes, imported and home cheeses, and ways to keep eggs. Recipe groups and set menus, such as a luncheon menu and a breakfast menu, appear in the plan. Home cooks were the clear target audience.

Volume Four of the Woman's Institute Library of Cookery covers salads, sandwiches, cold desserts, cakes, and pies. Pages present here give a contents list, while the recipes themselves do not appear. Listed salad topics include dressings, fruit salads, and high-protein salads. Sandwich types run from bread-and-butter to hot and open forms. Dessert sections promise custards, gelatine dishes, and frozen desserts made step by step.
zarlah-the-martian: R. Norman Grisewood published this Martian romance in 1909. Pages present here hold a contents list and a chapter heading, but no chapter text. The frontispiece shows Zarlah's car hurled upward into space at frightful speed. Chapter titles promise a strange shadow, a voice from another world, and an account of Martian life. Later titles promise flight at a hundred miles a minute and a race with death. The tale itself does not begin in these pages.
zone-policeman-88-a-close-range-study-of:
Harry A. Franck wrote this close-range study of the Panama Canal Zone and its workers. Chapter one opens as he climbs the Thousand Stairs to the Administration Building. Panama's bay and packed roofs spread below him. At police headquarters, the Captain asks what military service he has had. Franck answers none. A long, doubtful silence follows that reply.

Speaking Spanish saves his application on the spot. Franck thus joined the Zone police from inside a vagabond journey. The dated letter at the front places him in Quito at the end of 1912. Readers get canal life seen from a patrolman's daily round.
